abstract: This work introduces a new method called Self Organizing Neural Network (SONN) algorithm and demonstrates its use in a system identification task. The algorithm constructs the network, chooses the neuron functions, and adjusts the weights. It is compared to the Back-Propagation algorithm in the identification of the chaotic time series. The results shows that SONN constructs a simpler, more accurate model. requiring less training data and epochs. The algorithm can be applied and generalized to appilications as a classifier.

paragraphs: System identification involves learning a model of a process from observations of its behavior. This paper introduces the Self Organizing Neural Network algorithm, or SONN, and applies it to identifying a chaotic time series. The method makes several modeling decisions within the learning procedure, including how to construct the network itself.

SONN chooses the functions used by its neurons and adjusts their connection weights as well as building the network. This gives the procedure responsibility for both the form of the model and its fitted parameters. The authors compare it with backpropagation on the time-series identification task to assess the usefulness of that combined approach.

In the reported comparison, SONN produced a simpler and more accurate model while requiring fewer training examples and training epochs. The findings connect structural adaptation with both model quality and training requirements in this application. The authors also describe classification as a possible application and generalization of the algorithm, extending its intended use beyond the demonstrated identification problem.
summary.tldr: SONN learns network structure, neuron functions, and weights, producing a simpler and more accurate chaotic-series model than backpropagation in the reported comparison.

title: Self Organizing Neural Networks for the Identification Problem

abstract: Neural network models have been criticized for their inability to make use of compositional representations. In this paper, we describe a series of psychological phenomena that demonstrate the role of structured representations in cognition. These findings suggest that people compare relational representations via a process of structural alignment. This process will have to be captured by any model of cognition, symbolic or subsymbolic.
originalAbstract: Neural network models have been criticized for their inability to make use of compositional representations. In this paper, we describe a series of psychological phenomena that demonstrate the role of structured representations in cognition. These findings suggest that people compare relational representations via a process of structural alignment. This process will have to be captured by any model of cognition, symbolic or subsymbolic.

paragraphs: The paper examines a challenge for neural models of cognition: how to represent and compare information whose meaning depends on its internal organization. Compositional representations contain parts arranged into a structure. The authors focus on psychological findings showing that these structured representations matter for human thought, particularly when people make comparisons.

Their account centers on structural alignment. In this process, people compare relational representations by bringing their corresponding organization into alignment. The key issue is how elements relate within each representation, so a model of comparison needs a way to operate on those relationships as well as the elements themselves.

The paper describes a series of psychological phenomena supporting this view and uses them to establish a requirement for cognitive models. Structural alignment must be captured whether a model uses explicit symbols or distributed neural representations. The contribution is therefore a psychologically grounded target for model development: an adequate account of analogy must explain how structured relational information participates in comparison.
summary.tldr: Psychological evidence makes structural alignment of relational representations a core requirement for neural and symbolic models of analogy.

title: Analogy-- Watershed or Waterloo? Structural alignment and the development of connectionist models of analogy

The objective of this effort is to develop an adaptive Neural Network (NN) controller for the Ball C-Side 1m x 3m antenna with embedded actuators and the RAMS sensor system. A traditional optimal controller for the major modes is provided perturbations by the NN to compensate for unknown residual modes. paragraphs: This paper develops adaptive neural control for a flexible spacecraft antenna with embedded actuators and a sensor system. Its broader motivation is reducing spacecraft weight, volume, and cost through improved control of flexible structures. The immediate problem is suppressing vibration when some structural behavior is unknown or changes during operation.

A traditional optimal controller handles the major vibration modes, while a neural network adds adjustments to compensate for unknown residual modes. The network learns online, updating while the system operates. Training feedback for each actuator output is computed using Newton's method to reduce the difference between the desired and achieved antenna positions.

The authors report adaptive vibration control with both recurrent and feed-forward networks despite unknown modal variations and noisy measurements. This supports combining an established controller with learned corrections for behavior outside its main model. The demonstrated result concerns vibration adaptation under those conditions; the reductions in spacecraft weight, volume, and cost are the larger engineering goal motivating the work.
summary.tldr: Online neural corrections augment a conventional spacecraft-antenna controller to adapt to unknown vibration modes and noisy measurements.

title: Neural Network On-Line Learning Control of Spacecraft Smart Structures

abstract: In order to best understand a visual system one should attempt to characterize the natural images it processes. We gather images from the woods and find that these scenes possess an ensemble scale invariance. Further, they are highly non-Gaussian, and this non(cid:173) Gaussian character cannot be removed through local linear filter(cid:173) ing. We find that including a simple "gain control" nonlinearity in the filtering process makes the filter output quite Gaussian, mean(cid:173) ing information is maximized at fixed channel variance. Finally, we use the measured power spectrum to place an upper bound on the information conveyed about natural scenes by an array of receptors.

Further, they are highly non-Gaussian, and this non(cid:173) Gaussian character cannot be removed through local linear filter(cid:173) ing. Finally, we use the measured power spectrum to place an upper bound on the information conveyed about natural scenes by an array of receptors.

paragraphs: The paper studies woodland images to characterize the signals a visual system must process. Across the collected scenes, the authors find statistical scale invariance: the image ensemble retains statistical structure across changes of scale. They also find strongly non-Gaussian behavior, indicating that a Gaussian description does not adequately capture the observed image statistics.

Local linear filtering does not remove this non-Gaussian character. Adding a simple gain-control nonlinearity, however, makes the filter outputs approximately Gaussian. The important distinction is that changing local signal strength through a nonlinear operation alters the output statistics in a way the linear filters alone do not achieve.

The authors interpret the resulting Gaussian-like outputs in terms of maximizing information at fixed channel variance. They also use the measured power spectrum to bound how much information an array of receptors can convey about natural scenes. Together, these analyses connect measured environmental statistics to both a candidate visual-processing operation and an information constraint on sensory representation.
summary.tldr: Woodland image statistics reveal scale invariance and suggest that nonlinear gain control can produce approximately Gaussian visual-filter outputs.

title: Statistics of Natural Images: Scaling in the Woods

abstract: We present a method for learning, tracking, and recognizing human hand gestures recorded by a conventional CCD camera without any special gloves or other sensors. A view-based representation is used to model aspects of the hand relevant to the trained gestures, and is found using an unsupervised clustering technique. We use normalized correlation net(cid:173) works, with dynamic time warping in the temporal domain, as a distance function for unsupervised clustering. Views are computed separably for space and time dimensions; the distributed response of the combination of these units characterizes the input data with a low dimensional repre(cid:173) sentation. A supervised classification stage uses labeled outputs of the spatio-temporal units as training data. Our system can correctly classify gestures in real time with a low-cost image processing accelerator.

paragraphs: The paper presents a system for learning, tracking, and recognizing hand gestures from a conventional camera. It does not require instrumented gloves or additional sensors. The central task is to turn the recorded appearance and motion of a hand into a compact representation suitable for gesture classification.

An unsupervised clustering procedure discovers views that describe aspects of the hand relevant to the trained gestures. Similarity is measured using normalized correlation networks together with dynamic time warping for temporal comparisons. Spatial and temporal views are computed separately, and the combined pattern of responses across these units forms a low-dimensional description of the input.

A supervised stage then learns from labeled outputs of those spatial and temporal units. Representation discovery and gesture labeling thus play distinct roles in the system: one organizes the visual observations, while the other maps their responses to gesture categories. The authors report correct real-time classification using a low-cost image processing accelerator, demonstrating the practical use of this combined representation.
summary.tldr: A camera-based gesture system learns compact spatial and temporal representations and uses them for real-time supervised classification.

title: Classifying Hand Gestures with a View-Based Distributed Representation

abstract: In this paper we propose a method for learning Bayesian belief networks from data. The method uses artificial neural networks as probability estimators, thus avoiding the need for making prior assumptions on the nature of the probability distributions govern(cid:173) ing the relationships among the participating variables. This new method has the potential for being applied to domains containing both discrete and continuous variables arbitrarily distributed. We compare the learning performance of this new method with the performance of the method proposed by Cooper and Herskovits in [7]. The experimental results show that, although the learning scheme based on the use of ANN estimators is slower, the learning accuracy of the two methods is comparable. Category: Algorithms and Architectures.

The method uses artificial neural networks as probability estimators, thus avoiding the need for making prior assumptions on the nature of the probability distributions govern(cid:173) ing the relationships among the participating variables. This new method has the potential for being applied to domains containing both discrete and continuous variables arbitrarily distributed. We compare the learning performance of this new method with the performance of the method proposed by Cooper and Herskovits in [7]. The experimental results show that, although the learning scheme based on the use of ANN estimators is slower, the learning accuracy of the two methods is comparable. paragraphs: Learning a Bayesian belief network requires estimating probabilistic relationships among variables. This paper proposes using artificial neural networks for those probability estimates. The motivation is to avoid choosing a particular distributional form in advance for the relationships that the belief network is intended to capture.

Neural-network estimators provide the probability information used by the learning method. This gives the approach potential applicability to domains containing both discrete and continuous variables with arbitrarily shaped distributions. The flexibility concerns how relationships are represented probabilistically, allowing the data-driven estimators to take on a role that would otherwise depend on prior distributional assumptions.

The authors compare the method with the learning procedure of Cooper and Herskovits. Their experiments find comparable learning accuracy, while the neural-estimator approach is slower. The result identifies a concrete tradeoff: greater flexibility in the probability-estimation scheme comes with additional learning time in the reported comparison. The contribution is a way to connect neural probability estimation with belief-network learning while exposing that computational cost.
summary.tldr: Neural probability estimators enable flexible Bayesian belief-network learning, with comparable accuracy but slower learning than the compared method.

title: Learning Bayesian Belief Networks with Neural Network Estimators

abstract: A 80 x 78 pixel general purpose vision chip for spatial focal plane processing is presented. The size and configuration of the processing receptive field are programmable. The chip's architecture allows the photoreceptor cells to be small and densely packed by performing all computation on the read-out, away from the array. In addition to the raw intensity image, the chip outputs four processed images in parallel. Also presented is an application of the chip to line segment orientation detection, as found in the retinal receptive fields of toads.
originalAbstract: A 80 x 78 pixel general purpose vision chip for spatial focal plane processing is presented. The size and configuration of the processing receptive field are programmable. The chip's architecture allows the photoreceptor cells to be small and densely packed by performing all computation on the read-out, away from the array. In addition to the raw intensity image, the chip outputs four processed images in parallel. Also presented is an application of the chip to line segment orientation detection, as found in the retinal receptive fields of toads.

paragraphs: The paper presents an 80-by-78-pixel vision chip that performs spatial image processing. Its processing receptive field—the region used for a spatial computation—has a programmable size and configuration. This gives the hardware flexibility in how it combines information across an image, rather than restricting it to one fixed spatial arrangement.

The architecture places computation on the read-out, away from the photoreceptor array. That design allows the light-sensitive cells to remain small and closely packed. Alongside the raw intensity image, the chip produces four processed images in parallel, making multiple processing outputs available from the same imaging architecture.

The authors demonstrate an application to detecting line-segment orientation, motivated by orientation detection in toad retinal receptive fields. The example connects the general-purpose hardware to a specific visual operation. The contribution combines configurable spatial processing with an arrangement that preserves a dense sensor array, while providing both the original image and several processed views as outputs.
summary.tldr: A programmable vision chip keeps photoreceptors densely packed while producing a raw image and four parallel processed images.

title: A General Purpose Image Processing Chip: Orientation Detection

abstract: A circuit for fast, compact and low-power focal-plane motion centroid localization is presented. This chip, which uses mixed signal CMOS components to implement photodetection, edge detection, ON-set detection and centroid localization, models the retina and superior colliculus. The centroid localization circuit uses time-windowed asynchronously triggered row and column address events and two linear resistive grids to provide the analog coordinates of the motion centroid. This VLSI chip is used to realize fast lightweight autonavigating vehicles. The obstacle avoiding line-following algorithm is discussed.
originalAbstract: A circuit for fast, compact and low-power focal-plane motion centroid localization is presented. This chip, which uses mixed signal CMOS components to implement photodetection, edge detection, ON-set detection and centroid localization, models the retina and superior colliculus. The centroid localization circuit uses time-windowed asynchronously triggered row and column address events and two linear resistive grids to provide the analog coordinates of the motion centroid. This VLSI chip is used to realize fast lightweight autonavigating vehicles. The obstacle avoiding line-following algorithm is discussed.

paragraphs: The paper presents a compact, low-power vision chip that rapidly locates the center of detected motion. It performs this processing at the focal plane and models functions associated with the retina and superior colliculus. The intended application is fast, lightweight autonomous vehicles that need visual information for navigation.

Mixed-signal CMOS circuitry combines photodetection, edge detection, onset detection, and centroid localization. The localization stage receives asynchronously triggered row and column address events within a time window. Two linear resistive grids then produce analog coordinates for the motion centroid, converting distributed detection events into a spatial location.

This arrangement connects several stages of visual processing within a dedicated circuit, yielding a compact motion-location signal that can support vehicle behavior. The chip is used to realize autonomous navigation, and the paper discusses a line-following algorithm that also avoids obstacles. Its contribution brings together biologically motivated sensing, event-driven localization, and a navigation application in one hardware implementation.
summary.tldr: A compact mixed-signal vision chip converts motion events into centroid coordinates for lightweight autonomous navigation.

title: VLSI Implementation of Motion Centroid Localization for Autonomous Navigation

paragraphs: A product-of-experts model combines several probability models by multiplying their contributions into one distribution. This paper studies Gaussian experts. Their normalized product is also Gaussian, but combining individually simple covariance structures can produce a richer overall structure. Gaussian experts make this architecture especially amenable to mathematical analysis.

One construction uses Gaussian pancakes: distributions compressed along one direction and extended along the remaining directions. The authors show that maximum-likelihood learning of their product yields a probabilistic formulation of Minor Components Analysis. This complements the probabilistic formulation of Principal Components Analysis and connects the geometry of individual experts to a familiar component-analysis method.

The paper also examines products of one-factor probabilistic PCA models and a product-of-experts construction for a first-order autoregressive process. Across these examples, the central issue is how simple expert structures combine into an overall Gaussian model. The supplied derivation expresses this combination through addition of inverse covariance matrices, making the relationship between each expert’s constraints and the resulting distribution explicit.
summary.tldr: Products of simple Gaussian experts yield richer Gaussian structures, including a maximum-likelihood formulation of probabilistic Minor Components Analysis.

title: Products of Gaussians

abstract: We investigate the problem of automatically constructing efﬁcient rep- resentations or basis functions for approximating value functions based on analyzing the structure and topology of the state space. In particu- lar, two novel approaches to value function approximation are explored based on automatically constructing basis functions on state spaces that can be represented as graphs or manifolds: one approach uses the eigen- functions of the Laplacian, in effect performing a global Fourier analysis on the graph; the second approach is based on diffusion wavelets, which generalize classical wavelets to graphs using multiscale dilations induced by powers of a diffusion operator or random walk on the graph. Together, these approaches form the foundation of a new generation of methods for solving large Markov decision processes, in which the underlying repre- sentation and policies are simultaneously learned.
originalAbstract: We investigate the problem of automatically constructing efﬁcient rep- resentations or basis functions for approximating value functions based on analyzing the structure and topology of the state space. In particu- lar, two novel approaches to value function approximation are explored based on automatically constructing basis functions on state spaces that can be represented as graphs or manifolds: one approach uses the eigen- functions of the Laplacian, in effect performing a global Fourier analysis on the graph; the second approach is based on diffusion wavelets, which generalize classical wavelets to graphs using multiscale dilations induced by powers of a diffusion operator or random walk on the graph. Together, these approaches form the foundation of a new generation of methods for solving large Markov decision processes, in which the underlying repre- sentation and policies are simultaneously learned.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how to automatically build representations for approximating value functions in Markov decision processes. Its starting point is the structure and topology of the state space. When states can be represented as a graph or manifold, that organization can guide the construction of basis functions used to express a value function.

The authors explore two approaches. One uses eigenfunctions of the Laplacian, providing a graph analogue of global Fourier analysis. The other uses diffusion wavelets, extending wavelet ideas to graphs through multiple scales defined by powers of a diffusion operator or random walk. Both derive representation elements from relationships among states.

The approaches offer different ways to organize approximation around state-space structure: one uses global spectral functions, while the other introduces scales through diffusion. The authors present them as a foundation for methods addressing large Markov decision processes in which representations and policies are learned together. The contribution is therefore about constructing the ingredients of value-function approximation automatically, rather than taking the representation as fixed in advance.
summary.tldr: Laplacian eigenfunctions and diffusion wavelets construct value-function bases from state-space geometry, supporting joint learning of representations and policies.

title: Value Function Approximation with Diffusion Wavelets and Laplacian Eigenfunctions

abstract: We propose a new measure of conditional dependence of random variables, based on normalized cross-covariance operators on reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. Unlike previous kernel dependence measures, the proposed criterion does not de- pend on the choice of kernel in the limit of inﬁnite data, for a wide class of ker- nels. At the same time, it has a straightforward empirical estimate with good convergence behaviour. We discuss the theoretical properties of the measure, and demonstrate its application in experiments.
originalAbstract: We propose a new measure of conditional dependence of random variables, based on normalized cross-covariance operators on reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. Unlike previous kernel dependence measures, the proposed criterion does not de- pend on the choice of kernel in the limit of inﬁnite data, for a wide class of ker- nels. At the same time, it has a straightforward empirical estimate with good convergence behaviour. We discuss the theoretical properties of the measure, and demonstrate its application in experiments.

paragraphs: Conditional dependence concerns whether variables remain related after accounting for conditioning information. This paper proposes a measure of that relationship using kernel methods. Its construction uses normalized cross-covariance operators in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, providing a way to express statistical relationships through the feature representations associated with kernels.

The central theoretical property is independence from the particular kernel choice in the infinite-data limit, for a wide class of kernels. This distinguishes the proposed measure from earlier kernel dependence criteria. Both qualifications matter: the result concerns the limiting quantity, and the kernels must belong to the class covered by the theory.

The measure also has a straightforward empirical estimate with good convergence behavior, connecting its theoretical definition to calculations from observed samples. The paper discusses its mathematical properties and demonstrates applications experimentally. Its contribution is therefore a conditional-dependence criterion with a stable limiting interpretation across many kernel choices, together with an estimator intended to make that criterion usable with data.
summary.tldr: A kernel-based conditional-dependence measure has an empirical estimator and, for a wide kernel class, a kernel-independent infinite-data limit.

title: Kernel Measures of Conditional Dependence

abstract: Unexpected stimuli are a challenge to any machine learning algorithm. Here we identify distinct types of unexpected events, focusing on 'incongruent events' - when 'general level' and 'specific level' classifiers give conflicting predictions. We define a formal framework for the representation and processing of incongruent events: starting from the notion of label hierarchy, we show how partial order on labels can be deduced from such hierarchies. For each event, we compute its probability in different ways, based on adjacent levels (according to the partial order) in the label hierarchy . An incongruent event is an event where the probability computed based on some more specific level (in accordance with the partial order) is much smaller than the probability computed based on some more general level, leading to conflicting predictions. We derive algorithms to detect incongruent events from different types of hierarchies, corresponding to class membership or part membership. Respectively, we show promising results with real data on two specific problems: Out Of Vocabulary words in speech recognition, and the identification of a new sub-class (e.g., the face of a new individual) in audio-visual facial object recognition.

paragraphs: An unexpected input can still look familiar at a broad level while failing to fit a more specific interpretation. The paper calls this an incongruent event and studies it through disagreement between general and specific classifiers. This provides a way to distinguish one form of unexpectedness from novelty considered without hierarchical context.

The authors formalize relationships between labels using hierarchies and the partial orders they imply. For each event, they calculate probabilities through adjacent levels of that ordering. Incongruence occurs when a more specific level assigns a much smaller probability than a more general level, producing incompatible predictions about the same input.

They derive detection algorithms for hierarchies describing class membership and part membership. Real-data applications address words outside a speech recognizer’s vocabulary and previously unseen subclasses in audiovisual facial recognition, such as a new individual’s face. The reported results are promising. Their significance is that structured disagreement can help flag an input whose broad interpretation is plausible even when a finer interpretation does not fit.
summary.tldr: Disagreement between general and specific classifiers provides a structured signal for detecting certain unexpected inputs.

title: Beyond Novelty Detection: Incongruent Events, when General and Specific Classifiers Disagree

abstract: In this paper we address the problem of provably correct feature selection in arbitrary domains. An optimal solution to the problem is a Markov boundary, which is a minimal set of features that make the probability distribution of a target variable conditionally invariant to the state of all other features in the domain. While numerous algorithms for this problem have been proposed, their theoretical correctness and practical behavior under arbitrary probability distributions is unclear. We address this by introducing the Markov Boundary Theorem that precisely characterizes the properties of an ideal Markov boundary, and use it to develop algorithms that learn a more general boundary that can capture complex interactions that only appear when the values of multiple features are considered together. We introduce two algorithms: an exact, provably correct one as well a more practical randomized anytime version, and show that they perform well on artificial as well as benchmark and real-world data sets. Throughout the paper we make minimal assumptions that consist of only a general set of axioms that hold for every probability distribution, which gives these algorithms universal applicability.

paragraphs: The paper seeks a principled way to select the features needed to predict a target. An optimal solution is a Markov boundary: a minimal set of features such that, once their values are known, other features do not change the target's conditional distribution. The challenge is establishing correctness across arbitrary probability distributions.

The authors introduce a theorem characterizing an ideal Markov boundary and use it to develop algorithms for a more general boundary. This boundary can capture interactions that become visible only when several feature values are considered together. Accounting for such interactions matters because a feature's predictive role may depend on the accompanying features.

They provide an exact algorithm with a correctness proof and a more practical randomized anytime version. Both are evaluated on artificial, benchmark, and real-world datasets, with reported good performance. The analysis uses only general axioms that hold for every probability distribution, supporting the claimed universal applicability. That broad theoretical scope concerns the distributional assumptions; the abstract assigns the exact correctness guarantee specifically to the exact algorithm.
summary.tldr: A Markov-boundary theorem supports broadly applicable feature-selection algorithms that can capture interactions visible only among multiple features.

title: Toward Provably Correct Feature Selection in Arbitrary Domains

abstract: Bayesian approaches to utility elicitation typically adopt (myopic) expected value of information (EVOI) as a natural criterion for selecting queries. However, EVOI-optimization is usually computationally prohibitive. In this paper, we examine EVOI optimization using \emph{choice queries}, queries in which a user is ask to select her most preferred product from a set. We show that, under very general assumptions, the optimal choice query w.r.t.\ EVOI coincides with \emph{optimal recommendation set}, that is, a set maximizing expected utility of the user selection. Since recommendation set optimization is a simpler, submodular problem, this can greatly reduce the complexity of both exact and approximate (greedy) computation of optimal choice queries. We also examine the case where user responses to choice queries are error-prone (using both constant and follow mixed multinomial logit noise models) and provide worst-case guarantees. Finally we present a local search technique that works well with large outcome spaces.

paragraphs: Bayesian preference elicitation often chooses questions by their expected value of information: how useful the answer is expected to be for the next decision. Computing the best question under this myopic criterion can be expensive. This paper studies choice queries, where a user selects their preferred product from a presented set.

Under very general assumptions, the authors show that the optimal choice-query set also maximizes the expected utility of the user’s selection as a recommendation set. This equivalence turns query selection into a simpler submodular optimization problem. It can substantially reduce the computational burden of both exact methods and greedy approximation methods.

The paper also considers erroneous user responses under two specified noise models and provides worst-case guarantees. A local search method is presented for large outcome spaces and reported to work well. The central insight is a conditional equivalence between asking an informative choice question and offering a valuable set of options, which makes the myopic query-selection problem easier to compute.
summary.tldr: Under general assumptions, optimal recommendation sets are also myopically optimal choice queries, enabling simpler information-value optimization.

title: Optimal Bayesian Recommendation Sets and Myopically Optimal Choice Query Sets

abstract: A number of objective functions in clustering problems can be described with submodular functions. In this paper, we introduce the minimum average cost criterion, and show that the theory of intersecting submodular functions can be used for clustering with submodular objective functions. The proposed algorithm does not require the number of clusters in advance, and it will be determined by the property of a given set of data points. The minimum average cost clustering problem is parameterized with a real variable, and surprisingly, we show that all information about optimal clusterings for all parameters can be computed in polynomial time in total. Additionally, we evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithm through computational experiments.

paragraphs: Clustering requires an objective that defines which groupings of data are preferable. This paper considers objectives expressible through submodular functions and introduces a minimum average cost criterion. It shows how the theory of intersecting submodular functions can be used to solve clustering problems with this form of objective.

The proposed algorithm does not require the number of clusters as an input. Instead, the properties of the supplied data determine that number through the clustering formulation. This makes selecting the grouping and determining how many groups to use parts of the same problem, rather than requiring a cluster count to be chosen beforehand.

The authors also study a version of the problem controlled by a real-valued parameter. They prove that all information about optimal clusterings across all parameter values can be computed in polynomial total time. This is a result about the entire parameterized problem, not merely one selected value. Computational experiments additionally evaluate the algorithm, complementing the theoretical connection between submodularity and clustering.
summary.tldr: Minimum average cost clustering uses submodular structure to determine cluster counts and compute optimal-clustering information across all parameter values in polynomial time.

title: Minimum Average Cost Clustering

abstract: A new algorithm is proposed for a) unsupervised learning of sparse representations from subsampled measurements and b) estimating the parameters required for linearly reconstructing signals from the sparse codes. We verify that the new algorithm performs efficient data compression on par with the recent method of compressive sampling. Further, we demonstrate that the algorithm performs robustly when stacked in several stages or when applied in undercomplete or overcomplete situations. The new algorithm can explain how neural populations in the brain that receive subsampled input through fiber bottlenecks are able to form coherent response properties.
originalAbstract: A new algorithm is proposed for a) unsupervised learning of sparse representations from subsampled measurements and b) estimating the parameters required for linearly reconstructing signals from the sparse codes. We verify that the new algorithm performs efficient data compression on par with the recent method of compressive sampling. Further, we demonstrate that the algorithm performs robustly when stacked in several stages or when applied in undercomplete or overcomplete situations. The new algorithm can explain how neural populations in the brain that receive subsampled input through fiber bottlenecks are able to form coherent response properties.

paragraphs: This paper asks how useful representations can be learned when only subsampled measurements of a signal are available. The proposed algorithm learns sparse representations without supervision and estimates the parameters needed to reconstruct signals linearly from those representations. Learning the code and learning how to decode it are therefore both parts of the approach.

The authors report compression efficiency comparable to compressive sampling. They also demonstrate robust performance when several stages are stacked together and in both undercomplete and overcomplete settings. These evaluations address whether the method remains useful across different representation sizes and when processing is repeated through multiple stages.

The paper connects this computational result to communication between neural populations. Fiber bottlenecks mean that a population may receive subsampled input, yet still develop coherent response properties. The algorithm offers a possible explanation for how that can happen: sparse representations and reconstruction parameters can be learned from restricted measurements. This is presented as an explanatory possibility, rather than proof that the brain uses the proposed algorithm.
summary.tldr: An unsupervised algorithm learns sparse codes from subsampled inputs and offers a possible account of communication through neural bottlenecks.

title: Deciphering subsampled data: adaptive compressive sampling as a principle of brain communication

abstract: Variational Message Passing (VMP) is an algorithmic implementation of the Variational Bayes (VB) method which applies only in the special case of conjugate exponential family models. We propose an extension to VMP, which we refer to as Non-conjugate Variational Message Passing (NCVMP) which aims to alleviate this restriction while maintaining modularity, allowing choice in how expectations are calculated, and integrating into an existing message-passing framework: Infer.NET. We demonstrate NCVMP on logistic binary and multinomial regression. In the multinomial case we introduce a novel variational bound for the softmax factor which is tighter than other commonly used bounds whilst maintaining computational tractability.

We propose an extension to VMP, which we refer to as Non-conjugate Variational Message Passing (NCVMP) which aims to alleviate this restriction while maintaining modularity, allowing choice in how expectations are calculated, and integrating into an existing message-passing framework: Infer.NET. paragraphs: Variational Message Passing turns Variational Bayes inference into a modular algorithm, but its standard form applies only to conjugate exponential-family models. That mathematical restriction limits which model components can be handled directly. This paper proposes Non-conjugate Variational Message Passing to alleviate the restriction while retaining the organizational benefits of message-based inference.

The extension aims to preserve modularity, allow different ways of calculating expectations, and integrate with the existing Infer.NET framework. These goals matter together: broadening the model family is more useful when individual components can still be combined and inference calculations can be adapted to the components involved. The paper demonstrates the approach on logistic binary regression and multinomial regression.

For multinomial regression, the authors introduce a new variational bound for the softmax factor. It is tighter than other commonly used bounds while remaining computationally tractable. This supplies a more faithful tractable approximation for that part of the model. The work combines a broader message-passing framework with a specific mathematical improvement for handling multinomial outcomes.
summary.tldr: Non-conjugate Variational Message Passing extends modular Bayesian inference and introduces a tighter tractable softmax bound for multinomial regression.

title: Non-conjugate Variational Message Passing for Multinomial and Binary Regression

abstract: Variational methods have been previously explored as a tractable approximation to Bayesian inference for neural networks. However the approaches proposed so far have only been applicable to a few simple network architectures. This paper introduces an easy-to-implement stochastic variational method (or equivalently, minimum description length loss function) that can be applied to most neural networks. Along the way it revisits several common regularisers from a variational perspective. It also provides a simple pruning heuristic that can both drastically reduce the number of network weights and lead to improved generalisation. Experimental results are provided for a hierarchical multidimensional recurrent neural network applied to the TIMIT speech corpus.
originalAbstract: Variational methods have been previously explored as a tractable approximation to Bayesian inference for neural networks. However the approaches proposed so far have only been applicable to a few simple network architectures. This paper introduces an easy-to-implement stochastic variational method (or equivalently, minimum description length loss function) that can be applied to most neural networks. Along the way it revisits several common regularisers from a variational perspective. It also provides a simple pruning heuristic that can both drastically reduce the number of network weights and lead to improved generalisation. Experimental results are provided for a hierarchical multidimensional recurrent neural network applied to the TIMIT speech corpus.

paragraphs: The paper aims to make approximate Bayesian inference practical for a broad range of neural networks. Earlier variational approaches discussed in the abstract applied only to a few simple architectures. The proposed stochastic variational method is easy to implement and can be applied to most neural networks, broadening the architectural scope of this style of inference.

The method also has an equivalent interpretation as a minimum description length loss function. This gives a second perspective on the same training approach, linking probabilistic approximation with a description-length objective. The paper revisits several common regularizers from the variational viewpoint, connecting familiar training devices to that probabilistic interpretation.

A further contribution is a simple pruning heuristic that can drastically reduce the number of network weights and can improve generalization. These are possible benefits of the heuristic, rather than a universal outcome for every network. Experiments use a hierarchical multidimensional recurrent neural network on the TIMIT speech corpus, providing a concrete application of the proposed training approach.
summary.tldr: A practical stochastic variational method extends approximate Bayesian training to most neural networks and offers a weight-pruning heuristic.

title: Practical Variational Inference for Neural Networks

abstract: The combination of modern Reinforcement Learning and Deep Learning approaches holds the promise of making significant progress on challenging applications requiring both rich perception and policy-selection. The Arcade Learning Environment (ALE) provides a set of Atari games that represent a useful benchmark set of such applications. A recent breakthrough in combining model-free reinforcement learning with deep learning, called DQN, achieves the best real-time agents thus far. Planning-based approaches achieve far higher scores than the best model-free approaches, but they exploit information that is not available to human players, and they are orders of magnitude slower than needed for real-time play. Our main goal in this work is to build a better real-time Atari game playing agent than DQN. The central idea is to use the slow planning-based agents to provide training data for a deep-learning architecture capable of real-time play. We proposed new agents based on this idea and show that they outperform DQN.

paragraphs: Atari games require an agent to interpret visual information and choose actions quickly. The paper describes a gap between strong planning-based agents and practical real-time agents. Planning methods achieve much higher scores than the best model-free approaches discussed, but run far too slowly for real-time play and use information unavailable to human players.

The proposed approach uses those slow planners to generate training data for a deep-learning architecture. Expensive planning therefore supplies examples during training, while the learned architecture handles real-time play. The title identifies offline Monte Carlo tree search as the planning approach underlying this transfer from computationally demanding decisions to a faster agent.

The authors build agents around this idea and report that they outperform DQN, their stated real-time target. The result supports using a strong but slow planner as a source of training data for a practical game-playing system. The planner's access to additional information remains part of the described setup, so the findings concern the resulting trained agents rather than a demonstration of learning under human-equivalent information conditions.
summary.tldr: Training deep networks on data from slow planning agents produces real-time Atari agents that outperform DQN in the reported evaluation.

title: Deep Learning for Real-Time Atari Game Play Using Offline Monte-Carlo Tree Search Planning

abstract: We derive a second-order ordinary differential equation (ODE), which is the limit of Nesterov’s accelerated gradient method. This ODE exhibits approximate equivalence to Nesterov’s scheme and thus can serve as a tool for analysis. We show that the continuous time ODE allows for a better understanding of Nesterov’s scheme. As a byproduct, we obtain a family of schemes with similar convergence rates. The ODE interpretation also suggests restarting Nesterov’s scheme leading to an algorithm, which can be rigorously proven to converge at a linear rate whenever the objective is strongly convex.

paragraphs: This paper studies Nesterov’s accelerated gradient method by translating its sequence of optimization steps into a continuous-time mathematical model. The authors derive a second-order ordinary differential equation as a limit of the method. This gives them another way to examine the behavior of acceleration and reason about its convergence.

The differential equation is approximately equivalent to the discrete optimization scheme, making it an analytical tool rather than an exact description of every individual update. The authors use this perspective to gain insight into Nesterov’s method and derive a family of related schemes with similar convergence rates. The contribution thus extends beyond interpreting one existing algorithm.

The continuous-time interpretation also suggests restarting the accelerated method. This leads to an algorithm with a rigorous linear convergence guarantee whenever the objective is strongly convex. That condition matters: the stated linear-rate result applies to that class of objectives. Together, the results show how studying a continuous limit can guide both understanding and the construction of discrete optimization algorithms.
summary.tldr: A continuous-time model of Nesterov’s method yields related algorithms and motivates a restart scheme with linear convergence for strongly convex objectives.

title: A Differential Equation for Modeling Nesterov’s Accelerated Gradient Method: Theory and Insights

abstract: It is well-known that neural networks are computationally hard to train. On the other hand, in practice, modern day neural networks are trained efficiently using SGD and a variety of tricks that include different activation functions (e.g. ReLU), over-specification (i.e., train networks which are larger than needed), and regularization. In this paper we revisit the computational complexity of training neural networks from a modern perspective. We provide both positive and negative results, some of them yield new provably efficient and practical algorithms for training neural networks.
originalAbstract: It is well-known that neural networks are computationally hard to train. On the other hand, in practice, modern day neural networks are trained efficiently using SGD and a variety of tricks that include different activation functions (e.g. ReLU), over-specification (i.e., train networks which are larger than needed), and regularization. In this paper we revisit the computational complexity of training neural networks from a modern perspective. We provide both positive and negative results, some of them yield new provably efficient and practical algorithms for training neural networks.

paragraphs: This paper revisits the tension between the computational difficulty of training neural networks and the effectiveness of practical training procedures. Neural networks are known to be hard to train in general, yet practitioners successfully use stochastic gradient descent together with a range of design choices. The authors examine training complexity with that practical context in view.

The motivating choices include activation functions such as ReLU, networks larger than needed, and regularization. These practices make it useful to reconsider what existing hardness statements imply for the networks and procedures actually used. The paper frames computational efficiency as a question requiring both positive results and an account of the obstacles that remain.

The authors provide results on both sides, and some lead to new training algorithms described as provably efficient and practical. The significance lies in connecting complexity analysis to algorithm design: an analysis of difficulty also yields constructive ways to train networks. The stated findings support progress in particular settings while retaining the distinction between general training hardness and the possibility of efficient methods.
summary.tldr: Reexamining neural-network training complexity in light of modern practice yields both hardness results and new provably efficient training algorithms.

title: On the Computational Efficiency of Training Neural Networks

abstract: A popular approach to neural characterization describes neural responses in terms of a cascade of linear and nonlinear stages: a linear filter to describe stimulus integration, followed by a nonlinear function to convert the filter output to spike rate. However, real neurons respond to stimuli in a manner that depends on the nonlinear integration of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs. Here we introduce a biophysically inspired point process model that explicitly incorporates stimulus-induced changes in synaptic conductance in a dynamical model of neuronal membrane potential. Our work makes two important contributions. First, on a theoretical level, it offers a novel interpretation of the popular generalized linear model (GLM) for neural spike trains. We show that the classic GLM is a special case of our conductance-based model in which the stimulus linearly modulates excitatory and inhibitory conductances in an equal and opposite “push-pull” fashion. Our model can therefore be viewed as a direct extension of the GLM in which we relax these constraints; the resulting model can exhibit shunting as well as hyperpolarizing inhibition, and time-varying changes in both gain and membrane time constant. Second, on a practical level, we show that our model provides a tractable model of spike responses in early sensory neurons that is both more accurate and more interpretable than the GLM. Most importantly, we show that we can accurately infer intracellular synaptic conductances from extracellularly recorded spike trains. We validate these estimates using direct intracellular measurements of excitatory and inhibitory conductances in parasol retinal ganglion cells. We show that the model fit to extracellular spike trains can predict excitatory and inhibitory conductances elicited by novel stimuli with nearly the same accuracy as a model trained directly with intracellular conductances.

These changes enter a dynamical model of membrane potential, providing a more explicit account of neuronal input integration than a linear filter followed by a nonlinear conversion to spike rate. The resulting point process model connects observable spikes to internal physiological quantities.

summary.tldr: A conductance-based spike model extends the GLM and accurately infers excitatory and inhibitory conductances from extracellular recordings in the tested retinal cells.

title: Inferring synaptic conductances from spike trains with a biophysically inspired point process model

abstract: We introduce a framework for unsupervised learning of structured predictors with overlapping, global features. Each input's latent representation is predicted conditional on the observed data using a feature-rich conditional random field (CRF). Then a reconstruction of the input is (re)generated, conditional on the latent structure, using a generative model which factorizes similarly to the CRF. The autoencoder formulation enables efficient exact inference without resorting to unrealistic independence assumptions or restricting the kinds of features that can be used. We illustrate insightful connections to traditional autoencoders, posterior regularization and multi-view learning. Finally, we show competitive results with instantiations of the framework for two canonical tasks in natural language processing: part-of-speech induction and bitext word alignment, and show that training our model can be substantially more efficient than comparable feature-rich baselines.

Each input's latent representation is predicted conditional on the observed data using a feature-rich conditional random field (CRF). Then a reconstruction of the input is (re)generated, conditional on the latent structure, using a generative model which factorizes similarly to the CRF. The autoencoder formulation enables efficient exact inference without resorting to unrealistic independence assumptions or restricting the kinds of features that can be used. We illustrate insightful connections to traditional autoencoders, posterior regularization and multi-view learning. paragraphs: The paper introduces an unsupervised framework for learning structured predictions while using rich features of the input. Its goal is to accommodate features that overlap or describe global properties, which makes it valuable to have a formulation that supports expressive prediction together with tractable inference.

The framework works as an autoencoder. First, a conditional random field predicts a latent structure given the observed input. A generative model then reconstructs the input from that structure, using a factorization similar to the conditional random field's. This arrangement enables efficient exact inference without the unrealistic independence assumptions or restrictions on feature types that the authors seek to avoid.

The authors connect the framework to traditional autoencoders, posterior regularization, and multi-view learning. They instantiate it for inducing parts of speech and aligning words across bilingual text, reporting competitive results on both tasks. Training can also be substantially more efficient than comparable feature-rich baselines. The results show how a reconstruction objective can support unsupervised structured prediction while retaining a rich conditional model.
summary.tldr: CRF autoencoders combine rich conditional structure prediction with generative reconstruction to enable efficient unsupervised learning.

title: Conditional Random Field Autoencoders for Unsupervised Structured Prediction

abstract: In this paper, we present the mQA model, which is able to answer questions about the content of an image. The answer can be a sentence, a phrase or a single word. Our model contains four components: a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) to extract the question representation, a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to extract the visual representation, an LSTM for storing the linguistic context in an answer, and a fusing component to combine the information from the first three components and generate the answer. We construct a Freestyle Multilingual Image Question Answering (FM-IQA) dataset to train and evaluate our mQA model. It contains over 150,000 images and 310,000 freestyle Chinese question-answer pairs and their English translations. The quality of the generated answers of our mQA model on this dataset is evaluated by human judges through a Turing Test. Specifically, we mix the answers provided by humans and our model. The human judges need to distinguish our model from the human. They will also provide a score (i.e. 0, 1, 2, the larger the better) indicating the quality of the answer. We propose strategies to monitor the quality of this evaluation process. The experiments show that in 64.7% of cases, the human judges cannot distinguish our model from humans. The average score is 1.454 (1.918 for human). The details of this work, including the FM-IQA dataset, can be found on the project page: \url{http://idl.baidu.com/FM-IQA.html}.

Its mQA model combines an LSTM for representing the question, a CNN for visual content, another LSTM for the answer’s linguistic context, and a fusion component that generates the answer.

These results describe performance under this dataset and evaluation procedure; the remaining score gap matters even when a response’s source is difficult to identify.
summary.tldr: An image-question answering model combines visual and language networks and is evaluated by human judges.

title: Are You Talking to a Machine? Dataset and Methods for Multilingual Image Question

abstract: Offline handwriting recognition systems require cropped text line images for both training and recognition. On the one hand, the annotation of position and transcript at line level is costly to obtain. On the other hand, automatic line segmentation algorithms are prone to errors, compromising the subsequent recognition. In this paper, we propose a modification of the popular and efficient Multi-Dimensional Long Short-Term Memory Recurrent Neural Networks (MDLSTM-RNNs) to enable end-to-end processing of handwritten paragraphs. More particularly, we replace the collapse layer transforming the two-dimensional representation into a sequence of predictions by a recurrent version which can select one line at a time. In the proposed model, a neural network performs a kind of implicit line segmentation by computing attention weights on the image representation. The experiments on paragraphs of Rimes and IAM databases yield results that are competitive with those of networks trained at line level, and constitute a significant step towards end-to-end transcription of full documents.

This paper modifies a multidimensional recurrent neural network so that it can process handwritten paragraphs end to end.

Attention weights over the image representation provide an implicit form of line segmentation, bringing the selection of text lines into the recognition model itself.

Experiments on paragraphs from the Rimes and IAM databases produce results competitive with networks trained at line level. This shows that paragraph processing can reach comparable performance in the reported evaluations while integrating segmentation and transcription. The authors present the work as a significant step toward full-document transcription, with the demonstrated system operating at the paragraph level.
summary.tldr: A recurrent attention-based layer lets a handwriting network select and transcribe paragraph lines jointly, with competitive results on Rimes and IAM.

title: Joint Line Segmentation and Transcription for End-to-End Handwritten Paragraph Recognition

abstract: Missing records are a perennial problem in analysis of complex data of all types, when the target of inference is some function of the full data law. In simple cases, where data is missing at random or completely at random (Rubin, 1976), well-known adjustments exist that result in consistent estimators of target quantities. Assumptions underlying these estimators are generally not realistic in practical missing data problems. Unfortunately, consistent estimators in more complex cases where data is missing not at random, and where no ordering on variables induces monotonicity of missingness status are not known in general, with some notable exceptions (Robins, 1997), (Tchetgen Tchetgen et al, 2016), (Sadinle and Reiter, 2016). In this paper, we propose a general class of consistent estimators for cases where data is missing not at random, and missingness status is non-monotonic. Our estimators, which are generalized inverse probability weighting estimators, make no assumptions on the underlying full data law, but instead place independence restrictions, and certain other fairly mild assumptions, on the distribution of missingness status conditional on the data. The assumptions we place on the distribution of missingness status conditional on the data can be viewed as a version of a conditional Markov random field (MRF) corresponding to a chain graph. Assumptions embedded in our model permit identification from the observed data law, and admit a natural fitting procedure based on the pseudo likelihood approach of (Besag, 1975). We illustrate our approach with a simple simulation study, and an analysis of risk of premature birth in women in Botswana exposed to highly active anti-retroviral therapy.

paragraphs: Estimating a quantity about complete data becomes difficult when missingness depends on the data themselves. The paper addresses an especially complicated setting: missingness is not at random, and no ordering of the variables produces a monotonic pattern of which values are observed. Standard adjustments for simpler missing-data settings do not generally resolve this problem.

The authors propose generalized inverse probability weighting estimators that are consistent under their model assumptions. They leave the full-data distribution unrestricted, but impose independence restrictions and other assumptions on the missingness distribution conditional on the data. These conditions can be represented through a conditional Markov random field associated with a chain graph.

The assumptions make the target quantities identifiable from the observed-data distribution and support fitting through pseudolikelihood. The consistency claim consequently depends on the specified missingness model; it is not an assumption-free solution to arbitrary missing data. A simulation and an analysis of premature-birth risk among women in Botswana exposed to highly active antiretroviral therapy illustrate the approach.
summary.tldr: Generalized weighting estimators handle nonrandom, nonmonotonic missingness under structured assumptions on the missingness mechanism.

title: Consistent Estimation of Functions of Data Missing Non-Monotonically and Not at Random

abstract: We develop a Bayesian model for decision-making under time pressure with endogenous information acquisition. In our model, the decision-maker decides when to observe (costly) information by sampling an underlying continuous-time stochastic process (time series) that conveys information about the potential occurrence/non-occurrence of an adverse event which will terminate the decision-making process. In her attempt to predict the occurrence of the adverse event, the decision-maker follows a policy that determines when to acquire information from the time series (continuation), and when to stop acquiring information and make a final prediction (stopping). We show that the optimal policy has a "rendezvous" structure, i.e. a structure in which whenever a new information sample is gathered from the time series, the optimal "date" for acquiring the next sample becomes computable. The optimal interval between two information samples balances a trade-off between the decision maker’s "surprise", i.e. the drift in her posterior belief after observing new information, and "suspense", i.e. the probability that the adverse event occurs in the time interval between two information samples. Moreover, we characterize the continuation and stopping regions in the decision-maker’s state-space, and show that they depend not only on the decision-maker’s beliefs, but also on the "context", i.e. the current realization of the time series.

paragraphs: This paper studies decisions in which gathering information costs money or effort, while waiting carries its own risk. A decision-maker observes a continuous-time process to predict whether an adverse event will occur. That event can end the decision process, so the decision-maker must choose both when to collect another observation and when to stop and make a prediction.

The authors develop a Bayesian model and show that its optimal policy has a rendezvous structure. After each observation, the decision-maker can compute the optimal time for the next observation. The spacing balances two quantities: how new evidence may shift the current belief, called surprise, and the chance that the adverse event happens before the next observation, called suspense.

The paper also characterizes the states in which continuing or stopping is optimal. These choices depend on both the decision-maker’s beliefs and the current value of the observed process. Consequently, belief alone does not fully describe the decision situation: the surrounding context also affects when information is worth acquiring.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian model shows how to schedule costly observations and stop under time pressure by balancing belief changes against the risk of an adverse event.

title: Balancing Suspense and Surprise: Timely Decision Making with Endogenous Information Acquisition

abstract: Visual dialog is a task of answering a series of inter-dependent questions given an input image, and often requires to resolve visual references among the questions. This problem is different from visual question answering (VQA), which relies on spatial attention ({\em a.k.a. visual grounding}) estimated from an image and question pair. We propose a novel attention mechanism that exploits visual attentions in the past to resolve the current reference in the visual dialog scenario. The proposed model is equipped with an associative attention memory storing a sequence of previous (attention, key) pairs. From this memory, the model retrieves previous attention, taking into account recency, that is most relevant for the current question, in order to resolve potentially ambiguous reference(s). The model then merges the retrieved attention with the tentative one to obtain the final attention for the current question; specifically, we use dynamic parameter prediction to combine the two attentions conditioned on the question. Through extensive experiments on a new synthetic visual dialog dataset, we show that our model significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art (by ~16 % points) in the situation where the visual reference resolution plays an important role. Moreover, the proposed model presents superior performance (~2 % points improvement) in the Visual Dialog dataset, despite having significantly fewer parameters than the baselines.

paragraphs: Visual dialog requires answering connected questions about an image, so interpreting a reference may depend on earlier questions. A model that attends only to the current image-question pair may lack that conversational grounding. This paper introduces an attention memory that reuses earlier visual attention to help resolve the current reference.

The memory stores pairs of previous attention patterns and retrieval keys. For a new question, the model retrieves relevant past attention while accounting for recency. It then combines that retrieved pattern with tentative attention for the current question. Dynamic parameter prediction makes the combination depend on the question being answered.

On a new synthetic dialog dataset, the method outperforms the state of the art by about 16 percentage points when resolving visual references is important. On the Visual Dialog dataset, it improves performance by about two percentage points while using substantially fewer parameters than the baselines. These results support retaining visual attention history as a useful mechanism for connecting the current question to earlier conversational grounding.
summary.tldr: An attention memory retrieves and combines earlier visual grounding to resolve references across questions in visual dialog.

title: Visual Reference Resolution using Attention Memory for Visual Dialog

abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of learning a mixture of Gaussians with streaming data: given a stream of $N$ points in $d$ dimensions generated by an unknown mixture of $k$ spherical Gaussians, the goal is to estimate the model parameters using a single pass over the data stream. We analyze a streaming version of the popular Lloyd's heuristic and show that the algorithm estimates all the unknown centers of the component Gaussians accurately if they are sufficiently separated. Assuming each pair of centers are $C\sigma$ distant with $C=\Omega((k\log k)^{1/4}\sigma)$ and where $\sigma^2$ is the maximum variance of any Gaussian component, we show that asymptotically the algorithm estimates the centers optimally (up to certain constants); our center separation requirement matches the best known result for spherical Gaussians \citep{vempalawang}. For finite samples, we show that a bias term based on the initial estimate decreases at $O(1/{\rm poly}(N))$ rate while variance decreases at nearly optimal rate of $\sigma^2 d/N$. Our analysis requires seeding the algorithm with a good initial estimate of the true cluster centers for which we provide an online PCA based clustering algorithm. Indeed, the asymptotic per-step time complexity of our algorithm is the optimal $d\cdot k$ while space complexity of our algorithm is $O(dk\log k)$. In addition to the bias and variance terms which tend to $0$, the hard-thresholding based updates of streaming Lloyd's algorithm is agnostic to the data distribution and hence incurs an \emph{approximation error} that cannot be avoided. However, by using a streaming version of the classical \emph{(soft-thresholding-based)} EM method that exploits the Gaussian distribution explicitly, we show that for a mixture of two Gaussians the true means can be estimated consistently, with estimation error decreasing at nearly optimal rate, and tending to $0$ for $N\rightarrow \infty$.

paragraphs: This paper studies estimating the centers of spherical Gaussian mixture components from a single pass through streaming data. It analyzes a streaming form of Lloyd's clustering heuristic, with guarantees that require sufficiently separated centers and a good initial estimate. An online PCA-based clustering procedure supplies that initialization.

Under the stated separation conditions, the center estimates are asymptotically optimal up to constants. The finite-sample analysis separates initialization bias, which decays polynomially with sample count, from a variance term that decreases at a nearly optimal rate. The algorithm also has asymptotically optimal per-step time proportional to dimension times component count, with space growing as that product times the logarithm of component count.

A remaining approximation error arises because Lloyd's hard assignments do not explicitly exploit the Gaussian distribution. The authors therefore also analyze streaming EM, which uses soft assignments and the Gaussian model. For two Gaussian components, this approach estimates the true means consistently, with nearly optimal error decay toward zero. That consistency result is specifically stated for the two-component setting.
summary.tldr: Streaming clustering learns separated Gaussian centers efficiently, while a two-component streaming EM result removes the hard-assignment approximation error.

title: Learning Mixture of Gaussians with Streaming Data

abstract: A gated recurrent unit (GRU) is a successful recurrent neural network architecture for time-series data. The GRU is typically trained using a gradient-based method, which is subject to the exploding gradient problem in which the gradient increases significantly. This problem is caused by an abrupt change in the dynamics of the GRU due to a small variation in the parameters. In this paper, we find a condition under which the dynamics of the GRU changes drastically and propose a learning method to address the exploding gradient problem. Our method constrains the dynamics of the GRU so that it does not drastically change. We evaluated our method in experiments on language modeling and polyphonic music modeling. Our experiments showed that our method can prevent the exploding gradient problem and improve modeling accuracy.

paragraphs: Gated recurrent units model time-series data and are commonly trained with gradient-based optimization. Their gradients can sometimes increase sharply, disrupting learning. This paper examines that problem through the dynamics of the recurrent model: a small change in parameters can trigger an abrupt change in how the GRU behaves over time.

The authors identify a condition under which such a drastic dynamical change occurs. They use that analysis to design a learning method that constrains the GRU's dynamics, aiming to keep parameter updates from producing those abrupt transitions. The proposed intervention therefore acts on the behavior associated with the gradient explosion.

Experiments evaluate the method on language modeling and polyphonic music modeling. The authors report that it can prevent exploding gradients and improve modeling accuracy in those evaluations. These findings connect training stability with predictive performance: controlling the identified dynamical behavior helped both in the tested tasks. The abstract presents experimental support for this effect rather than a claim that every possible GRU training run is protected.
summary.tldr: Constraining GRU dynamics can prevent gradient explosions and improve accuracy, as shown in language and music modeling experiments.

title: Preventing Gradient Explosions in Gated Recurrent Units

abstract: For many classic structured prediction problems, probability distributions over the dependent variables can be efficiently computed using widely-known algorithms and data structures (such as forward-backward, and its corresponding trellis for exact probability distributions in Markov models). However, we know of no previous work studying efficient representations of exact distributions over clusterings. This paper presents definitions and proofs for a dynamic-programming inference procedure that computes the partition function, the marginal probability of a cluster, and the MAP clustering---all exactly. Rather than the Nth Bell number, these exact solutions take time and space proportional to the substantially smaller powerset of N. Indeed, we improve upon the time complexity of the algorithm introduced by Kohonen and Corander (2016) for this problem by a factor of N. While still large, this previously unknown result is intellectually interesting in its own right, makes feasible exact inference for important real-world small data applications (such as medicine), and provides a natural stepping stone towards sparse-trellis approximations that enable further scalability (which we also explore). In experiments, we demonstrate the superiority of our approach over approximate methods in analyzing real-world gene expression data used in cancer treatment.
