paragraphs: NeuPhysics learns the three-dimensional geometry and physical parameters of a dynamic scene from a single RGB video stream. Its representation separates a stable description of shape from changes over time. A time-invariant signed distance function provides the reference geometry, while a time-conditioned deformation field describes motion relative to that reference.

The method connects this neural representation to a differentiable physics simulator through a two-way conversion involving a hexahedral mesh. This connection allows the system to estimate physical parameters from the source video by minimizing a cycle-consistency loss. The neural field and mesh serve complementary roles within the same reconstruction process, linking visual geometry with simulated physical behavior.

The mesh also provides an editing interface: users modify recovered three-dimensional objects, and those changes propagate back into the neural field. Experiments report better mesh and video reconstruction of dynamic scenes than competing neural-field approaches. Examples using consumer-camera videos demonstrate useful recovered representations. The contribution therefore combines reconstruction, physics estimation, and interactive editing within a method that takes monocular video as its input.
summary.tldr: NeuPhysics connects neural geometry with a physics simulator to reconstruct and edit dynamic 3D scenes from monocular video.

title: NeuPhysics: Editable Neural Geometry and Physics from Monocular Videos

abstract: Recently a wide variety of NAS methods have been proposed and achieved considerable success in automatically identifying highly-performing architectures of neural networks for the sake of reducing the reliance on human experts. Existing NAS methods ignore the fact that different input data elements (e.g., image pixels) have different importance (or saliency) in determining the prediction outcome. They treat all data elements as being equally important and therefore lead to suboptimal performance. To address this problem, we propose an end-to-end framework which dynamically detects saliency of input data, reweights data using saliency maps, and searches architectures on saliency-reweighted data. Our framework is based on four-level optimization, which performs four learning stages in a unified way. At the first stage, a model is trained with its architecture tentatively fixed. At the second stage, saliency maps are generated using the trained model. At the third stage, the model is retrained on saliency-reweighted data. At the fourth stage, the model is evaluated on a validation set and the architecture is updated by minimizing the validation loss. Experiments on several datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search automates the choice of network structure. This paper argues that the search should account for differences in the importance of input elements, such as image pixels. If some parts of an input matter more for a prediction, that information can also guide how candidate architectures are trained and evaluated.

The proposed framework joins four learning stages. First, it trains a model while temporarily fixing its architecture. Second, it generates saliency maps from that model. Third, it retrains using inputs reweighted by those maps. Fourth, it evaluates validation loss and updates the architecture to improve that loss.

These stages form a unified four-level optimization problem, allowing the saliency information to change during the search. Architecture selection is therefore linked to what the current model considers informative in the data. Experiments on several datasets demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness, supporting the use of dynamic input importance as part of automated architecture design.
summary.tldr: A four-stage optimization framework uses dynamically estimated input saliency to guide neural architecture search.

title: Saliency-Aware Neural Architecture Search

abstract: Creating high-quality articulated 3D models of animals is challenging either via manual creation or using 3D scanning tools. Therefore, techniques to reconstruct articulated 3D objects from 2D images are crucial and highly useful. In this work, we propose a practical problem setting to estimate 3D pose and shape of animals given only a few (10-30) in-the-wild images of a particular animal species (say, horse). Contrary to existing works that rely on pre-defined template shapes, we do not assume any form of 2D or 3D ground-truth annotations, nor do we leverage any multi-view or temporal information. Moreover, each input image ensemble can contain animal instances with varying poses, backgrounds, illuminations, and textures. Our key insight is that 3D parts have much simpler shape compared to the overall animal and that they are robust w.r.t. animal pose articulations. Following these insights, we propose LASSIE, a novel optimization framework which discovers 3D parts in a self-supervised manner with minimal user intervention. A key driving force behind LASSIE is the enforcing of 2D-3D part consistency using self-supervisory deep features. Experiments on Pascal-Part and self-collected in-the-wild animal datasets demonstrate considerably better 3D reconstructions as well as both 2D and 3D part discovery compared to prior arts. Project page: https://chhankyao.github.io/lassie/

paragraphs: LASSIE reconstructs articulated animal shape and pose from a small collection of 10–30 images of one species. The images can show different animal instances, poses, backgrounds, lighting, and textures. The method does not assume predefined template shapes, ground-truth 2D or 3D annotations, or information linking images through multiple views or time.

The approach builds on the observation that individual body parts have simpler shapes than a complete animal and remain useful units as the animal changes pose. Its optimization framework discovers 3D parts through self-supervision with minimal user intervention. A central constraint encourages agreement between 2D and 3D parts using self-supervisory deep features.

This part-based organization gives the reconstruction process structure without requiring a complete animal template in advance. Evaluations on Pascal-Part and collected animal images report considerably better 3D reconstructions and better part discovery in both two and three dimensions than prior approaches. The stated setting is particularly relevant to reconstructing a species from a sparse, varied image collection rather than coordinated captures.
summary.tldr: LASSIE discovers 3D animal parts to reconstruct articulated shapes from 10–30 varied images with minimal user intervention.

title: LASSIE: Learning Articulated Shapes from Sparse Image Ensemble via 3D Part Discovery

abstract: We present simultaneous generation and mapping (SGAM), a novel 3D scene generation algorithm. Our goal is to produce a realistic, globally consistent 3D world on a large scale. Achieving this goal is challenging and goes beyond the capacities of existing 3D generation or video generation approaches, which fail to scale up to create large, globally consistent 3D scene structures. Towards tackling the challenges, we take a hybrid approach that integrates generative sensor model- ing with 3D reconstruction. Our proposed approach is an autoregressive generative framework that simultaneously generates sensor data at novel viewpoints and builds a 3D map at each timestamp. Given an arbitrary camera trajectory, our method repeatedly applies this generation-and-mapping process for thousands of steps, allowing us to create a gigantic virtual world. Our model can be trained from RGB-D sequences without having access to the complete 3D scene structure. The generated scenes are readily compatible with various interactive environments and rendering engines. originalAbstract: We present simultaneous generation and mapping (SGAM), a novel 3D scene generation algorithm. Our goal is to produce a realistic, globally consistent 3D world on a large scale. Achieving this goal is challenging and goes beyond the capacities of existing 3D generation or video generation approaches, which fail to scale up to create large, globally consistent 3D scene structures. Towards tackling the challenges, we take a hybrid approach that integrates generative sensor model- ing with 3D reconstruction. Our proposed approach is an autoregressive generative framework that simultaneously generates sensor data at novel viewpoints and builds a 3D map at each timestamp. Given an arbitrary camera trajectory, our method repeatedly applies this generation-and-mapping process for thousands of steps, allowing us to create a gigantic virtual world. Our model can be trained from RGB-D sequences without having access to the complete 3D scene structure. The generated scenes are readily compatible with various interactive environments and rendering engines. Experiments on CLEVER and GoogleEarth datasets demon- strates ours can generate consistent, realistic, and geometrically-plausible scenes that compare favorably to existing view synthesis methods. Our project page is available at https://yshen47.github.io/sgam.

paragraphs: Creating a large virtual world requires generated views to agree about a shared three-dimensional scene. SGAM tackles this challenge by combining generative sensor modeling with 3D reconstruction. Its goal is to extend scene generation over large spaces while maintaining realistic appearance and globally consistent geometry.

The method follows an autoregressive process: at each step, it generates sensor data from a new viewpoint and builds a 3D map. Given a camera trajectory, it repeats this coupled generation-and-mapping operation for thousands of steps. Training uses RGB-D sequences, which provide color and depth observations, without requiring access to the complete structure of the scene.

Experiments on CLEVER and GoogleEarth report realistic, consistent, and geometrically plausible generated scenes that compare favorably with existing view-synthesis methods. The resulting scenes are also compatible with interactive environments and rendering engines. The contribution is therefore both a way to extend generation across many viewpoints and a way to produce a mapped world usable beyond the generation process itself.
summary.tldr: SGAM repeatedly generates new-view sensor data and reconstructs a 3D map to build large, consistent virtual worlds from RGB-D training sequences.

title: SGAM: Building a Virtual 3D World through Simultaneous Generation and Mapping

abstract: Self-supervised multi-view stereopsis (MVS) attracts increasing attention for learning dense surface predictions from only a set of images without onerous ground-truth 3D training data for supervision. However, existing methods highly rely on the local photometric consistency, which fails to identify accurately dense correspondence in broad textureless and reflectance areas.In this paper, we show that geometric proximity such as surface connectedness and occlusion boundaries implicitly inferred from images could serve as reliable guidance for pixel-wise multi-view correspondences. With this insight, we present a novel elastic part representation which encodes physically-connected part segmentations with elastically-varying scales, shapes and boundaries. Meanwhile, a self-supervised MVS framework namely ElasticMVS is proposed to learn the representation and estimate per-view depth following a part-aware propagation and evaluation scheme. Specifically, the pixel-wise part representation is trained by a contrastive learning-based strategy, which increases the representation compactness in geometrically concentrated areas and contrasts otherwise. ElasticMVS iteratively optimizes a part-level consistency loss and a surface smoothness loss, based on a set of depth hypotheses propagated from the geometrically concentrated parts. Extensive evaluations convey the superiority of ElasticMVS in the reconstruction completeness and accuracy, as well as the efficiency and scalability. Particularly, for the challenging large-scale reconstruction benchmark, ElasticMVS demonstrates significant performance gain over both the supervised and self-supervised approaches.

A contrastive training strategy makes representations more compact within geometrically concentrated areas while separating others. The reconstruction framework uses these parts to propagate candidate depth values and evaluate them, repeatedly optimizing part-level consistency and surface smoothness.

The approach matters because correspondence is informed by connected surface structure rather than only nearby pixel appearance. Reported evaluations show advantages in reconstruction completeness, accuracy, efficiency, and scalability. On the challenging large-scale reconstruction benchmark considered, ElasticMVS produces significant gains over both supervised and self-supervised approaches. These results support the value of learning flexible geometric parts as guidance for depth estimation.
summary.tldr: ElasticMVS learns flexible connected surface parts to guide self-supervised depth estimation where appearance matching is unreliable.

title: ElasticMVS: Learning elastic part representation for self-supervised multi-view stereopsis

abstract: The ever-increasing computational complexity of deep learning models makes their training and deployment difficult on various cloud and edge platforms. Replacing floating-point arithmetic with low-bit integer arithmetic is a promising approach to save energy, memory footprint, and latency of deep learning models. As such, quantization has attracted the attention of researchers in recent years. However, using integer numbers to form a fully functional integer training pipeline including forward pass, back-propagation, and stochastic gradient descent is not studied in detail. Our empirical and mathematical results reveal that integer arithmetic seems to be enough to train deep learning models. Unlike recent proposals, instead of quantization, we directly switch the number representation of computations. Our novel training method forms a fully integer training pipeline that does not change the trajectory of the loss and accuracy compared to floating-point, nor does it need any special hyper-parameter tuning, distribution adjustment, or gradient clipping. Our experimental results show that our proposed method is effective in a wide variety of tasks such as classification (including vision transformers), object detection, and semantic segmentation.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether integer arithmetic can support the entire training process for deep neural networks. The motivation is the growing computational burden of training and deployment, with lower-bit arithmetic offering potential savings in energy, memory, and latency. The question extends beyond computing predictions to back-propagation and stochastic gradient descent.

The authors propose changing the number representation used in computations directly, distinguishing their approach from recent quantization proposals. Their method forms a fully integer training pipeline. They report that it preserves the loss and accuracy trajectories of floating-point training without requiring special hyperparameter tuning, distribution adjustment, or gradient clipping.

Mathematical analysis and experiments lead the authors to conclude that integer arithmetic appears sufficient for training deep models. Evaluations cover classification, including vision transformers, object detection, and semantic segmentation. This breadth supports the method's applicability across several tasks. The stated conclusion remains qualified: the findings support integer training in the studied settings, rather than proving that every model and training procedure can be converted identically.
summary.tldr: A fully integer training pipeline preserves reported floating-point learning trajectories across several tasks without special training adjustments.

title: Is Integer Arithmetic Enough for Deep Learning Training?

abstract: A finite set of invariants can identify many interesting transformation groups. For example, distances, inner products and angles are preserved by Euclidean, Orthogonal and Conformal transformations, respectively. In an equivariant representation, the group invariants should remain constant on the embedding as we transform the input. This gives a procedure for learning equivariant representations without knowing the possibly nonlinear action of the group in the input space. Rather than enforcing such hard invariance constraints on the latent space, we show how to use invariants for "symmetry regularization" of the latent, while guaranteeing equivariance through other means. We also show the feasibility of learning disentangled representations using this approach and provide favorable qualitative and quantitative results on downstream tasks, including world modeling and reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Transformations can be characterized by quantities they preserve. Distances, inner products, and angles provide examples for different transformation groups. The paper uses this observation to structure learned representations: when an input is transformed, corresponding invariant quantities in its representation should remain constant even though the representation itself may change.

This offers a route to learning equivariant representations without knowing the possibly nonlinear way the group acts on the input space. The authors use invariants as a symmetry regularizer on the latent representation instead of imposing them as hard constraints. Equivariance is guaranteed through other means, so regularization shapes the representation without carrying the entire guarantee.

The paper also demonstrates the feasibility of learning disentangled representations with this approach. Qualitative and quantitative results are favorable on downstream tasks including world modeling and reinforcement learning. Its central contribution is a way to use knowledge of preserved quantities to organize latent structure, connecting an abstract description of symmetry to representations that can support practical learning tasks.
summary.tldr: Group invariants provide a symmetry regularizer for learning structured, equivariant representations without knowing the group's full input-space action.

title: Structuring Representations Using Group Invariants

abstract: Sampling methods, as important inference and learning techniques, are typically designed for unconstrained domains. However, constraints are ubiquitous in machine learning problems, such as those on safety, fairness, robustness, and many other properties that must be satisfied to apply sampling results in real-life applications. Enforcing these constraints often leads to implicitly-defined manifolds, making efficient sampling with constraints very challenging. In this paper, we propose a new variational framework with a designed orthogonal-space gradient flow (O-Gradient) for sampling on a manifold $\mathcal{G}_0$ defined by general equality constraints. O-Gradient decomposes the gradient into two parts: one decreases the distance to $\mathcal{G}_0$ and the other decreases the KL divergence in the orthogonal space. While most existing manifold sampling methods require initialization on $\mathcal{G}_0$, O-Gradient does not require such prior knowledge. We prove that O-Gradient converges to the target constrained distribution with rate $\widetilde{O}(1/\text{the number of iterations})$ under mild conditions. Our proof relies on a new Stein characterization of conditional measure which could be of independent interest. We implement O-Gradient through both Langevin dynamics and Stein variational gradient descent and demonstrate its effectiveness in various experiments, including Bayesian deep neural networks.

paragraphs: Sampling methods often assume that samples can move freely through their domain. Equality constraints change this problem by restricting valid samples to a manifold, which may be defined only implicitly. This paper develops a variational framework for sampling from a target distribution on such a constrained space.

Its O-Gradient flow splits the gradient into two components with distinct roles. One moves toward the constraint manifold, while the other reduces the discrepancy from the target distribution through an orthogonal-space KL-divergence objective. This separation allows the process to begin away from the manifold, avoiding the need to already know a valid initialization.

Under conditions described as mild, the authors prove convergence to the constrained target distribution at an approximately inverse-iteration rate, up to logarithmic factors. The proof introduces a new Stein characterization of a conditional measure. Implementations through Langevin dynamics and Stein variational gradient descent demonstrate effectiveness in experiments, including Bayesian deep neural networks. The framework therefore connects movement toward constraint satisfaction with distributional learning in one sampling process.
summary.tldr: O-Gradient samples under equality constraints by separating movement toward the feasible manifold from improvement toward the target distribution.

title: Sampling in Constrained Domains with Orthogonal-Space Variational Gradient Descent

abstract: Despite their wide adoption, the underlying training and memorization dynamics of very large language models is not well understood. We empirically study exact memorization in causal and masked language modeling, across model sizes and throughout the training process. We measure the effects of dataset size, learning rate, and model size on memorization, finding that larger language models memorize training data faster across all settings. Surprisingly, we show that larger models can memorize a larger portion of the data before over-fitting and tend to forget less throughout the training process. We also analyze the memorization dynamics of different parts of speech and find that models memorize nouns and numbers first; we hypothesize and provide empirical evidence that nouns and numbers act as a unique identifier for memorizing individual training examples. Together, these findings present another piece of the broader puzzle of trying to understand what actually improves as models get bigger.

paragraphs: This paper examines how exact memorization develops during language-model training. The authors study both causal and masked language modeling, tracking models of different sizes throughout training. They also measure how dataset size and learning rate affect memorization, making the timing and persistence of memorized material central objects of study.

Across the studied settings, larger models memorize training data faster. They can also memorize a larger portion of the data before overfitting and tend to forget less during training. These observations show that exact memorization and overfitting do not move together in a simple way: greater memorization can appear before the point at which overfitting emerges.

The analysis also separates words by their grammatical roles and finds that nouns and numbers are memorized first. The authors hypothesize that these elements help identify individual training examples and provide empirical evidence for that explanation. The work contributes an empirical account of what changes with model scale, including how quickly examples are memorized and how reliably that memorization persists.
summary.tldr: Larger language models memorize faster and retain more in the studied settings, with substantial memorization occurring before overfitting.

title: Memorization Without Overfitting: Analyzing the Training Dynamics of Large Language Models

abstract: Recently, there has been increased interest in fair generative models. In this work,we conduct, for the first time, an in-depth study on fairness measurement, acritical component in gauging progress on fair generative models. We make threecontributions. First, we conduct a study that reveals that the existing fairnessmeasurement framework has considerable measurement errors, even when highlyaccurate sensitive attribute (SA) classifiers are used. These findings cast doubtson previously reported fairness improvements. Second, to address this issue,we propose CLassifier Error-Aware Measurement (CLEAM), a new frameworkwhich uses a statistical model to account for inaccuracies in SA classifiers. Ourproposed CLEAM reduces measurement errors significantly, e.g., 4.98%→0.62%for StyleGAN2 w.r.t. Gender. Additionally, CLEAM achieves this with minimaladditional overhead. Third, we utilize CLEAM to measure fairness in importanttext-to-image generator and GANs, revealing considerable biases in these modelsthat raise concerns about their applications. Code and more resources: https://sutd-visual-computing-group.github.io/CLEAM/.

paragraphs: Evaluating fairness in generated images often depends on classifiers that identify sensitive attributes. This paper finds that the existing measurement framework can produce substantial errors even when those classifiers are highly accurate. As a result, apparent improvements in a generator's fairness may partly reflect errors in the measurement process.

The authors introduce CLassifier Error-Aware Measurement, or CLEAM, to account statistically for inaccuracies in sensitive-attribute classification. The framework substantially reduces measurement error while adding little overhead. In the reported StyleGAN2 gender example, the measurement error falls from 4.98% to 0.62%. This improvement concerns the reliability of evaluation rather than a change to the generator itself.

The paper also uses CLEAM to assess text-to-image generators and generative adversarial networks, finding considerable biases in the models examined. Together, the results show why measuring fairness requires attention to the evaluator's own errors. They cast doubt on previously reported improvements without establishing that all such improvements are invalid, and provide a more error-aware approach to assessing future claims.
summary.tldr: CLEAM accounts for sensitive-attribute classifier errors to make generative-model fairness measurements substantially more accurate.

title: On Measuring Fairness in Generative Models

abstract: Cross-modal Retrieval methods build similarity relations between vision and language modalities by jointly learning a common representation space. However, the predictions are often unreliable due to the Aleatoric uncertainty, which is induced by low-quality data, e.g., corrupt images, fast-paced videos, and non-detailed texts. In this paper, we propose a novel Prototype-based Aleatoric Uncertainty Quantification (PAU) framework to provide trustworthy predictions by quantifying the uncertainty arisen from the inherent data ambiguity. Concretely, we first construct a set of various learnable prototypes for each modality to represent the entire semantics subspace. Then Dempster-Shafer Theory and Subjective Logic Theory are utilized to build an evidential theoretical framework by associating evidence with Dirichlet Distribution parameters. The PAU model induces accurate uncertainty and reliable predictions for cross-modal retrieval. Extensive experiments are performed on four major benchmark datasets of MSR-VTT, MSVD, DiDeMo, and MS-COCO, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method. The code is accessible at https://github.com/leolee99/PAU.

paragraphs: Cross-modal retrieval matches visual content with language by learning a shared representation space. Its predictions can become unreliable when the data itself is ambiguous, such as damaged images, rapidly changing videos, or vague descriptions. PAU focuses on quantifying this data-driven, or aleatoric, uncertainty alongside retrieval predictions.

The framework first learns a collection of prototypes for each modality to represent its semantic space. It then uses Dempster-Shafer theory and subjective logic to build an evidence-based uncertainty framework, linking evidence to parameters of a Dirichlet distribution. This connects the model's representation of semantic content with a formal account of uncertainty about its predictions.

Experiments on MSR-VTT, MSVD, DiDeMo, and MS-COCO demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The authors report accurate uncertainty estimates and reliable retrieval predictions. The contribution is a mechanism for making ambiguity in the input data explicit, so a retrieval system can characterize uncertainty as well as produce a match. Its prototype-based construction ties that characterization to learned semantic representations in both vision and language.
summary.tldr: PAU uses learned semantic prototypes and an evidential framework to quantify data ambiguity in vision-language retrieval.

title: Prototype-based Aleatoric Uncertainty Quantification for Cross-modal Retrieval

abstract: Equivariance has gained strong interest as a desirable network property that inherently ensures robust generalization. However, when dealing with complex systems such as articulated objects or multi-object scenes, effectively capturing inter-part transformations poses a challenge, as it becomes entangled with the overall structure and local transformations. The interdependence of part assignment and per-part group action necessitates a novel equivariance formulation that allows for their co-evolution. In this paper, we present Banana, a Banach fixed-point network for equivariant segmentation with inter-part equivariance by construction. Our key insight is to iteratively solve a fixed-point problem, where point-part assignment labels and per-part SE(3)-equivariance co-evolve simultaneously. We provide theoretical derivations of both per-step equivariance and global convergence, which induces an equivariant final convergent state. Our formulation naturally provides a strict definition of inter-part equivariance that generalizes to unseen inter-part configurations. Through experiments conducted on both articulated objects and multi-object scans, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in achieving strong generalization under inter-part transformations, even when confronted with substantial changes in pointcloud geometry and topology.

paragraphs: Segmenting a point cloud becomes difficult when different parts of an object or scene move independently. Identifying a part and understanding its transformation depend on each other: the model needs part assignments to describe separate motions, yet those motions affect the evidence used for assignment. Banana addresses this coupled problem through a network designed for inter-part equivariance.

The method repeatedly updates point-to-part assignments together with per-part SE(3)-equivariance, which concerns rotations and translations in three dimensions. These updates solve a fixed-point problem, seeking a state that remains unchanged under further iteration. The authors derive both equivariance at each step and global convergence, yielding an equivariant final state.

This formulation gives a precise treatment of how segmentation should respond to transformations of individual parts. Experiments on articulated objects and scans containing multiple objects show strong generalization to inter-part transformations, including substantial changes in point-cloud geometry and topology. The findings support jointly evolving the assignments and transformation behavior as a way to handle previously unseen arrangements of parts.
summary.tldr: Banana jointly refines part assignments and transformation behavior to produce convergent, inter-part-equivariant point-cloud segmentation.

title: Banana: Banach Fixed-Point Network for Pointcloud Segmentation with Inter-Part Equivariance

abstract: 3D sensing for monocular in-the-wild images, e.g., depth estimation and 3D object detection, has become increasingly important.However, the unknown intrinsic parameter hinders their development and deployment.Previous methods for the monocular camera calibration rely on specific 3D objects or strong geometry prior, such as using a checkerboard or imposing a Manhattan World assumption.This work instead calibrates intrinsic via exploiting the monocular 3D prior.Given an undistorted image as input, our method calibrates the complete 4 Degree-of-Freedom (DoF) intrinsic parameters.First, we show intrinsic is determined by the two well-studied monocular priors: monocular depthmap and surface normal map.However, this solution necessitates a low-bias and low-variance depth estimation.Alternatively, we introduce the incidence field, defined as the incidence rays between points in 3D space and pixels in the 2D imaging plane.We show that: 1) The incidence field is a pixel-wise parametrization of the intrinsic invariant to image cropping and resizing.2) The incidence field is a learnable monocular 3D prior, determined pixel-wisely by up-to-sacle monocular depthmap and surface normal.With the estimated incidence field, a robust RANSAC algorithm recovers intrinsic.We show the effectiveness of our method through superior performance on synthetic and zero-shot testing datasets.Beyond calibration, we demonstrate downstream applications in image manipulation detection \& restoration, uncalibrated two-view pose estimation, and 3D sensing.

paragraphs: Recovering 3D information from an ordinary image is harder when the camera’s intrinsic parameters are unknown. This paper estimates the complete four-degree-of-freedom intrinsic parameters from a single undistorted image. Its approach uses learned monocular 3D information instead of relying on calibration objects or strong scene-geometry assumptions.

The authors first show that depth and surface-normal maps determine the intrinsics, but this route requires depth estimates with low bias and variance. They introduce an alternative representation called the incidence field, which describes the rays connecting 3D points with image pixels. It provides a pixel-wise parameterization of the intrinsics that is invariant to cropping and resizing and can be learned from monocular 3D cues.

A robust RANSAC procedure recovers camera intrinsics from the estimated incidence field. The authors report superior performance on synthetic and zero-shot test datasets. They also demonstrate applications in detecting and restoring image manipulations, estimating relative pose from uncalibrated image pairs, and 3D sensing. The contribution makes learned ray geometry the intermediate representation linking an image to its camera calibration.
summary.tldr: A learned incidence field enables recovery of four camera intrinsic parameters from one undistorted image.

title: Tame a Wild Camera: In-the-Wild Monocular Camera Calibration

abstract: Graph contrastive learning (GCL) aims to learn representations by capturing the agreements between different graph views. Traditional GCL methods generate views in the spatial domain, but it has been recently discovered that the spectral domain also plays a vital role in complementing spatial views. However, existing spectral-based graph views either ignore the eigenvectors that encode valuable positional information or suffer from high complexity when trying to address the instability of spectral features. To tackle these challenges, we first design an informative, stable, and scalable spectral encoder, termed EigenMLP, to learn effective representations from the spectral features. Theoretically, EigenMLP is invariant to the rotation and reflection transformations on eigenvectors and robust against perturbations. Then, we propose a spatial-spectral contrastive framework (Sp$^{2}$GCL) to capture the consistency between the spatial information encoded by graph neural networks and the spectral information learned by EigenMLP, thus effectively fusing these two graph views. Experiments on the node- and graph-level datasets show that our method not only learns effective graph representations but also achieves a 2--10x speedup over other spectral-based methods.

Then, we propose a spatial-spectral contrastive framework (Sp$^{2}$GCL) to capture the consistency between the spatial information encoded by graph neural networks and the spectral information learned by EigenMLP, thus effectively fusing these two graph views. Experiments on the node- and graph-level datasets show that our method not only learns effective graph representations but also achieves a 2--10x speedup over other spectral-based methods.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning builds representations by finding agreement between different views of a graph. Spatial views describe graph structure through connections, while spectral views provide complementary information, including positional information carried by eigenvectors. Existing spectral approaches either discard this useful information or incur substantial computational costs when addressing its instability.

The paper introduces EigenMLP, an encoder designed to retain spectral information while remaining stable and scalable. The authors prove invariance to rotations and reflections of eigenvectors and robustness against perturbations. This matters because the encoded representation should not change simply because the spectral description undergoes one of these transformations.

Their Sp²GCL framework contrasts the spatial information learned by a graph neural network with the spectral information learned by EigenMLP. Encouraging consistency combines the two views within learned representations. Experiments on both node-level and graph-level datasets demonstrate effective representations and a reported two- to tenfold speedup over other spectral methods. The contribution therefore addresses representation quality and the computational burden of using spectral features together.
summary.tldr: EigenMLP enables stable spectral encoding that complements spatial graph features while accelerating the evaluated spectral methods.

title: Graph Contrastive Learning with Stable and Scalable Spectral Encoding

abstract: Object detection in aerial images is a growing area of research, with maritime object detection being a particularly important task for reliable surveillance, monitoring, and active rescuing. Notwithstanding astonishing advances of computer visiontechnologies, detecting ships and floating matters in these images are challenging due to factors such as object distance. What makes it worse is pervasive sea surface effects such as sunlight reflection, wind, and waves. Hyperspectral image (HSI) sensors, providing more than 100 channels in wavelengths of visible and near-infrared, can extract intrinsic information of materials from a few pixels of HSIs.The advent of HSI sensors motivates us to leverage HSIs to circumvent false positives due to the sea surface effects.Unfortunately, there are few public HSI datasets due to the high cost and labor involved in collecting them, hindering object detection research based on HSIs. We have collected and annotated a new dataset called ``Multi-Modal Ship and flOating matter Detection in Aerial Images (M$^{2}$SODAI),'', which includes synchronized image pairs of RGB and HSI data, along with bounding box labels for nearly 6,000 instances per category. We also propose a new multi-modal extension of the feature pyramid network called DoubleFPN.Extensive experiments on our benchmark demonstrate that fusion of RGB and HSI data can enhance mAP, especially in the presence of the sea surface effects.

Hyperspectral sensors offer more than 100 visible and near-infrared channels, which can reveal material information from only a few pixels. The paper investigates this information as a way to reduce confusion caused by the water surface.

The authors collect and annotate M²SODAI, a dataset of synchronized RGB and hyperspectral image pairs. It includes bounding boxes for nearly 6,000 instances per category. Providing paired observations addresses the scarcity of public hyperspectral detection datasets and enables direct study of how these sensor types can complement one another.

The paper also introduces DoubleFPN, a multimodal extension of a feature pyramid network. Experiments on the new benchmark show that combining RGB and hyperspectral data can improve mean average precision, particularly when sea-surface effects are present. The dataset and model together establish a concrete setting for evaluating spectral information in maritime object detection.
summary.tldr: M²SODAI pairs RGB and hyperspectral maritime imagery, and DoubleFPN shows detection gains from fusing the two sensor types.

title: M$^{2}$SODAI: Multi-Modal Maritime Object Detection Dataset With RGB and Hyperspectral Image Sensors

abstract: Infants possess a remarkable ability to rapidly learn and process visual inputs. As an infant's mobility increases, so does the variety and dynamics of their visual inputs. Is this change in the properties of the visual inputs beneficial or even critical for the proper development of the visual system? To address this question, we used video recordings from infants wearing head-mounted cameras to train a variety of self-supervised learning models. Critically, we separated the infant data by age group and evaluated the importance of training with a curriculum aligned with developmental order. We found that initiating learning with the data from the youngest age group provided the strongest learning signal and led to the best learning outcomes in terms of downstream task performance. We then showed that the benefits of the data from the youngest age group are due to the slowness and simplicity of the visual experience. The results provide strong empirical evidence for the importance of the properties of the early infant experience and developmental progression in training. More broadly, our approach and findings take a noteworthy step towards reverse engineering the learning mechanisms in newborn brains using image-computable models from artificial intelligence.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether the changing visual experiences of infants can help explain how visual learning develops. As infants become more mobile, what they see becomes more varied and dynamic. The researchers used videos recorded by infant head-mounted cameras to investigate whether the order of those experiences matters when training artificial visual learning systems.

They divided the recordings by age and trained several self-supervised models with curricula that reflected developmental order. Starting with footage from the youngest infants produced the strongest learning signal and the best performance on subsequent tasks. The study further attributes the usefulness of this early footage to its slower changes and simpler visual content.

The findings suggest that training data matter through their progression as well as their contents. Relatively simple, slowly changing experiences can provide a useful starting point before more complex inputs arrive. These are empirical results from artificial learning models, supporting the importance of early experience without establishing that the models reproduce the learning mechanisms of infant brains.
summary.tldr: Models trained first on the youngest infants’ slower, simpler visual experiences achieved the best downstream learning outcomes.

title: Curriculum Learning With Infant Egocentric Videos

abstract: Particle-based deep generative models, such as gradient flows and score-based diffusion models, have recently gained traction thanks to their striking performance. Their principle of displacing particle distributions using differential equations is conventionally seen as opposed to the previously widespread generative adversarial networks (GANs), which involve training a pushforward generator network. In this paper we challenge this interpretation, and propose a novel framework that unifies particle and adversarial generative models by framing generator training as a generalization of particle models. This suggests that a generator is an optional addition to any such generative model. Consequently, integrating a generator into a score-based diffusion model and training a GAN without a generator naturally emerge from our framework. We empirically test the viability of these original models as proofs of concepts of potential applications of our framework.

paragraphs: Particle-based generative models transform sample distributions through differential equations. Generative adversarial networks are commonly described differently, through training a generator network that maps inputs into generated samples. This paper questions that separation and develops a framework connecting the two views. The goal is to understand their relationship at the level of the generative process.

The framework treats generator training as a generalization of particle models. Under this interpretation, a generator network becomes an optional component of such a model rather than the defining boundary between particle-based and adversarial generation. This opens up combinations that are less natural when the two model families are treated as fundamentally separate.

Two constructions follow from the framework: adding a generator to a score-based diffusion model and training a GAN without a generator. The authors test their viability empirically as proofs of concept. These experiments support the possibility of the proposed combinations; their stated role is to illustrate potential applications of the unifying framework, rather than establish universal performance superiority.
summary.tldr: A shared particle-model framework connects GANs and score-based diffusion, motivating diffusion with a generator and adversarial generation without one.

title: Unifying GANs and Score-Based Diffusion as Generative Particle Models

abstract: In high-stakes domains such as legal, banking, hiring, and healthcare, learning models frequently rely on sensitive user information for inference, necessitating the complete set of features. This not only poses significant privacy risks for individuals but also demands substantial human effort from organizations to verify information accuracy. This study asks whether it is necessary to use all input features for accurate predictions at inference time. The paper demonstrates that, in a personalized setting, individuals may only need to disclose a small subset of features without compromising decision-making accuracy. The paper also provides an efficient sequential algorithm to determine the appropriate attributes for each individual to provide. Evaluations across various learning tasks show that individuals can potentially report as little as 10\% of their information while maintaining the same accuracy level as a model that employs the full set of user information.

paragraphs: Prediction systems in areas such as banking, hiring, healthcare, and legal decision-making often request a complete set of personal features. Collecting those features creates privacy exposure for individuals and work for organizations that must verify the information. This paper asks whether accurate predictions actually require every feature from every person at inference time.

The proposed approach personalizes which information an individual needs to disclose. Instead of treating the full feature set as a universal requirement, an efficient sequential algorithm determines appropriate attributes for each person. The central result is that, in a personalized setting, a small subset of features may be enough to preserve decision-making accuracy.

Across the evaluated learning tasks, individuals can potentially provide as little as ten percent of their information while retaining the accuracy of a model using the full set. This is a reported possibility, rather than a guaranteed disclosure level for every person or task. The contribution connects prediction accuracy to selective information collection, showing why inference-time data requirements can be reconsidered at the individual level.
summary.tldr: Personalized feature selection can let individuals disclose substantially less information while preserving prediction accuracy in evaluated settings.

title: Data Minimization at Inference Time

abstract: We study learning-based approaches to semantic route planning, which concerns producing routes in response to rich queries that specify various criteria and preferences. Semantic routing is already widely found in industry applications, especially navigational services like Google Maps; however, existing implementations only support limited route criteria and narrow query sets as they rely on repurposing classical route optimization algorithms. We argue for a learning-based approach to semantic routing as a more scalable and general alternative. To foster interest in this important application of graph learning, we are releasing a large-scale publicly-licensed benchmark for semantic routing consisting of real-world multi-objective navigation problems---expressed via natural language queries---on the richly annotated road networks of US cities. In addition to being intractable with existing approaches to semantic routing, our benchmark poses a significant scaling challenge for graph learning methods. As a proof-of-concept, we show that---at scale---even a standard transformer network is a powerful semantic routing system and achieves non-trivial performance on our benchmark. In the process, we demonstrate a simple solution to the challenge of scaling up graph learning: an autoregressive approach that decomposes semantic routing into smaller ``next-edge'' prediction problems.

paragraphs: Semantic routing asks for routes that satisfy rich requests containing multiple criteria and preferences. Existing implementations adapt classical route optimization algorithms and consequently support limited criteria and query types. This paper argues that learning-based routing offers a more scalable and general way to respond to such requests.

The authors release a large, publicly licensed benchmark built from annotated road networks in US cities. Its navigation problems express multiple objectives through natural-language queries. The benchmark challenges existing semantic-routing approaches and also creates a scaling problem for graph learning: a system must handle rich requests over large, structured road networks.

Their proof of concept uses a standard transformer with an autoregressive formulation. It breaks route generation into a sequence of smaller predictions about the next edge, making the overall graph problem manageable through repeated local prediction tasks. At scale, the transformer achieves non-trivial benchmark performance. The result establishes a promising learning-based approach while presenting its demonstrated capability as a proof of concept.
summary.tldr: A semantic-routing benchmark and transformer proof of concept show how next-edge prediction can tackle routes specified by rich natural-language requests.

title: Semantic Routing via Autoregressive Modeling

abstract: Tokenizer, serving as a translator to map the intricate visual data into a compact latent space, lies at the core of visual generative models. Based on the finding that existing tokenizers are tailored to either image or video inputs, this paper presents OmniTokenizer, a transformer-based tokenizer for joint image and video tokenization. OmniTokenizer is designed with a spatial-temporal decoupled architecture, which integrates window attention and causal attention for spatial and temporal modeling, respectively. To exploit the complementary nature of image and video data, we further propose a progressive training strategy, where OmniTokenizer is first trained on image data on a fixed resolution to develop the spatial encoding capacity and then jointly trained on image and video data on multiple resolutions to learn the temporal dynamics. OmniTokenizer, for the first time, handles both image and video inputs within a unified framework and proves the possibility of realizing their synergy. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OmniTokenizer achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) reconstruction performance on various image and video datasets, e.g., 1.11 reconstruction FID on ImageNet and 42 reconstruction FVD on UCF-101, beating the previous SOTA methods by 13% and 26%, respectively. Additionally, we also show that when integrated with OmniTokenizer, both language model-based approaches and diffusion models can realize advanced visual synthesis performance, underscoring the superiority and versatility of our method.

paragraphs: Visual tokenizers translate images or videos into compact representations for generative models. OmniTokenizer provides one transformer-based framework for both input types, addressing the separation between existing image and video tokenizers. The goal is to let spatial information from images and temporal information from videos contribute to a shared representation system.

Its architecture separates spatial and temporal modeling, using window attention for space and causal attention for time. Training also proceeds in stages. The tokenizer first learns spatial encoding from images at a fixed resolution, then trains jointly on images and videos at multiple resolutions to learn temporal dynamics and exploit their complementary information.

These improve on previous leading results by 13% and 26%, respectively. Integration with both language-model-based generators and diffusion models also produces strong visual synthesis results. The findings support a common tokenizer as a useful component across multiple visual generation approaches.
summary.tldr: OmniTokenizer jointly encodes images and videos using separated spatial-temporal attention and progressive training, achieving strong reconstruction and generation results.

title: OmniTokenizer: A Joint Image-Video Tokenizer for Visual Generation

abstract: Modern machine learning models deployed often encounter distribution shifts in real-world applications, manifesting as covariate or semantic out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts. These shifts give rise to challenges in OOD generalization and OOD detection. This paper introduces a novel, integrated approach AHA (Adaptive Human-Assisted OOD learning) to simultaneously address both OOD generalization and detection through a human-assisted framework by labeling data in the wild. Our approach strategically labels examples within a novel maximum disambiguation region, where the number of semantic and covariate OOD data roughly equalizes. By labeling within this region, we can maximally disambiguate the two types of OOD data, thereby maximizing the utility of the fixed labeling budget. Our algorithm first utilizes a noisy binary search algorithm that identifies the maximal disambiguation region with high probability. The algorithm then continues with annotating inside the identified labeling region, reaping the full benefit of human feedback. Extensive experiments validate the efficacy of our framework. We observed that with only a few hundred human annotations, our method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods that do not involve human assistance, in both OOD generalization and OOD detection.

paragraphs: Deployed models encounter unfamiliar data for different reasons. Covariate shifts change the input distribution, while semantic shifts introduce unfamiliar meaning or categories. AHA addresses both the challenge of generalizing under distribution changes and the challenge of detecting out-of-distribution examples, using a limited amount of human labeling.

Its central decision is where to spend that labeling budget. The method targets a region where semantic and covariate out-of-distribution examples occur in roughly equal numbers. The authors identify this as a maximum disambiguation region: labels obtained there are especially useful for distinguishing the two kinds of shift. A noisy binary search locates the region with high probability, after which annotation continues inside it.

Experiments show that a few hundred human annotations yield significant improvements in both generalization and detection over state-of-the-art methods without human assistance. The finding supports targeted human feedback as a way to address two related deployment problems together. The comparison specifically includes the added information supplied by people, with the algorithm determining which examples make that information most useful.
summary.tldr: AHA strategically requests human labels to improve both generalization under distribution shifts and detection of unfamiliar data.

title: AHA: Human-Assisted Out-of-Distribution Generalization and Detection

abstract: Autoregressively trained transformers have brought a profound revolution to the world, especially with their in-context learning (ICL) ability to address downstream tasks. Recently, several studies suggest that transformers learn a mesa-optimizer during autoregressive (AR) pretraining to implement ICL. Namely, the forward pass of the trained transformer is equivalent to optimizing an inner objective function in-context.However, whether the practical non-convex training dynamics will converge to the ideal mesa-optimizer is still unclear.Towards filling this gap, we investigate the non-convex dynamics of a one-layer linear causal self-attention model autoregressively trained by gradient flow, where the sequences are generated by an AR process $x_{t+1} = W x_t$. First, under a certain condition of data distribution, we prove that an autoregressively trained transformer learns $W$ by implementing one step of gradient descent to minimize an ordinary least squares (OLS) problem in-context. It then applies the learned $\widehat{W}$ for next-token prediction, thereby verifying the mesa-optimization hypothesis. Next, under the same data conditions, we explore the capability limitations of the obtained mesa-optimizer. We show that a stronger assumption related to the moments of data is the sufficient and necessary condition that the learned mesa-optimizer recovers the distribution. Besides, we conduct exploratory analyses beyond the first data condition and prove that generally, the trained transformer will not perform vanilla gradient descent for the OLS problem. Finally, our simulation results verify the theoretical results.

paragraphs: The paper examines whether training a transformer to predict the next item in a sequence can make it learn an optimization procedure that runs inside its forward pass. This is the mesa-optimization explanation of in-context learning: the trained model uses the current context to solve an inner learning problem. The authors investigate whether this behavior emerges from non-convex training dynamics.

Their analysis concerns a one-layer linear causal self-attention model trained through gradient flow on sequences following the rule x_{t+1} = W x_t. Under a particular condition on the data distribution, they prove that the model implements one gradient-descent step on an ordinary least-squares problem within the context. It then uses the resulting estimate of W to predict the next item. This establishes the proposed mechanism within the stated setting.

Learning this optimization procedure does not by itself establish distribution recovery. Under the same initial data condition, the authors identify a stronger condition involving data moments that is both necessary and sufficient for recovery. Beyond the initial condition, their exploratory analysis shows that the trained model generally does not implement ordinary gradient descent on that least-squares problem. Simulations support the theoretical findings.
summary.tldr: Under specified data conditions, a simplified autoregressively trained transformer learns an internal gradient-descent step, while distribution recovery requires a stronger condition.

title: On Mesa-Optimization in Autoregressively Trained Transformers: Emergence and Capability

abstract: Image restoration (IR) in real-world scenarios presents significant challenges due to the lack of high-capacity models and comprehensive datasets.To tackle these issues, we present a dual strategy: GenIR, an innovative data curation pipeline, and DreamClear, a cutting-edge Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based image restoration model.**GenIR**, our pioneering contribution, is a dual-prompt learning pipeline that overcomes the limitations of existing datasets, which typically comprise only a few thousand images and thus offer limited generalizability for larger models. GenIR streamlines the process into three stages: image-text pair construction, dual-prompt based fine-tuning, and data generation \& filtering. This approach circumvents the laborious data crawling process, ensuring copyright compliance and providing a cost-effective, privacy-safe solution for IR dataset construction. The result is a large-scale dataset of one million high-quality images.Our second contribution, **DreamClear**, is a DiT-based image restoration model. It utilizes the generative priors of text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models and the robust perceptual capabilities of multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) to achieve photorealistic restoration. To boost the model's adaptability to diverse real-world degradations, we introduce the Mixture of Adaptive Modulator (MoAM). It employs token-wise degradation priors to dynamically integrate various restoration experts, thereby expanding the range of degradations the model can address.Our exhaustive experiments confirm DreamClear's superior performance, underlining the efficacy of our dual strategy for real-world image restoration. Code and pre-trained models are available at: https://github.com/shallowdream204/DreamClear.

paragraphs: DreamClear addresses two connected obstacles in real-world image restoration: insufficient model capacity and limited training datasets. The paper proposes both a data creation pipeline, GenIR, and a restoration model based on a Diffusion Transformer. The motivation is that larger restoration models need broader training material than datasets containing only a few thousand images can provide.

GenIR constructs image-text pairs, performs dual-prompt fine-tuning, and then generates and filters data. It produces one million high-quality images. The authors present this pipeline as a cost-effective, privacy-safe and copyright-compliant approach that avoids laborious data crawling. Its role is to supply the scale of training material needed by the accompanying restoration approach.

DreamClear combines the generative knowledge of text-to-image diffusion models with the perceptual capabilities of multimodal language models. Its Mixture of Adaptive Modulator uses degradation information for individual tokens to dynamically combine restoration experts, helping it address varied image damage. The reported experiments find superior restoration performance, supporting the combined strategy of expanding the dataset and making the model adaptive to different degradations.
summary.tldr: DreamClear pairs a million-image generation pipeline with an adaptive diffusion transformer to improve real-world image restoration.

title: DreamClear: High-Capacity Real-World Image Restoration with Privacy-Safe Dataset Curation

abstract: Neural Collapse (NC) was a recently discovered phenomenon that the output features and the classifier weights of the neural network converge to optimal geometric structures at the Terminal Phase of Training (TPT) under various losses. However, the relationship between these optimal structures at TPT and the classification performance remains elusive, especially in imbalanced learning. Even though it is noticed that fixing the classifier to an optimal structure can mitigate the minority collapse problem, the performance is still not comparable to the classical imbalanced learning methods with a learnable classifier. In this work, we find that the optimal structure can be designed to represent a better classification rule, and thus achieve better performance. In particular, we justify that, to achieve better classification, the features from the minor classes should align with more directions. This justification then yields a decision rule called the Generalized Classification Rule (GCR) and we also term these directions as the centers of the classes. Then we study the NC under an MSE-type loss via the Unconstrained Features Model (UFM) framework where (1) the features from a class tend to collapse to the mean of the corresponding centers of that class (named Neural Collapse to Multiple Centers (NCMC)) at the global optimum, and (2) the original classifier approximates a surrogate to GCR when NCMC occurs. Based on the analysis, we develop a strategy for determining the number of centers and propose a Cosine Loss function for the fixed classifier that induces NCMC. Our experiments have shown that the Cosine Loss can induce NCMC and has performance on long-tail classification comparable to the classical imbalanced learning methods.
originalAbstract: Neural Collapse (NC) was a recently discovered phenomenon that the output features and the classifier weights of the neural network converge to optimal geometric structures at the Terminal Phase of Training (TPT) under various losses. However, the relationship between these optimal structures at TPT and the classification performance remains elusive, especially in imbalanced learning. Even though it is noticed that fixing the classifier to an optimal structure can mitigate the minority collapse problem, the performance is still not comparable to the classical imbalanced learning methods with a learnable classifier. In this work, we find that the optimal structure can be designed to represent a better classification rule, and thus achieve better performance. In particular, we justify that, to achieve better classification, the features from the minor classes should align with more directions. This justification then yields a decision rule called the Generalized Classification Rule (GCR) and we also term these directions as the centers of the classes. Then we study the NC under an MSE-type loss via the Unconstrained Features Model (UFM) framework where (1) the features from a class tend to collapse to the mean of the corresponding centers of that class (named Neural Collapse to Multiple Centers (NCMC)) at the global optimum, and (2) the original classifier approximates a surrogate to GCR when NCMC occurs. Based on the analysis, we develop a strategy for determining the number of centers and propose a Cosine Loss function for the fixed classifier that induces NCMC. Our experiments have shown that the Cosine Loss can induce NCMC and has performance on long-tail classification comparable to the classical imbalanced learning methods.

paragraphs: Neural collapse describes geometric organization of learned features and classifier weights near the end of training. For imbalanced data, imposing an optimal geometry can reduce minority collapse without matching established methods that learn their classifiers. This paper asks whether a different geometry can encode a better classification rule.

The authors justify assigning minority classes more directions, called centers, and derive a Generalized Classification Rule from this idea. Under an MSE-type loss in the Unconstrained Features Model, they show that features from a class tend to collapse to the mean of its assigned centers at the global optimum. When this occurs, the original classifier approximates a surrogate for the proposed rule.

They use the analysis to develop a strategy for choosing center counts and a Cosine Loss for a fixed classifier. Experiments show that this loss can induce the proposed multiple-center collapse and achieve long-tail classification performance comparable to classical imbalance-learning methods. The work links a specific feature geometry to a practical classification strategy.
summary.tldr: Assigning multiple centers to classes yields a new collapse geometry and a fixed-classifier training method competitive on long-tail classification.

title: Neural Collapse To Multiple Centers For Imbalanced Data

abstract: Quantization of large language models (LLMs) faces significant challenges, particularly due to the presence of outlier activations that impede efficient low-bit representation. Traditional approaches predominantly address Normal Outliers, which are activations across all tokens with relatively large magnitudes. However, these methods struggle with smoothing Massive Outliers that display significantly larger values, which leads to significant performance degradation in low-bit quantization. In this paper, we introduce DuQuant, a novel approach that utilizes rotation and permutation transformations to more effectively mitigate both massive and normal outliers. First, DuQuant starts by constructing the rotation matrix, using specific outlier dimensions as prior knowledge, to redistribute outliers to adjacent channels by block-wise rotation. Second, We further employ a zigzag permutation to balance the distribution of outliers across blocks, thereby reducing block-wise variance. A subsequent rotation further smooths the activation landscape, enhancing model performance. DuQuant simplifies the quantization process and excels in managing outliers, outperforming the state-of-the-art baselines across various sizes and types of LLMs on multiple tasks, even with 4-bit weight-activation quantization. Our code is available at https://github.com/Hsu1023/DuQuant.

paragraphs: Low-bit quantization represents a language model's numerical values with fewer bits, but unusually large activations make that representation difficult. The paper distinguishes ordinary large activations from much more extreme massive outliers. Existing approaches mainly address the former and can lose substantial performance when the latter remain poorly controlled.

DuQuant redistributes these activations through a sequence of transformations. It first builds a rotation using known outlier dimensions and applies it within blocks, spreading outliers into neighboring channels. A zigzag permutation then balances the outlier distribution across blocks, reducing differences between them. A further rotation smooths the activations again before quantization.

The reported evaluations span multiple tasks and language models of different types and sizes. DuQuant outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods, including when both weights and activations use four-bit quantization. The findings support addressing outliers at two levels: their concentration within a block and their uneven distribution across blocks. This provides a concrete explanation for why the combination of rotations and permutation improves the quantized models.
summary.tldr: DuQuant combines block rotations and a balancing permutation to redistribute activation outliers and improve low-bit language models.

title: DuQuant: Distributing Outliers via Dual Transformation Makes Stronger Quantized LLMs

abstract: The poor performance of transformers on arithmetic tasks seems to stem in large part from their inability to keep track of the exact position of each digit inside of a large span of digits. We mend this problem by adding an embedding to each digit that encodes its position relative to the start of the number. In addition to the boost these embeddings provide on their own, we show that this fix enables architectural modifications such as input injection and recurrent layers to improve performance even further.With positions resolved, we can study the logical extrapolation ability of transformers. Can they solve arithmetic problems that are larger and more complex than those in their training data? We find that training on only 20 digit numbers with a single GPU for one day, we can reach state-of-the-art performance, achieving up to 99% accuracy on 100 digit addition problems. Finally, we show that these gains in numeracy also unlock improvements on other multi-step reasoning tasks including sorting and multiplication.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why transformers struggle with arithmetic involving long numbers. Their intervention adds an embedding to every digit that records its position relative to the beginning of that number.

These embeddings improve performance on their own and also enable further gains from input injection and recurrent layers. With digit positions made explicit, the authors examine logical extrapolation: whether a model can solve arithmetic problems larger and more complex than those encountered during training. This makes the representation of numbers central to the study of generalization.

They also find improvements in sorting and multiplication. The results demonstrate strong extrapolation in the studied tasks and support the view that resolving digit positions can unlock both arithmetic gains and benefits from architectural changes.
summary.tldr: Explicit digit-position embeddings help transformers extrapolate from 20-digit training numbers to 100-digit addition, reaching up to 99% accuracy.

title: Transformers Can Do Arithmetic with the Right Embeddings

abstract: Inverse rendering methods have achieved remarkable performance in reconstructing high-fidelity 3D objects with disentangled geometries, materials, and environmental light. However, they still face huge challenges in reflective surface reconstruction. Although recent methods model the light trace to learn specularity, the ignorance of indirect illumination makes it hard to handle inter-reflections among multiple smooth objects. In this work, we propose Ref-MC2 that introduces the multi-time Monte Carlo sampling which comprehensively computes the environmental illumination and meanwhile considers the reflective light from object surfaces. To address the computation challenge as the times of Monte Carlo sampling grow, we propose a specularity-adaptive sampling strategy, significantly reducing the computational complexity. Besides the computational resource, higher geometry accuracy is also required because geometric errors accumulate multiple times. Therefore, we further introduce a reflection-aware surface model to initialize the geometry and refine it during inverse rendering. We construct a challenging dataset containing scenes with multiple objects and inter-reflections. Experiments show that our method outperforms other inverse rendering methods on various object groups. We also show downstream applications, e.g., relighting and material editing, to illustrate the disentanglement ability of our method.

paragraphs: Inverse rendering attempts to recover geometry, materials, and illumination separately from images. Reflective objects complicate this separation because their appearance includes light reflected from other surfaces. Methods that neglect indirect illumination can therefore struggle with scenes containing several smooth objects whose reflections interact.

Ref-MC2 uses repeated Monte Carlo sampling to account for both environmental illumination and light reflected from object surfaces. Because additional sampling increases computation, a specularity-adaptive strategy reduces the computational burden. The method also addresses geometry: errors can accumulate across repeated reflections, so a reflection-aware surface model initializes the geometry and refines it during inverse rendering.

The authors introduce a challenging dataset of multiple objects with inter-reflections and report better results than other inverse-rendering methods across various object groups. Relighting and material-editing demonstrations illustrate the recovered separation of scene properties. The work connects illumination modeling, sampling efficiency, and geometric accuracy, showing why all three matter when reconstructing scenes in which objects visibly reflect one another.
summary.tldr: Ref-MC2 reconstructs mutually reflective objects using repeated light sampling, specularity-adaptive computation, and reflection-aware geometry refinement.

title: Multi-times Monte Carlo Rendering for Inter-reflection Reconstruction

abstract: In-context learning is an emergent paradigm in large language models (LLMs) that enables them to generalize to new tasks and domains by simply prompting these models with a few exemplars without explicit parameter updates. Many attempts have been made to understand in-context learning in LLMs as a function of model scale, pretraining data, and other factors. In this work, we propose a new mechanism to probe and understand in-context learning from the lens of decision boundaries for in-context binary classification. Decision boundaries are straightforward to visualize and provide important information about the qualitative behavior of the inductive biases of standard classifiers. To our surprise, we find that the decision boundaries learned by current LLMs in simple binary classification tasks are often irregularly non-smooth, regardless of task linearity. This paper investigates the factors influencing these decision boundaries and explores methods to enhance their generalizability. We assess various approaches, including training-free and fine-tuning methods for LLMs, the impact of model architecture, and the effectiveness of active prompting techniques for smoothing decision boundaries in a data-efficient manner. Our findings provide a deeper understanding of in-context learning dynamics and offer practical improvements for enhancing robustness and generalizability of in-context learning.
