paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model respond to a new task using examples in its prompt, without updating its parameters. This paper studies that behavior through binary classification decision boundaries: the dividing regions where the model switches from predicting one class to the other. These boundaries make aspects of the model's learned behavior visible.

The authors find that current language models often produce irregular, nonsmooth boundaries on simple classification tasks, including linear ones. This observation reveals behavior that a single accuracy score may not describe: the model's classification rule can have an uneven shape even when the task admits a simple relationship between inputs and labels.

The study investigates factors affecting these boundaries and ways to improve their generalization. It assesses methods with and without fine-tuning, architectural differences, and active prompting techniques intended to smooth boundaries using data efficiently. The findings offer a way to inspect in-context learning and provide practical improvements for robustness and generalizability, with the reported irregularity framed as a frequent observation rather than a universal property.
summary.tldr: Decision-boundary probes reveal frequent irregularities in in-context classification and help investigate methods for improving its generalization.

title: Probing the Decision Boundaries of In-context Learning in Large Language Models

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) exhibit a surprising structure in their final layer known as neural collapse (NC), and a growing body of works is currently investigated the propagation of neural collapse to earlier layers of DNNs -- a phenomenon called deep neural collapse (DNC). However, existing theoretical results are restricted to either linear models, the last two layers or binary classification. In contrast, we focus on non-linear models of arbitrary depth in multi-class classification and reveal a surprising qualitative shift. As soon as we go beyond two layers or two classes, DNC stops being optimal for the deep unconstrained features model (DUFM) -- the standard theoretical framework for the analysis of collapse. The main culprit is the low-rank bias of multi-layer regularization schemes. This bias leads to optimal solutions of even lower rank than the neural collapse. We support our theoretical findings with experiments on both DUFM and real data, which show the emergence of the low-rank structure in the solution found by gradient descent.

In contrast, we focus on non-linear models of arbitrary depth in multi-class classification and reveal a surprising qualitative shift. As soon as we go beyond two layers or two classes, DNC stops being optimal for the deep unconstrained features model (DUFM) -- the standard theoretical framework for the analysis of collapse. paragraphs: Neural collapse describes a structured arrangement that appears in the final layer of deep neural networks. Deep neural collapse asks whether this organization also extends to earlier layers. Previous theoretical analyses were restricted to linear models, the final two layers, or classification with two classes. This paper investigates nonlinear models of arbitrary depth in multiclass classification.

The authors work within the deep unconstrained features model, a standard theoretical framework for studying collapse. They find a qualitative change beyond the two-layer or two-class settings: deep neural collapse ceases to be optimal in that framework. The explanation is the low-rank bias introduced by regularization across multiple layers, which favors solutions with even lower rank than the collapse structure.

Experiments on the theoretical model and on real data support the analysis by showing low-rank structures in solutions found through gradient descent. The result challenges the idea that extending neural collapse through a network necessarily describes the preferred solution. It identifies multilayer regularization as a competing organizing force in the studied optimization setting.
summary.tldr: In the studied deep unconstrained features model, multilayer regularization favors lower-rank solutions over deep neural collapse beyond simpler settings.

title: Neural collapse vs. low-rank bias: Is deep neural collapse really optimal?

abstract: Gaussian processes (GPs) are widely used for regression and optimization tasks such as Bayesian optimization (BO) due to their expressiveness and principled uncertainty estimates. However, in settings with large datasets corrupted by outliers, standard GPs and their sparse approximations struggle with computational tractability and robustness. We introduce Robust Computation-aware Gaussian Process (RCaGP), a novel GP model that jointly addresses these challenges by combining a principled treatment of approximation-induced uncertainty with robust generalized Bayesian updating. The key insight is that robustness and approximation-awareness are not orthogonal but intertwined: approximations can exacerbate the impact of outliers, and mitigating one without the other is insufficient. Unlike previous work that focuses narrowly on either robustness or approximation quality, RCaGP combines both in a principled and scalable framework, thus effectively managing both outliers and computational uncertainties introduced by approximations such as low-rank matrix multiplications. Our model ensures more conservative and reliable uncertainty estimates, a property we rigorously demonstrate. Additionally, we establish a robustness property and show that the mean function is key to preserving it, motivating a tailored model selection scheme for robust mean functions. Empirical results confirm that solving these challenges jointly leads to superior performance across both clean and outlier-contaminated settings, both on regression and high-throughput Bayesian optimization benchmarks.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes provide predictions with uncertainty estimates, but large datasets containing outliers create two interacting difficulties. Computation requires approximations, and those approximations can worsen the influence of unusual observations. The paper argues that handling outliers and handling approximation error separately is insufficient because each can affect the reliability of the other.

Robust Computation-aware Gaussian Process combines uncertainty about computational approximations with robust generalized Bayesian updating. summary.tldr: RCaGP jointly accounts for outliers and computational approximation uncertainty to improve Gaussian-process reliability and benchmark performance.

title: Robust and Computation-Aware Gaussian Processes

abstract: Long-Tailed Recognition (LTR) presents a significant challenge due to extreme class imbalance, where existing methods often struggle to balance performance across head and tail classes. Directly applying multi-objective optimization (MOO) to leverage multiple LTR strategies can be complex and unstable. To address this, we propose TS-MOF (Two-Stage Multi-Objective Fine-tuning), a novel framework that strategically decouples feature learning from classifier adaptation. After standard pre-training, TS-MOF freezes the feature backbone and focuses on an efficient multi-objective fine-tuning of specialized classifier heads. The core of TS-MOF's second stage lies in two innovations: Refined Performance Level Agreement for adaptive task weighting based on real-time per-class performance, and Robust Deterministic Projective Conflict Gradient for stable gradient conflict resolution and constructive fusion. This approach enables effective synergy between diverse LTR strategies, leading to significant and balanced performance improvements. Extensive experiments on CIFAR100-LT, ImageNet-LT, and iNaturalist 2018 demonstrate that TS-MOF achieves state-of-the-art results, particularly enhancing tail class accuracy (e.g., +3.3\% on CIFAR100-LT IR=100 tail) while improving head class performance, all within a remarkably short fine-tuning period of 20 epochs.

paragraphs: Long-tailed recognition involves classes with very different amounts of training data. TS-MOF separates representation learning from classifier adaptation to make that combination more manageable.

The findings support focused classifier adaptation as an efficient way to combine long-tailed recognition strategies without retraining the feature backbone.
summary.tldr: TS-MOF freezes pretrained features and coordinates classifier objectives to improve both common and rare class recognition.

title: TS-MOF: Two-Stage Multi-Objective Fine-tuning for Long-Tailed Recognition

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now pivotal in real-world applications. Model editing has emerged as a promising paradigm for efficiently modifying LLMs without full retraining. However, current editing approaches face significant limitations due to parameter drift, which stems from inconsistencies between newly edited knowledge and the model's existing knowledge. In sequential editing scenarios, cumulative drifts progressively lead to model collapse characterized by general capability degradation and balance between acquiring new knowledge and catastrophic forgetting of existing knowledge. Drawing inspiration from the hippocampal trisynaptic circuit for continual memorizing and forgetting, we propose a Hippocampal-like Sequential Editing (HSE) framework that designs the unlearning of obsolete knowledge, domain-specific knowledge update separation and replay for edited knowledge. Specifically, the HSE framework designs three core mechanisms: (1) Machine unlearning selectively erases outdated knowledge to facilitate integration of new information, (2) Fisher Information Matrix-guided parameter updates prevents cross-domain knowledge interference, and (3) Parameter replay consolidates long-term editing memory through lightweight and global replay of editing data in a parametric form. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that HSE achieves smaller generalization error bounds, more stable convergence and higher computational efficiency. Experimental results validate its effective balance between acquiring new knowledge and mitigating catastrophic forgetting, maintaining or even slightly enhancing general capabilities. In practical applications, experiments confirm its effectiveness in multi-domain hallucination mitigation, healthcare knowledge injecting, and societal bias reduction.

paragraphs: Repeatedly editing a language model can create conflicts between new information and existing knowledge. The resulting parameter drift can accumulate, degrading general capabilities and causing forgetting. HSE addresses this sequential-update problem through mechanisms inspired by the hippocampal circuit's roles in retaining and forgetting information.

The framework combines three operations. Machine unlearning selectively removes outdated knowledge before integrating replacements. Updates guided by the Fisher Information Matrix separate changes across knowledge domains to prevent interference. Parameter replay consolidates earlier edits through lightweight, global replay of editing information represented in parameter form. Together, these mechanisms address obsolete information, cross-domain interactions, and retention of previous updates.

The paper's theoretical analysis reports smaller generalization-error bounds, more stable convergence, and greater computational efficiency. Experiments show a balance between incorporating new knowledge and reducing catastrophic forgetting, while preserving or slightly improving general capabilities. Additional applications demonstrate effectiveness for reducing hallucinations across domains, incorporating healthcare knowledge, and reducing societal bias, supporting the framework's use for continued model maintenance.
summary.tldr: HSE combines selective unlearning, domain-aware updates, and parameter replay to stabilize repeated knowledge edits in language models.

title: Hippocampal-like Sequential Editing for Continual Knowledge Updates in Large Language Models

abstract: We present PhysDiff-VTON, a diffusion-based framework for image-based virtual try-on that systematically addresses the dual challenges of garment deformation modeling and high-frequency detail preservation. The core innovation lies in integrating physics-inspired mechanisms into the diffusion process: a pose-guided deformable warping module simulates fabric dynamics by predicting spatial offsets conditioned on human pose semantics, while wavelet-enhanced feature decomposition explicitly preserves texture fidelity through frequency-aware attention. Further enhancing generation quality, a novel sampling strategy optimizes the denoising trajectory via least action principles, enforcing temporal coherence, spatial smoothness, and multi-scale structural consistency. Comprehensive evaluations across multiple datasets demonstrate significant improvements in both geometric plausibility and perceptual quality compared to existing approaches. The framework establishes a new paradigm for synthesizing photorealistic try-on images that adhere to physical constraints while maintaining intricate garment details, advancing the practical applicability of diffusion models in fashion technology.

paragraphs: Virtual try-on must make clothing fit a person's pose while preserving fabric textures and other fine details. PhysDiff-VTON addresses both demands within a diffusion-based image-generation framework. Its design introduces physics-inspired mechanisms into garment deformation and the sequence of denoising steps used to create the final image.

A pose-guided warping module predicts spatial offsets from human pose information to simulate fabric dynamics. A separate wavelet-based decomposition supports attention to different frequency content, helping preserve detailed textures. The sampling strategy then optimizes the denoising trajectory using least-action principles, enforcing coherence across that trajectory, spatial smoothness, and structural consistency at multiple scales.

Evaluations across multiple datasets report significant gains in geometric plausibility and perceptual quality compared with existing approaches. These findings connect the framework's two concerns: plausible garment shape and faithful appearance. The physics-inspired treatment guides both how clothing features move and how the image is progressively generated, supporting more realistic try-on images without treating fine garment detail as a separate finishing step.
summary.tldr: PhysDiff-VTON combines pose-guided deformation, frequency-aware detail preservation, and physics-inspired diffusion sampling for more plausible virtual try-on.

title: PhysDiff-VTON: Cross-Domain Physics Modeling and Trajectory Optimization for Virtual Try-On

abstract: Effective robotic autonomy in unknown environments demands proactive exploration and precise understanding of both geometry and semantics. In this paper, we propose ActiveSGM, an active semantic mapping framework designed to predict the informativeness of potential observations before execution. Built upon a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) mapping backbone, our approach employs semantic and geometric uncertainty quantification, coupled with a sparse semantic representation, to guide exploration. By enabling robots to strategically select the most beneficial viewpoints, ActiveSGM efficiently enhances mapping completeness, accuracy, and robustness to noisy semantic data, ultimately supporting more adaptive scene exploration. Our experiments on the Replica and Matterport3D datasets highlight the effectiveness of ActiveSGM in active semantic mapping tasks.

paragraphs: ActiveSGM addresses how a robot should explore an unfamiliar environment while building a map that captures both geometry and semantic information. These goals are connected: deciding where to look next affects what the robot can learn about shapes and scene meaning. The framework therefore estimates the usefulness of possible observations before the robot executes them.

The mapping system uses a 3D Gaussian Splatting backbone. It combines estimates of geometric uncertainty and semantic uncertainty with a sparse semantic representation to guide exploration. These signals support selecting viewpoints expected to provide the most useful information. In this formulation, uncertainty is part of the decision process for acquiring new observations, connecting the current map's weaknesses to future exploration.

The authors report improvements in mapping completeness, accuracy, and resilience to noisy semantic data. Experiments on Replica and Matterport3D demonstrate the framework's effectiveness for active semantic mapping. The stated significance is more adaptive exploration: the robot's choices respond to what remains uncertain about both the physical structure and the semantic content of the environment.
summary.tldr: ActiveSGM uses geometric and semantic uncertainty to choose informative viewpoints and improve robotic mapping during exploration.

title: Understanding while Exploring: Semantics-driven Active Mapping

abstract: Recently, test-time scaling of Large Language Models (LLMs) has emerged as a practical alternative to parameter and data scaling. Reasoning tasks often require large-scale, RLVR-based LLMs, while more economical LLMs can handle simpler tasks. Routing an LLM tailored to *suitability* (*i.e.*, capability and cost) ensures usability and efficiency. We introduce LLMRec, which routes the most suitable LLM to the user query without pre-inference on the candidate LLM zoo. It pioneeringly reframes the LLM routing problem as a comprehensive recommendation system (RecSys) task. Our core insight is that an LLM's suitability for a query is a complex, latent signal equal to user-item preference. LLMRec systematically engineers features for candidate LLMs (intrinsic attributes and capability distributions), queries (general semantics and meta-dimensional info), and context (inference type, cost budgets). It also incorporates behavioral features to learn high-order interactions. LLMRec is designed to generalize to out-of-domain datasets and adapt to new LLMs as the model zoo evolves. We define the metric with the Pareto frontier under user-specified cost budgets. Across six datasets, LLMRec achieves an average cost reduction of over 38% while maintaining accuracy and consistently outperforming baselines in converging toward the Pareto frontier.

LLMRec treats this choice as a recommendation problem: the suitability of a model for a query is a hidden preference signal to be learned. It selects a candidate without first running inference on the candidate models.

The system combines model attributes and capability distributions with query meaning, additional query characteristics, and context such as inference type and budget. Behavioral features help it learn more complex interactions among these factors. Its design also targets unfamiliar datasets and newly added models, addressing the changing set of choices available to a routing system.

Evaluation considers the accuracy-cost Pareto frontier under user-specified budgets. Across six datasets, LLMRec reports an average cost reduction exceeding 38% while maintaining accuracy and outperforming baselines in approaching that frontier. The findings support learning which model suits each request as a practical way to reduce spending without sacrificing measured answer quality.
summary.tldr: LLMRec recommends a suitable language model for each query and budget, reporting over 38% average cost savings while maintaining accuracy.

title: Let the LLM Stick to Its Strengths: Learning to Route Economical LLM

abstract: Event cameras, with their capacity to provide high temporal resolution information between frames, are increasingly utilized for video frame interpolation (VFI) in challenging scenarios characterized by high-speed motion and significant occlusion. However, prevalent issues of blur and distortion within the keyframes and ground truth data used for training and inference in these demanding conditions are frequently overlooked. This oversight impedes the perceptual realism and multi-scene generalization capabilities of existing event-based VFI (E-VFI) methods when generating interpolated frames. Motivated by the observation that semantic-perceptual discrepancies between degraded and pristine images are considerably smaller than their image-level differences, we introduce EPA. This novel E-VFI framework diverges from approaches reliant on direct image-level supervision by constructing multilevel, degradation-insensitive semantic perceptual supervisory signals to enhance the perceptual realism and multi-scene generalization of the model's predictions. Specifically, EPA operates in two phases: it first employs a DINO-based perceptual extractor, a customized style adapter, and a reconstruction generator to derive multi-layered, degradation-insensitive semantic-perceptual features ($\mathcal{S}$). Second, a novel Bidirectional Event-Guided Alignment (BEGA) module utilizes deformable convolutions to align perceptual features from keyframes to ground truth with inter-frame temporal guidance extracted from event signals. By decoupling the learning process from direct image-level supervision, EPA enhances model robustness against degraded keyframes and unreliable ground truth information. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this approach yields interpolated frames more consistent with human perceptual preferences. *The code will be released upon acceptance.*

Its first phase combines a DINO-based perceptual extractor, a customized style adapter, and a reconstruction generator to obtain features at several levels that are relatively insensitive to degradation. These features provide the learning signals.

A second component, Bidirectional Event-Guided Alignment, uses event timing and deformable convolutions to align perceptual features between keyframes and target frames. This reduces dependence on direct image-level supervision and improves robustness to degraded inputs and unreliable targets. Experiments report interpolated frames that better match human perceptual preferences, supporting the use of semantic-perceptual learning signals when the available imagery is imperfect.
summary.tldr: EPA uses degradation-insensitive perceptual supervision and event-guided alignment to produce more perceptually realistic interpolated video frames.

title: EPA: Boosting Event-based Video Frame Interpolation with Perceptually Aligned Learning

abstract: We present Genesis, a unified world model for joint generation of multi-view driving videos and LiDAR sequences with spatio-temporal and cross-modal consistency. Genesis employs a two-stage architecture that integrates a DiT-based video diffusion model with 3D-VAE encoding, and a BEV-represented LiDAR generator with NeRF-based rendering and adaptive sampling. Both modalities are directly coupled through a shared condition input, enabling coherent evolution across visual and geometric domains. To guide the generation with structured semantics, we introduce DataCrafter, a captioning module built on vision-language models that provides scene-level and instance-level captions. Extensive experiments on the nuScenes benchmark demonstrate that Genesis achieves state-of-the-art performance across video and LiDAR metrics (FVD 16.95, FID 4.24, Chamfer 0.611), and benefits downstream tasks including segmentation and 3D detection, validating the semantic fidelity and practical utility of the synthetic data.

paragraphs: Genesis generates driving scenes in two forms together: videos from multiple viewpoints and sequences of LiDAR measurements. The objective is consistency across space, time, and sensor modalities. A generated scene therefore needs coherent visual and geometric evolution, so that the video and LiDAR describe compatible aspects of the same changing environment.

The system uses a two-stage architecture. Its video component combines a diffusion transformer with a three-dimensional variational autoencoder. Its LiDAR component uses a bird's-eye-view representation, neural radiance field rendering, and adaptive sampling. Shared conditioning directly connects the two modalities. A vision-language captioning module called DataCrafter supplies descriptions at both the scene and individual-instance levels to guide generation.

On nuScenes, the authors report state-of-the-art results across video and LiDAR metrics, including FVD of 16.95, FID of 4.24, and Chamfer of 0.611. They also find benefits for segmentation and three-dimensional detection. These downstream results support the practical value of the synthetic scenes alongside the reported improvements in generation quality.
summary.tldr: Genesis jointly generates driving videos and LiDAR sequences using shared conditioning to maintain spatial, temporal, and cross-modal consistency.

title: Genesis: Multimodal Driving Scene Generation with Spatio-Temporal and Cross-Modal Consistency

abstract: Cluster DAGs (C-DAGs) provide an abstraction of causal graphs in which nodes represent clusters of variables, and edges encode both cluster-level causal relationships and dependencies arisen from unobserved confounding. C-DAGs define an equivalence class of acyclic causal graphs that agree on cluster-level relationships, enabling causal reasoning at a higher level of abstraction. However, when the chosen clustering induces cycles in the resulting C-DAG, the partition is deemed inadmissible under conventional C-DAG semantics. In this work, we extend the C-DAG framework to support arbitrary variable clusterings by relaxing the partition admissibility constraint, thereby allowing cyclic C-DAG representations. We extend the notions of d-separation and causal calculus to this setting, significantly broadening the scope of causal reasoning across clusters and enabling the application of C-DAGs in previously intractable scenarios. Our calculus is both sound and atomically complete with respect to the do-calculus: all valid interventional queries at the cluster level can be derived using our rules, each corresponding to a primitive do-calculus step.

paragraphs: Cluster causal graphs group variables into larger units, allowing causal reasoning without specifying every relationship inside each group. They represent a class of underlying acyclic causal graphs that agree at the cluster level, including dependencies from unobserved confounding. Conventional rules reject a grouping if it creates cycles between clusters, restricting which abstractions can be used.

This paper relaxes that restriction and permits cyclic cluster-level representations for arbitrary variable groupings. The cycles arise in the clustered description; the framework still concerns classes of underlying acyclic causal graphs. The authors extend both d-separation and causal calculus so that reasoning can proceed with these more flexible abstractions.

The resulting calculus is sound and atomically complete relative to do-calculus. In the paper’s formulation, valid cluster-level interventional queries can be derived through rules corresponding to primitive do-calculus steps. This matters because users can choose meaningful variable groupings without having to discard them solely because aggregation creates a cycle, while retaining a formally justified calculus.
summary.tldr: The paper extends causal reasoning to arbitrary variable clusters, allowing cyclic cluster representations with a sound, atomically complete calculus.

title: Relaxing partition admissibility in Cluster-DAGs: a causal calculus with arbitrary variable clustering

abstract: LLM serving systems typically treat user prompts as monolithic inputs, optimizing inference through decoding tricks or inter-query batching. However, many real-world prompts contain *latent semantic parallelism*—decomposable structures where subtasks can be executed independently to reduce latency while preserving meaning.We introduce PARALLELPROMPT, the first benchmark for measuring intra-query parallelism in natural user prompts. Our dataset comprises over 37,000 real-world prompts from public LLM chat logs, each annotated with a structured schema capturing task templates, shared context, and iteration inputs. These schemas are extracted using LLM-assisted prompting with rule-based multilingual validation.To evaluate the benefits of decomposition, we provide an execution suite that benchmarks serial vs. parallel strategies, measuring latency, structural adherence, and semantic fidelity. Our results show that intra-query parallelism can be successfully parsed in over 75\% of curated datasets, unlocking up to *$5\times$ speedups* on tasks like translation, comprehension, and comparative analysis, with minimal quality degradation.By releasing this benchmark, curation pipeline, and evaluation suite, we provide the first standardized testbed for studying structure-aware execution in LLM serving pipelines.

paragraphs: A single user prompt can contain several independent tasks, yet language-model serving systems commonly process it as one unit. PARALLELPROMPT studies whether that internal structure can be extracted so the parts run concurrently. Its focus is parallel work within a query, complementing serving techniques that batch separate queries.

The benchmark contains more than 37,000 prompts from public chat logs. Each prompt has a structured description of its task template, shared context, and inputs to repeated operations. The authors obtain these descriptions through language-model-assisted prompting and rule-based multilingual validation. An accompanying execution suite compares serial and parallel strategies on latency, adherence to the requested structure, and preservation of meaning.

The results report successful extraction of internal parallelism in over 75% of the curated data and speedups reaching fivefold on tasks such as translation, comprehension, and comparative analysis, with minimal quality loss. These are task- and dataset-dependent findings. The released benchmark, curation pipeline, and evaluation suite provide a common basis for studying when structure-aware execution delivers useful latency reductions.
summary.tldr: PARALLELPROMPT benchmarks splitting individual prompts into independent subtasks, reporting up to fivefold speedups with minimal quality degradation.

title: PARALLELPROMPT: Extracting Parallelism from Large Language Model Queries

abstract: Human intelligence effortlessly interprets visual scenes along a rich spectrum of semantic dimensions. However, existing approaches to language-grounded visual concept learning are limited to a few predefined primitive axes, such as color and shape, and are typically explored in synthetic datasets. In this work, we propose a scalable framework that adaptively identifies image-related concept axes and grounds visual concepts along these axes in real-world scenes. Leveraging a pretrained vision-language model and our universal prompting strategy, our framework identifies a diverse image-related axes without any prior knowledge. Our universal concept encoder adaptively binds visual features to the discovered axes without introducing additional model parameters for each concept. To ground visual concepts along the discovered axes, we optimize a compositional anchoring objective, which ensures that each axis can be independently manipulated without affecting others. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on subsets of ImageNet, CelebA-HQ, and AFHQ, showcasing superior editing capabilities across diverse real-world concepts that are too varied to be manually predefined. Our method also exhibits strong compositional generalization, outperforming existing visual concept learning and text-based editing methods. The code is available at https://github.com/whieya/Language-grounded-VCL.

paragraphs: Visual concept learning often begins with a short, predefined list of attributes, such as color or shape. This paper addresses the richer variety found in real images by developing a framework that discovers relevant semantic axes and connects visual concepts to them, instead of requiring those axes to be specified beforehand.

A pretrained vision-language model and a universal prompting strategy identify image-related axes without prior knowledge of which axes to use. A shared concept encoder then connects visual features to the discovered axes without adding parameters for every concept. The compositional anchoring objective is designed to make each axis independently controllable while leaving other axes unaffected.

Evaluations on subsets of ImageNet, CelebA-HQ, and AFHQ report improved editing across diverse real-world concepts. The framework also shows strong compositional generalization and outperforms existing concept-learning and text-based editing methods. These findings support the value of discovering and organizing concepts adaptively when a fixed, manually chosen attribute vocabulary cannot cover the available visual variety.
summary.tldr: The framework discovers semantic axes in real images and learns independently controllable visual concepts without adding parameters per concept.

title: Bridging the gap to real-world language-grounded visual concept learning

abstract: The sequential nature of modern LLMs makes them expensive and slow, and speculative sam- pling has proven to be an effective solution to this problem. Methods like EAGLE perform autoregression at the feature level, reusing top- layer features from the target model to achieve better results than vanilla speculative sampling. A growing trend in the LLM community is scaling up training data to improve model intelligence without increasing inference costs. However, we observe that scaling up data provides limited improvements for EAGLE. We identify that this limitation arises from EAGLE’s feature prediction constraints. In this paper, we introduce EAGLE-3, which abandons feature prediction in favor of direct token prediction and replaces reliance on top-layer features with multi-layer feature fusion via a technique named training-time test. These improvements significantly enhance performance and enable the draft model to fully benefit from scaling up training data. Our experiments include both chat models and reasoning models, evaluated on five tasks. The results show that EAGLE-3 achieves a speedup ratio up to 6.5x, with about 1.4x improvement over EAGLE-2. In the SGLang framework, EAGLE- 3 achieves a 1.38x throughput improvement at a batch size of 64.

EAGLE accelerates this process through speculative sampling that reuses features from the target model. summary.tldr: EAGLE-3 combines direct token prediction with features from multiple layers to improve speculative inference and benefit from more training data.

title: EAGLE-3: Scaling up Inference Acceleration of Large Language Models via Training-Time Test

abstract: Graph Transformers (GTs) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for graph representation learning due to their ability to model diverse node interactions. However, existing GTs often rely on intricate architectural designs tailored to specific interactions, limiting their flexibly. To address this, we propose a unified hierarchical mask framework that reveals an underlying equivalence between model architecture and attention mask construction. This framework enables a consistent modeling paradigm by capturing diverse interactions through carefully designed attention masks. Theoretical analysis under this framework demonstrates that the probability of correct classification positively correlates with the receptive field size and label consistency, leading to a fundamental design principle: An effective attention mask should ensure both a sufficiently large receptive field and a high level of label consistency. While no single existing mask satisfies this principle across all scenarios, our analysis reveals that hierarchical masks offer complementary strengths—motivating their effective integration. Then, we introduce M$^3$Dphormer, a Mixture-of-Experts based Graph Transformer with Multi-Level Masking and Dual Attention Computation. M$^3$Dphormer incorporates three theoretically grounded hierarchical masks and employs a bi-level expert routing mechanism to adaptively integrate multi-level interaction information. To ensure scalability, we further introduce a dual attention computation scheme that dynamically switches between dense and sparse modes based on local mask sparsity. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that M$^3$Dphormer achieves state-of-the-art performance, validating the effectiveness of our unified framework and model design.

That perspective offers a common way to represent diverse node interactions without developing a separate intricate architecture for each interaction pattern.

The contribution connects a theoretical account of useful graph interactions to an adaptive model and a computation scheme that responds to the structure of its masks.
summary.tldr: M³Dphormer combines complementary attention masks and adaptive computation to improve graph Transformer performance.

title: Unifying and Enhancing Graph Transformers via a Hierarchical Mask Framework

abstract: We present MaskWM, a simple, efficient, and flexible framework for image watermarking. MaskWM has two variants: (1) MaskWM-D, which supports global watermark embedding, watermark localization, and local watermark extraction for applications such as tamper detection; (2) MaskWM-ED, which focuses on local watermark embedding and extraction, offering enhanced robustness in small regions to support fine-grined image protection. MaskWM-D builds on the classical encoder-distortion layer-decoder training paradigm. In MaskWM-D, we introduce a simple masking mechanism during the decoding stage that enables both global and local watermark extraction. During training, the decoder is guided by various types of masks applied to watermarked images before extraction, helping it learn to localize watermarks and extract them from the corresponding local areas. MaskWM-ED extends this design by incorporating the mask into the encoding stage as well, guiding the encoder to embed the watermark in designated local regions, which improves robustness under regional attacks. Extensive experiments show that MaskWM achieves state-of-the-art performance in global and local watermark extraction, watermark localization, and multi-watermark embedding. It outperforms all existing baselines, including the recent leading model WAM for local watermarking, while preserving high visual quality of the watermarked images. In addition, MaskWM is highly efficient and adaptable. It requires only 20 hours of training on a single A6000 GPU, achieving 15× computational efficiency compared to WAM. By simply adjusting the distortion layer, MaskWM can be quickly fine-tuned to meet varying robustness requirements.

Its two variants support different needs: MaskWM-D embeds globally and enables local extraction, while MaskWM-ED embeds and extracts within designated areas.

MaskWM-D follows an encoder, distortion layer, and decoder training design. Before extraction, different masks are applied to watermarked images, teaching the decoder to locate marks and recover them from local areas. MaskWM-ED also supplies the mask to the encoder, directing where the watermark is placed and improving robustness against regional attacks.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance in global and local extraction, localization, and multiple-watermark embedding while maintaining high visual quality. The authors report 20 hours of training on one A6000 GPU and 15-fold computational efficiency relative to WAM. They also describe adjusting the distortion layer to fine-tune robustness requirements. The result is a shared, adaptable framework for both whole-image watermarking and protection of smaller image regions.
summary.tldr: MaskWM uses training-time masks to enable efficient global and regional image watermarking, localization, and extraction.

title: Mask Image Watermarking

abstract: We address the open question of counterfactual identification for high-dimensional multivariate outcomes from observational data. Pearl (2000) argues that counterfactuals must be identifiable (i.e., recoverable from the observed data distribution) to justify causal claims. A recent line of work on counterfactual inference shows promising results but lacks identification, undermining the causal validity of its estimates. To address this, we establish a foundation for multivariate counterfactual identification using continuous-time flows, including non-Markovian settings under standard criteria. We characterise the conditions under which flow matching yields a unique, monotone and rank-preserving counterfactual transport map with tools from dynamic optimal transport, ensuring consistent inference. Building on this, we validate the theory in controlled scenarios with counterfactual ground-truth and demonstrate improvements in axiomatic counterfactual soundness on real images.

A recent line of work on counterfactual inference shows promising results but lacks identification, undermining the causal validity of its estimates. To address this, we establish a foundation for multivariate counterfactual identification using continuous-time flows, including non-Markovian settings under standard criteria. We characterise the conditions under which flow matching yields a unique, monotone and rank-preserving counterfactual transport map with tools from dynamic optimal transport, ensuring consistent inference. paragraphs: Counterfactual inference asks what an outcome would have been under a different condition. For high-dimensional outcomes, producing a convincing alternative is only part of the challenge: the counterfactual must also be recoverable from the observed data distribution to justify the causal interpretation. This paper develops theoretical foundations for that identification problem.

The approach represents changes through continuous-time flows and analyzes them using dynamic optimal transport. The authors characterize conditions under which flow matching produces a unique counterfactual transport map with monotonicity and rank-preservation properties. Their framework also includes non-Markovian settings under standard criteria. The identification claim depends on these conditions; it is not an unrestricted guarantee for arbitrary learned flows.

The theory is evaluated in controlled scenarios where true counterfactual outcomes are available for comparison. Experiments on real images additionally report improvements in adherence to counterfactual soundness axioms. These two forms of evidence serve different purposes: controlled cases check behavior against known answers, while the image results assess consistency with specified counterfactual principles. Together, they connect the identification analysis to practical inference.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes conditions under which continuous-time flows identify unique multivariate counterfactual maps from observational data.

title: Counterfactual Identifiability via Dynamic Optimal Transport

abstract: When some parameters of a constrained optimization problem (COP) are uncertain, this gives rise to a predict-then-optimize (PtO) problem, comprising two stages: the \textit{prediction} of the unknown parameters from contextual information and the subsequent \textit{optimization} using those predicted parameters. Decision-focused learning (DFL) implements the first stage by training a machine learning (ML) model to optimize the quality of the decisions made using the predicted parameters. When the predicted parameters occur in the constraints, they can lead to infeasible solutions. Therefore, it is important to simultaneously manage both feasibility and decision quality. We develop a DFL framework for predicting constraint parameters in a generic COP. While prior works typically assume that the underlying optimization problem is a linear program (LP) or integer LP (ILP), our approach makes no such assumption. We derive two novel loss functions based on maximum likelihood estimation (MLE): the first one penalizes infeasibility (by penalizing predicted parameters that lead to infeasible solutions), while the second one penalizes suboptimal decisions (by penalizing predicted parameters that make the true optimal solution infeasible). We introduce a single tunable parameter to form a weighted average of the two losses, allowing decision-makers to balance suboptimality and feasibility. We experimentally demonstrate that adjusting this parameter provides decision-makers control over this trade-off. Moreover, across several COP instances, we show that adjusting the tunable parameter allows a decision-maker to prioritize either suboptimality or feasibility, outperforming the performance of existing baselines in either objective.

Decision-focused learning trains the predictor according to the quality of the resulting decisions. When the predicted quantities appear in constraints, prediction errors can also make the chosen decision infeasible. This paper develops a framework that explicitly balances those two concerns.

The framework applies to generic constrained optimization problems without assuming they are linear or integer linear programs. It introduces two losses derived from maximum likelihood estimation. One penalizes predictions that produce infeasible solutions. The other penalizes predictions that exclude the true optimal solution, addressing a different failure: an inaccurate feasible region can rule out the best decision.

A single adjustable parameter combines the losses and lets a decision-maker emphasize feasibility or decision quality. Experiments across several constrained optimization instances demonstrate control over this trade-off. With suitable choices of the parameter, the method exceeds existing baselines on the prioritized objective. The result is a tunable approach to competing goals, rather than a claim that one setting simultaneously optimizes both.
summary.tldr: Two complementary training losses let prediction-driven optimization balance feasible decisions against decision quality.

title: Feasibility-Aware Decision-Focused Learning for Predicting Parameters in the Constraints

abstract: The modeling of samples of distributions is a major challenge since distributions do not form a vector space. While various approaches exist for univariate distributions, including transformations to a Hilbert space, far less is known about the multivariate case. We utilize a transformation approach to map multivariate distributions to a Hilbert space via a Wasserstein slicing method that is invertible. This approach combines functional data analysis tools, such as functional principal component analysis and modes of variation, with the facility to map back to interpretable distributions. We also provide convergence guarantees for the Hilbert space representations under a broad class of such transforms. The method is illustrated using joint systolic and diastolic blood pressure data.

paragraphs: Sometimes each observation in a dataset is an entire probability distribution rather than a single measurement. Analyzing variation between these observations is difficult because distributions do not form a vector space. Although transformation methods exist for distributions of one variable, the paper addresses the less developed case of distributions involving multiple variables.

The authors use an invertible Wasserstein slicing transformation to represent multivariate distributions in a Hilbert space, where functional data analysis tools can be applied. This enables techniques such as functional principal component analysis and the examination of modes of variation. Invertibility is central: patterns identified in the transformed space can be mapped back into distributions that retain an interpretable meaning.

The paper also establishes convergence guarantees for Hilbert space representations under a broad class of these transformations. An application to joint systolic and diastolic blood pressure distributions illustrates the method. The contribution connects a mathematically convenient representation with a route back to the original statistical objects, allowing variation to be studied without leaving the results solely in an abstract transformed space.
summary.tldr: An invertible Wasserstein slicing transform enables functional analysis of multivariate distributions and maps discovered patterns back into interpretable distributions.

title: Functional data analysis for multivariate distributions through Wasserstein slicing

abstract: We present an algorithm for minimizing a sum of functions that combines the computational efficiency of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with the second order curvature information leveraged by quasi-Newton methods. We unify these disparate approaches by maintaining an independent Hessian approximation for each contributing function in the sum. We maintain computational tractability and limit memory requirements even for high dimensional optimization problems by storing and manipulating these quadratic approximations in a shared, time evolving, low dimensional subspace. This algorithm contrasts with earlier stochastic second order techniques that treat the Hessian of each contributing function as a noisy approximation to the full Hessian, rather than as a target for direct estimation. Each update step requires only a single contributing function or minibatch evaluation (as in SGD), and each step is scaled using an approximate inverse Hessian and little to no adjustment of hyperparameters is required (as is typical for quasi-Newton methods). We experimentally demonstrate improved convergence on seven diverse optimization problems. The algorithm is released as open source Python and MATLAB packages.

paragraphs: The paper presents an optimizer for objectives written as sums of functions. It aims to combine the inexpensive updates of stochastic gradient descent with the curvature information used by quasi-Newton methods. Each update evaluates only one contributing function or minibatch, while an approximate inverse Hessian scales the update.

Earlier stochastic second-order approaches treated an individual function's Hessian as a noisy estimate of the whole objective's Hessian. Here, each component's curvature is itself a target for estimation. The resulting quadratic approximations are stored and manipulated within a shared low-dimensional subspace that evolves over time.

That shared representation is intended to control memory and computational demands even when the original optimization space is large. The method requires little or no hyperparameter adjustment, according to the abstract. Experiments report improved convergence across seven diverse optimization problems, and implementations are released in Python and MATLAB. These findings support the proposed combination of component-level curvature modeling and inexpensive incremental evaluation.
summary.tldr: The optimizer combines inexpensive stochastic updates with separate component-level curvature estimates stored in a shared evolving subspace.

title: Fast large-scale optimization by unifying stochastic gradient and quasi-Newton methods

abstract: Semi-supervised learning, which uses unlabeled data to help learn a discriminative model, is especially important for structured output problems, as considerably more effort is needed to label its multidimensional outputs versus standard single output problems. We propose a new max-margin framework for semi-supervised structured output learning, that allows the use of powerful discrete optimization algorithms and high order regularizers defined directly on model predictions for the unlabeled examples. We show that our framework is closely related to Posterior Regularization, and the two frameworks optimize special cases of the same objective. The new framework is instantiated on two image segmentation tasks, using both a graph regularizer and a cardinality regularizer. Experiments also demonstrate that this framework can utilize unlabeled data from a different source than the labeled data to significantly improve performance while saving labeling effort.

paragraphs: Structured prediction produces multidimensional outputs, making labeled examples more expensive to obtain than in single-output learning. This paper develops a semi-supervised framework that uses unlabeled examples to help train a discriminative model. Its goal is to make those examples useful through restrictions on the model's predictions, reducing the dependence on costly complete annotations.

The proposed framework uses a max-margin formulation and permits high-order regularizers defined directly on predictions for unlabeled data. It also supports powerful discrete optimization algorithms. The authors establish a connection with Posterior Regularization: both approaches optimize special cases of a common objective. This relationship places the new formulation alongside an existing way of incorporating constraints into learning.

The framework is instantiated on two image segmentation tasks with graph and cardinality regularizers. Experiments show that it can significantly improve performance using unlabeled data drawn from a different source than the labeled examples. In these applications, prediction-level regularization allows additional data to contribute useful information while saving labeling effort, even when the two data sources differ.
summary.tldr: A max-margin framework uses high-order regularization of unlabeled predictions to improve structured learning and reduce labeling effort.

title: High Order Regularization for Semi-Supervised Learning of Structured Output Problems

abstract: There has been a lot of recent interest in designing neural network models to estimate a distribution from a set of examples. We introduce a simple modification for autoencoder neural networks that yields powerful generative models. Our method masks the autoencoder’s parameters to respect autoregressive constraints: each input is reconstructed only from previous inputs in a given ordering. Constrained this way, the autoencoder outputs can be interpreted as a set of conditional probabilities, and their product, the full joint probability. We can also train a single network that can decompose the joint probability in multiple different orderings. Our simple framework can be applied to multiple architectures, including deep ones. Vectorized implementations, such as on GPUs, are simple and fast. Experiments demonstrate that this approach is competitive with state-of-the-art tractable distribution estimators. At test time, the method is significantly faster and scales better than other autoregressive estimators.

paragraphs: MADE turns an autoencoder into a model that assigns probabilities to complete inputs. The key change is to mask network parameters so that each input component is reconstructed using only earlier components in a chosen ordering. This restriction gives the network the dependency structure needed for an autoregressive probability model.

With those dependencies enforced, each output represents a conditional probability, and multiplying the conditionals gives the joint probability of the input. The authors also show how a single network can support multiple orderings. Their framework applies to several network architectures, including deep networks, so the construction is not tied to one shallow design.

The masking approach supports simple, fast vectorized implementations, including on GPUs. Experiments find it competitive with leading tractable distribution estimators, while test-time computation is significantly faster and scales better than other autoregressive estimators. The contribution is therefore both a probabilistic reinterpretation of a familiar network and an implementation approach with demonstrated computational advantages.
summary.tldr: MADE masks autoencoder connections to produce a fast autoregressive probability model with competitive density-estimation performance.

title: MADE: Masked Autoencoder for Distribution Estimation

abstract: We give faster algorithms and improved sample complexities for the fundamental problem of estimating the top eigenvector. Given an explicit matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$, we show how to compute an $\epsilon$-approximate top eigenvector of $A^TA$ in time $\tilde O\left( \left[\text{nnz}(A) + \frac{d \text{sr}(A)}{\text{gap}^2} \right] \cdot \log 1/\epsilon\right)$. Here $\text{nnz}(A)$ is the number of nonzeros in $A$, $\text{sr}(A)$ is the stable rank, and gap is the relative eigengap. We also consider an online setting in which, given a stream of i.i.d. samples from a distribution D with covariance matrix $\Sigma$ and a vector $x_0$ which is an $O(\text{gap})$ approximate top eigenvector for $\Sigma$, we show how to refine $x_0$ to an $\epsilon$ approximation using $O \left( \frac{\text{var}(\mathcal{D})}{\text{gap}-\epsilon}\right)$ samples from $\mathcal{D}$. Here $\text{var}(\mathcal{D})$ is a natural notion of variance. Combining our algorithm with previous work to initialize $x_0$, we obtain improved sample complexities and runtimes under a variety of assumptions on D. We achieve our results via a robust analysis of the classic shift-and-invert preconditioning method. This technique lets us reduce eigenvector computation to approximately solving a series of linear systems with fast stochastic gradient methods.

paragraphs: The paper improves algorithms for estimating a matrix’s top eigenvector. For an explicitly available matrix A, it computes an approximate top eigenvector of A transpose times A. The runtime depends on the number of nonzero entries, the dimension, stable rank, and relative eigenvalue gap, with logarithmic dependence on the inverse target error.

The main technique is a robust analysis of shift-and-invert preconditioning. It turns eigenvector computation into a sequence of approximately solved linear systems, which fast stochastic-gradient methods can handle. The analysis makes these approximate intermediate computations usable within the eigenvector algorithm and establishes the resulting runtime improvements.

The authors also study an online setting with independent, identically distributed samples from a distribution with a covariance matrix. Their refinement procedure assumes an initial vector already approximates the top eigenvector to a gap-dependent accuracy. Combining refinement with earlier initialization methods improves sample complexity and runtime under various distributional assumptions. Thus, the results cover both explicit matrices and sample-based estimation, while retaining the initialization and distribution conditions relevant to the online guarantees.
summary.tldr: Robust shift-and-invert analysis accelerates top-eigenvector estimation by reducing it to approximate linear-system solves.

title: Faster Eigenvector Computation via Shift-and-Invert Preconditioning

abstract: We consider online content recommendation with implicit feedback through pairwise comparisons, formalized as the so-called dueling bandit problem. We study the dueling bandit problem in the Condorcet winner setting, and consider two notions of regret: the more well-studied strong regret, which is 0 only when both arms pulled are the Condorcet winner; and the less well-studied weak regret, which is 0 if either arm pulled is the Condorcet winner. We propose a new algorithm for this problem, Winner Stays (WS), with variations for each kind of regret: WS for weak regret (WS-W) has expected cumulative weak regret that is $O(N^2)$, and $O(N\log(N))$ if arms have a total order; WS for strong regret (WS-S) has expected cumulative strong regret of $O(N^2 + N \log(T))$, and $O(N\log(N)+N\log(T))$ if arms have a total order. WS-W is the first dueling bandit algorithm with weak regret that is constant in time. WS is simple to compute, even for problems with many arms, and we demonstrate through numerical experiments on simulated and real data that WS has significantly smaller regret than existing algorithms in both the weak- and strong-regret settings.

paragraphs: Dueling bandits learn from pairwise comparisons, as when a recommendation system observes which of two items a user prefers. This paper assumes a Condorcet winner: an option that wins against each other option in pairwise preference. It distinguishes strong regret, which vanishes only when both selected options are the winner, from weak regret, which vanishes when either is.

The authors propose Winner Stays variants for both objectives. For N options, the weak-regret version has expected cumulative regret O(N²), improving to O(N log N) when the options have a total order. Crucially, these bounds do not grow with the number of rounds, T.

The strong-regret version adds an O(N log T) term to the corresponding bounds. Thus the two objectives lead to different time dependence even within the same algorithm family. Numerical experiments using simulated and real data report substantially smaller regret than existing algorithms in both settings, while the method remains computationally simple even with many options.
summary.tldr: Winner Stays achieves expected cumulative weak regret bounded independently of time under the Condorcet-winner assumption.

title: Dueling Bandits with Weak Regret

abstract: Contextual bandits are widely used in Internet services from news recommendation to advertising, and to Web search. Generalized linear models (logistical regression in particular) have demonstrated stronger performance than linear models in many applications where rewards are binary. However, most theoretical analyses on contextual bandits so far are on linear bandits. In this work, we propose an upper confidence bound based algorithm for generalized linear contextual bandits, which achieves an $\sim O(\sqrt{dT})$ regret over T rounds with d dimensional feature vectors. This regret matches the minimax lower bound, up to logarithmic terms, and improves on the best previous result by a $\sqrt{d}$ factor, assuming the number of arms is fixed. A key component in our analysis is to establish a new, sharp finite-sample confidence bound for maximum likelihood estimates in generalized linear models, which may be of independent interest. We also analyze a simpler upper confidence bound algorithm, which is useful in practice, and prove it to have optimal regret for certain cases.

paragraphs: Contextual bandits choose actions using available features while learning from the rewards those actions produce. Generalized linear models are useful when rewards are binary, but much prior theory focused on linear reward models. This paper develops upper-confidence-bound algorithms and guarantees for the generalized linear setting.

The main algorithm achieves regret on the order of the square root of d times T, up to logarithmic factors, for d-dimensional features over T rounds. With the number of arms fixed, this matches the minimax lower bound up to those logarithmic terms and improves the best previous result by a square-root-of-d factor. The fixed-arm assumption is part of the stated comparison.

A key technical contribution is a sharp finite-sample confidence bound for maximum-likelihood estimates in generalized linear models. That bound supports decisions that account for uncertainty in estimated rewards. The authors also analyze a simpler, practically useful upper-confidence-bound algorithm and prove optimal regret in certain cases, distinguishing its conditional guarantee from the main result.
summary.tldr: An upper-confidence-bound method achieves near-minimax regret for generalized linear contextual bandits with a fixed number of arms.

title: Provably Optimal Algorithms for Generalized Linear Contextual Bandits

abstract: In this paper we propose Reward Machines {—} a type of finite state machine that supports the specification of reward functions while exposing reward function structure to the learner and supporting decomposition. We then present Q-Learning for Reward Machines (QRM), an algorithm which appropriately decomposes the reward machine and uses off-policy q-learning to simultaneously learn subpolicies for the different components. QRM is guaranteed to converge to an optimal policy in the tabular case, in contrast to Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning methods which might converge to suboptimal policies. We demonstrate this behavior experimentally in two discrete domains. We also show how function approximation methods like neural networks can be incorporated into QRM, and that doing so can find better policies more quickly than hierarchical methods in a domain with a continuous state space.

paragraphs: A reward function tells a reinforcement learning agent what outcomes to pursue, but its structure can also help organize learning. This paper introduces reward machines, finite-state machines that specify rewards while exposing their internal task structure. That representation supports dividing a larger learning problem into components.

The authors develop Q-Learning for Reward Machines, or QRM, which decomposes the machine and learns subpolicies for its components simultaneously through off-policy Q-learning. The authors also incorporate function approximation, including neural networks, into QRM and show faster learning of better policies than hierarchical methods in a continuous-state domain. The optimality guarantee belongs to the tabular setting; the continuous-state result is empirical evidence that the structured approach can also be useful with function approximation.
summary.tldr: Reward machines expose task structure for simultaneous subpolicy learning, with optimal-policy convergence guaranteed for tabular QRM.

title: Using Reward Machines for High-Level Task Specification and Decomposition in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Embedding representation learning via neural networks is at the core foundation of modern similarity based search. While much effort has been put in developing algorithms for learning binary hamming code representations for search efficiency, this still requires a linear scan of the entire dataset per each query and trades off the search accuracy through binarization. To this end, we consider the problem of directly learning a quantizable embedding representation and the sparse binary hash code end-to-end which can be used to construct an efficient hash table not only providing significant search reduction in the number of data but also achieving the state of the art search accuracy outperforming previous state of the art deep metric learning methods. We also show that finding the optimal sparse binary hash code in a mini-batch can be computed exactly in polynomial time by solving a minimum cost flow problem. Our results on Cifar-100 and on ImageNet datasets show the state of the art search accuracy in precision@k and NMI metrics while providing up to 98X and 478X search speedup respectively over exhaustive linear search. The source code is available at https://github.com/maestrojeong/Deep-Hash-Table-ICML18.

paragraphs: Similarity search needs representations that capture meaningful resemblance while allowing relevant items to be found quickly. The paper argues that binary Hamming representations still require scanning the dataset and can sacrifice accuracy through binarization. It instead learns a representation together with a sparse binary hash code that supports an efficient hash table.

The representation is designed to be quantizable, so its learned structure can work with the discrete codes used for retrieval. Learning both parts end to end connects the representation-learning objective with the mechanism used to reduce search. The authors also show that the optimal sparse binary codes for a mini-batch can be found exactly in polynomial time by solving a minimum-cost-flow problem.

They report search speedups of up to 98 times and 478 times, respectively, relative to exhaustive linear search. These results support the value of jointly designing useful representations and an indexing mechanism that reduces the number of items searched.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning quantizable embeddings and sparse hash codes improves reported retrieval accuracy while enabling substantial speedups over exhaustive search.

title: Efficient end-to-end learning for quantizable representations

abstract: We propose a framework to learn deep generative models via \textbf{V}ariational \textbf{Gr}adient Fl\textbf{ow} (VGrow) on probability spaces. The evolving distribution that asymptotically converges to the target distribution is governed by a vector field, which is the negative gradient of the first variation of the $f$-divergence between them. We prove that the evolving distribution coincides with the pushforward distribution through the infinitesimal time composition of residual maps that are perturbations of the identity map along the vector field. The vector field depends on the density ratio of the pushforward distribution and the target distribution, which can be consistently learned from a binary classification problem. Connections of our proposed VGrow method with other popular methods, such as VAE, GAN and flow-based methods, have been established in this framework, gaining new insights of deep generative learning. We also evaluated several commonly used divergences, including Kullback-Leibler, Jensen-Shannon, Jeffreys divergences as well as our newly discovered “logD” divergence which serves as the objective function of the logD-trick GAN. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that VGrow can generate high-fidelity images in a stable and efficient manner, achieving competitive performance with state-of-the-art GANs.

paragraphs: VGrow treats generative learning as the gradual movement of a probability distribution toward a target distribution. An f-divergence measures their discrepancy, and a vector field determines how the evolving distribution moves to reduce it. The proposed mathematical flow converges asymptotically to the target, connecting generation with optimization over probability distributions.

The authors prove that this evolution corresponds to repeatedly applying infinitesimally small residual maps. Each map makes a small change to its input in the direction specified by the vector field. The field depends on the ratio between the evolving density and the target density, which the framework can consistently learn through binary classification.

This formulation establishes connections with variational autoencoders, GANs, and flow-based generative methods. The paper evaluates several divergences, including a newly identified logD divergence corresponding to the logD-trick GAN objective. Benchmark experiments report stable, efficient generation of high-fidelity images and performance competitive with state-of-the-art GANs. The mathematical distributional evolution and the empirical image-generation results provide complementary support for the framework.
summary.tldr: VGrow learns generative models through divergence-driven distributional flows, connecting residual transformations and density-ratio estimation with competitive image generation.

title: Deep Generative Learning via Variational Gradient Flow

abstract: It is often desirable in recommender systems and other information retrieval applications to provide diverse results, and determinantal point processes (DPPs) have become a popular way to capture the trade-off between the quality of individual results and the diversity of the overall set. However, sampling from a DPP is inherently expensive: if the underlying collection contains N items, then generating each DPP sample requires time linear in N following a one-time preprocessing phase. Additionally, results often need to be personalized to a user, but standard approaches to personalization invalidate the preprocessing, making personalized samples especially expensive. In this work we address both of these shortcomings. First, we propose a new algorithm for generating DPP samples in time logarithmic in N, following a slightly more expensive preprocessing phase. We then extend the algorithm to support arbitrary query-time feature weights, allowing us to generate samples customized to individual users while still retaining logarithmic runtime; experiments show our approach runs over 300 times faster than traditional DPP sampling on collections of 100,000 items for samples of size 10.

paragraphs: Determinantal point processes provide a way to select sets that balance individual item quality with diversity across the selected items. This is useful in recommendation and information retrieval, but repeatedly drawing such sets can be expensive. Standard sampling takes time proportional to the collection size after preprocessing, and personalization can invalidate that preparatory work.

The paper introduces a tree-based sampling method that changes this trade-off. It spends slightly more effort on preprocessing so that subsequent samples take time logarithmic in the number of items. An extension supports arbitrary feature weights supplied at query time, allowing the same approach to produce personalized samples while retaining that logarithmic dependence.

In experiments with collections of 100,000 items and samples containing 10 items, the method runs more than 300 times faster than traditional DPP sampling. That result illustrates the practical benefit of preparing for repeated sampling in advance. The contribution also addresses personalization directly, so its speed advantage is not restricted to repeatedly serving an unchanged selection preference.
summary.tldr: A tree-based DPP sampler supports fast repeated and personalized sampling with logarithmic dependence on collection size after preprocessing.

title: A Tree-Based Method for Fast Repeated Sampling of Determinantal Point Processes

abstract: Generative models have become significantly more powerful in recent years. However, these models continue to have difficulty capturing global structure in data. For example, images of buildings typically contain spatial patterns such as windows repeating at regular intervals, but state-of-the-art models have difficulty generating these patterns. We propose to address this problem by incorporating programs representing global structure into generative models{—}e.g., a 2D for-loop may represent a repeating pattern of windows{—}along with a framework for learning these models by leveraging program synthesis to obtain training data. On both synthetic and real-world data, we demonstrate that our approach substantially outperforms state-of-the-art at both generating and completing images with global structure.

We propose to address this problem by incorporating programs representing global structure into generative models{—}e.g., a 2D for-loop may represent a repeating pattern of windows{—}along with a framework for learning these models by leveraging program synthesis to obtain training data. paragraphs: Generative image models can struggle with structure that must remain consistent across a whole image. A building's regularly spaced windows illustrate the problem: producing individual windows is only part of the task, because their overall arrangement also matters. This paper addresses that difficulty by incorporating programs that explicitly represent global structure into a generative model.

The programs provide a way to describe repeated spatial organization. For example, a two-dimensional loop can represent a repeating arrangement of windows. The authors also introduce a learning framework that uses program synthesis to obtain training data for these models. The approach therefore connects a structured description of the image with a procedure for learning to generate it.

On synthetic and real-world data, the paper reports substantial improvements over leading methods in both image generation and image completion when global structure is involved. These findings suggest that representing regularity explicitly can help a model coordinate different image regions. The benefit applies to creating structured images and to filling in missing portions of them.
summary.tldr: Programs that represent global image structure, learned using program-synthesized training data, improve generation and completion of structured images.

title: Learning Neurosymbolic Generative Models via Program Synthesis

abstract: Variance-reduced algorithms, although achieve great theoretical performance, can run slowly in practice due to the periodic gradient estimation with a large batch of data. Batch-size adaptation thus arises as a promising approach to accelerate such algorithms. However, existing schemes either apply prescribed batch-size adaption rule or exploit the information along optimization path via additional backtracking and condition verification steps. In this paper, we propose a novel scheme, which eliminates backtracking line search but still exploits the information along optimization path by adapting the batch size via history stochastic gradients. We further theoretically show that such a scheme substantially reduces the overall complexity for popular variance-reduced algorithms SVRG and SARAH/SPIDER for both conventional nonconvex optimization and reinforcement learning problems. To this end, we develop a new convergence analysis framework to handle the dependence of the batch size on history stochastic gradients. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed batch-size adaptation scheme.
