paragraphs: Variance-reduced optimization methods can have strong theoretical guarantees yet remain slow because they periodically estimate gradients using large batches. Adjusting batch size offers a way to reduce that expense. Existing approaches either follow a predetermined schedule or inspect the optimization path through extra backtracking and condition-checking steps.

This paper proposes choosing batch sizes using stochastic gradients already collected during optimization. The method therefore responds to the observed optimization history without requiring a backtracking line search. Its central idea is to use past gradient information to guide how much data should be used for subsequent gradient estimation.

The authors develop a convergence-analysis framework that handles the dependence between batch size and earlier stochastic gradients. They show substantial reductions in overall complexity for SVRG and SARAH/SPIDER in both conventional nonconvex optimization and reinforcement-learning problems. Extensive experiments support the effectiveness of the adaptation scheme. The contribution combines a practical way to avoid extra search steps with theoretical treatment of the history dependence that the adaptive rule introduces.
summary.tldr: Using past stochastic gradients to adapt batch sizes reduces the complexity of variance-reduced optimization without backtracking line searches.

title: History-Gradient Aided Batch Size Adaptation for Variance Reduced Algorithms

abstract: We give a local search based algorithm for $k$-median and $k$-means (and more generally for any $k$-clustering with $\ell_p$ norm cost function) from the perspective of individual fairness. More precisely, for a point $x$ in a point set $P$ of size $n$, let $r(x)$ be the minimum radius such that the ball of radius $r(x)$ centered at $x$ has at least $n/k$ points from $P$. Intuitively, if a set of $k$ random points are chosen from $P$ as centers, every point $x\in P$ expects to have a center within radius $r(x)$. In this work, we show how to get an approximately optimal such fair $k$-clustering: The $k$-median ($k$-means) cost of our solution is within a constant factor of the cost of an optimal fair $k$-clustering, and our solution approximately satisfies the fairness condition (also within a constant factor).

paragraphs: Clustering quality is usually summarized by an overall cost, but this paper also asks whether each individual point has reasonable access to a center. For a dataset of n points and k centers, it defines a local radius for each point: the smallest radius containing at least n/k dataset points around it.

This radius gives each point its own distance scale for assessing fairness. The authors motivate it through the intuition of selecting k random data points as centers. They then develop a local-search algorithm for approximately fair clustering, covering k-median, k-means, and more generally clustering costs based on an lp norm.

The guarantees address both cost and fairness. For k-median and k-means, the solution’s cost is within a constant factor of the best fair clustering, and its fairness condition is satisfied within a constant factor as well. Thus, the paper provides an approximate trade-off with formal guarantees on both requirements, using a fairness standard that adapts to each point’s local neighborhood.
summary.tldr: A local-search clustering algorithm achieves constant-factor guarantees for both individual fairness and cost relative to an optimal fair clustering.

title: Individual Fairness for k-Clustering

abstract: Traditional supervised learning aims to train a classifier in the closed-set world, where training and test samples share the same label space. In this paper, we target a more challenging and re_x0002_alistic setting: open-set learning (OSL), where there exist test samples from the classes that are unseen during training. Although researchers have designed many methods from the algorith_x0002_mic perspectives, there are few methods that pro_x0002_vide generalization guarantees on their ability to achieve consistent performance on different train_x0002_ing samples drawn from the same distribution. Motivated by the transfer learning and probably approximate correct (PAC) theory, we make a bold attempt to study OSL by proving its general_x0002_ization error-given training samples with size n, the estimation error will get close to order Op(1/$\sqrt{}$n). This is the first study to provide a generalization bound for OSL, which we do by theoretically investigating the risk of the tar_x0002_get classifier on unknown classes. According to our theory, a novel algorithm, called auxiliary open-set risk (AOSR) is proposed to address the OSL problem. Experiments verify the efficacy of AOSR. The code is available at github.com/AnjinLiu/Openset_Learning_AOSR.

paragraphs: Ordinary supervised classification assumes that every test example belongs to a class represented during training. Open-set learning allows test examples from previously unseen classes. This changes what successful generalization requires: the learner’s behavior on unknown classes becomes part of the problem, beyond distinguishing the classes it has already encountered.

The paper develops a theoretical account of this setting using ideas from transfer learning and probably approximately correct learning theory. Its analysis explicitly investigates the target classifier’s risk on unknown classes. For a training sample of size n, the authors obtain an estimation-error result approaching an order of 1/√n in probability. This concerns the estimation error, rather than asserting that all classification error disappears at that rate.

The theory motivates an algorithm called auxiliary open-set risk, or AOSR. Experiments support its effectiveness. The contribution thus links a generalization analysis to a concrete learning method: it provides a way to reason about performance across training samples while explicitly including the unknown-class behavior that distinguishes open-set learning.
summary.tldr: The paper derives an open-set generalization bound by analyzing unknown-class risk and uses that theory to develop the AOSR algorithm.

title: Learning Bounds for Open-Set Learning

abstract: Multi-agent settings in the real world often involve tasks with varying types and quantities of agents and non-agent entities; however, common patterns of behavior often emerge among these agents/entities. Our method aims to leverage these commonalities by asking the question: “What is the expected utility of each agent when only considering a randomly selected sub-group of its observed entities?” By posing this counterfactual question, we can recognize state-action trajectories within sub-groups of entities that we may have encountered in another task and use what we learned in that task to inform our prediction in the current one. We then reconstruct a prediction of the full returns as a combination of factors considering these disjoint groups of entities and train this “randomly factorized" value function as an auxiliary objective for value-based multi-agent reinforcement learning. By doing so, our model can recognize and leverage similarities across tasks to improve learning efficiency in a multi-task setting. Our approach, Randomized Entity-wise Factorization for Imagined Learning (REFIL), outperforms all strong baselines by a significant margin in challenging multi-task StarCraft micromanagement settings.

paragraphs: Multi-agent tasks can differ in the number and kinds of agents and other entities they contain, even when useful behavioral patterns recur. REFIL seeks to exploit those recurring patterns. It asks what utility an agent would expect if it considered only a randomly selected subgroup of the entities it observes.

This counterfactual view lets the model recognize trajectories within smaller groups that resemble situations encountered in another task. Predictions associated with disjoint entity groups are then combined to reconstruct a prediction of the full return. The randomly factorized value function is trained as an auxiliary objective alongside value-based multi-agent reinforcement learning.

The intended benefit is more efficient learning across tasks: knowledge about a familiar subgroup can help evaluate a new situation with a different overall collection of entities. In challenging multi-task StarCraft micromanagement experiments, REFIL significantly outperforms all strong baselines considered. The results support subgroup-based value learning as a way to use common structure across tasks with varying entity compositions.
summary.tldr: REFIL learns auxiliary values for random entity subgroups to reuse behavioral patterns across multi-agent tasks and improve learning efficiency.

title: Randomized Entity-wise Factorization for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Machine learning is predicated on the concept of generalization: a model achieving low error on a sufficiently large training set should also perform well on novel samples from the same distribution. We show that both data whitening and second order optimization can harm or entirely prevent generalization. In general, model training harnesses information contained in the sample-sample second moment matrix of a dataset. For a general class of models, namely models with a fully connected first layer, we prove that the information contained in this matrix is the only information which can be used to generalize. Models trained using whitened data, or with certain second order optimization schemes, have less access to this information, resulting in reduced or nonexistent generalization ability. We experimentally verify these predictions for several architectures, and further demonstrate that generalization continues to be harmed even when theoretical requirements are relaxed. However, we also show experimentally that regularized second order optimization can provide a practical tradeoff, where training is accelerated but less information is lost, and generalization can in some circumstances even improve.

paragraphs: Preprocessing and optimization choices can affect which information a model uses to generalize. This paper shows that data whitening and certain second-order optimization schemes can reduce or even prevent generalization. Its explanation centers on the sample-sample second moment matrix, which captures relationships among examples that training can exploit.

For the studied class of models with a fully connected first layer, the authors prove that this matrix contains the only information available for generalization under their theoretical setup. Whitening or certain second-order updates reduce access to that information. The resulting loss of usable structure explains why better-conditioned training need not lead to better performance on new examples.

Experiments on several architectures verify the predictions and show that generalization can still suffer when the theoretical requirements are relaxed. However, regularized second-order optimization provides an empirical tradeoff: it can accelerate training while discarding less information, and sometimes even improve generalization. The findings therefore distinguish harmful information loss from cases where regularization preserves a useful balance between optimization speed and predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Whitening and certain second-order updates can remove usable generalization information, while regularization can provide a better speed–generalization tradeoff.

title: Whitening and Second Order Optimization Both Make Information in the Dataset Unusable During Training, and Can Reduce or Prevent Generalization

abstract: Newton-type methods are popular in federated learning due to their fast convergence. Still, they suffer from two main issues, namely: low communication efficiency and low privacy due to the requirement of sending Hessian information from clients to parameter server (PS). In this work, we introduced a novel framework called FedNew in which there is no need to transmit Hessian information from clients to PS, hence resolving the bottleneck to improve communication efficiency. In addition, FedNew hides the gradient information and results in a privacy-preserving approach compared to the existing state-of-the-art. The core novel idea in FedNew is to introduce a two level framework, and alternate between updating the inverse Hessian-gradient product using only one alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) step and then performing the global model update using Newton’s method. Though only one ADMM pass is used to approximate the inverse Hessian-gradient product at each iteration, we develop a novel theoretical approach to show the converging behavior of FedNew for convex problems. Additionally, a significant reduction in communication overhead is achieved by utilizing stochastic quantization. Numerical results using real datasets show the superiority of FedNew compared to existing methods in terms of communication costs.

paragraphs: Newton-type methods are attractive for federated learning because they can converge quickly. Their communication requirements are a problem, however: sending Hessian information from clients to a central server creates overhead and privacy concerns. FedNew changes how the Newton update is constructed so clients do not need to transmit that information.

The method alternates between two levels of computation. First, it approximates the inverse Hessian-gradient product using a single step of the alternating direction method of multipliers, or ADMM. It then uses that approximation for the global Newton model update. This focuses the computation on the product needed for updating the model. The framework also hides gradient information.

The authors establish convergence behavior for convex problems despite using only one ADMM pass per iteration. They further reduce communication overhead through stochastic quantization. Numerical experiments on real datasets report lower communication costs than existing methods. The paper therefore combines a cheaper way to construct Newton-type updates with a convex convergence analysis and empirical communication gains, while describing privacy improvement relative to existing approaches.
summary.tldr: FedNew approximates federated Newton updates with one ADMM step per iteration, avoiding Hessian transmission, hiding gradients, and reducing communication costs.

title: FedNew: A Communication-Efficient and Privacy-Preserving Newton-Type Method for Federated Learning

abstract: State-of-the-art deep learning methods achieve human-like performance on many tasks, but make errors nevertheless. Characterizing these errors in easily interpretable terms gives insight into whether a classifier is prone to making systematic errors, but also gives a way to act and improve the classifier. We propose to discover those feature-value combinations (i.e., patterns) that strongly correlate with correct resp. erroneous predictions to obtain a global and interpretable description for arbitrary classifiers. We show this is an instance of the more general label description problem, which we formulate in terms of the Minimum Description Length principle. To discover a good pattern set, we develop the efficient Premise algorithm. Through an extensive set of experiments we show it performs very well in practice on both synthetic and real-world data. Unlike existing solutions, it ably recovers ground truth patterns, even on highly imbalanced data over many features. Through two case studies on Visual Question Answering and Named Entity Recognition, we confirm that Premise gives clear and actionable insight into the systematic errors made by modern NLP classifiers.

paragraphs: Knowing a classifier’s overall performance does not explain whether its errors follow recognizable patterns. This paper seeks interpretable combinations of feature values that strongly correlate with correct or incorrect predictions. The aim is a global description of a classifier’s behavior that can reveal systematic weaknesses and suggest where improvement efforts should focus.

The authors cast this task as a broader label-description problem and formulate it using the Minimum Description Length principle. They develop Premise, an efficient algorithm for finding a useful set of descriptive patterns. Because the patterns describe relationships between features and prediction outcomes, the approach can be applied to arbitrary classifiers.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show strong practical performance, including recovery of ground-truth patterns in highly imbalanced data with many features. Case studies in Visual Question Answering and Named Entity Recognition show clear, actionable descriptions of systematic errors. The result is a way to turn collections of mistakes into interpretable regularities, while keeping the stated relationship correlational.
summary.tldr: Premise discovers interpretable feature patterns associated with classifier successes and errors, helping characterize systematic weaknesses.

title: Label-Descriptive Patterns and Their Application to Characterizing Classification Errors

abstract: Winning lottery tickets refer to sparse subgraphs of deep neural networks which have classification accuracy close to the original dense networks. Resilient connectivity properties of such sparse networks play an important role in their performance. The attempt is to identify a sparse and yet well-connected network to guarantee unhindered information flow. Connectivity in a graph is best characterized by its spectral expansion property. Ramanujan graphs are robust expanders which lead to sparse but highly-connected networks, and thus aid in studying the winning tickets. A feedforward neural network consists of a sequence of bipartite graphs representing its layers. We analyze the Ramanujan graph property of such bipartite layers in terms of their spectral characteristics using the Cheeger’s inequality for irregular graphs. It is empirically observed that the winning ticket networks preserve the Ramanujan graph property and achieve a high accuracy even when the layers are sparse. Accuracy and robustness to noise start declining as many of the layers lose the property. Next we find a robust winning lottery ticket by pruning individual layers while retaining their respective Ramanujan graph property. This strategy is observed to improve the performance of existing network pruning algorithms.

paragraphs: A winning lottery ticket is a sparse part of a neural network that retains accuracy close to the original dense model. This paper investigates whether the connectivity of these subnetworks helps explain their performance. The central question is how a network can lose many connections while still allowing information to pass effectively through its layers.

The authors represent each feedforward layer as a bipartite graph and examine its spectral properties. They focus on the Ramanujan property, associated with graphs that remain strongly connected despite being sparse. Their analysis uses Cheeger’s inequality for irregular graphs to connect spectral characteristics with connectivity.

Empirically, winning tickets retain this property even at substantial sparsity. Accuracy and resistance to noise begin to decline when many layers lose it. These observations motivate pruning layers individually while preserving their Ramanujan property. The resulting strategy improves existing pruning algorithms in the reported experiments, supporting connectivity preservation as a useful practical guide rather than establishing a universal accuracy guarantee.
summary.tldr: Preserving a spectral connectivity property during pruning empirically helps sparse neural networks retain accuracy and robustness.

title: A Study on the Ramanujan Graph Property of Winning Lottery Tickets

abstract: Transformers have made progress in miscellaneous tasks, but suffer from quadratic computational and memory complexities. Recent works propose sparse transformers with attention on sparse graphs to reduce complexity and remain strong performance. While effective, the crucial parts of how dense a graph needs to be to perform well are not fully explored. In this paper, we propose Normalized Information Payload (NIP), a graph scoring function measuring information transfer on graph, which provides an analysis tool for trade-offs between performance and complexity. Guided by this theoretical analysis, we present Hypercube Transformer, a sparse transformer that models token interactions in a hypercube and shows comparable or even better results with vanilla transformer while yielding $O(N\log N)$ complexity with sequence length $N$. Experiments on tasks requiring various sequence lengths lay validation for our graph function well.

This paper develops an analysis tool for examining that trade-off.

The authors use this theoretical perspective to design Hypercube Transformer, whose token interactions follow a hypercube structure. The resulting sparse model has O(N log N) complexity for sequence length N, providing a more favorable scaling pattern than quadratic attention.

Experiments on tasks with different sequence lengths support the proposed graph-scoring function. Hypercube Transformer produces results comparable to, or better than, a vanilla transformer in the reported evaluations. The contribution pairs a concrete sparse architecture with a way to reason about connectivity, helping explain how reduced attention graphs can retain effective information exchange.
summary.tldr: A graph information-transfer score guides Hypercube Transformer, which achieves O(N log N) complexity with competitive reported performance.

title: What Dense Graph Do You Need for Self-Attention?

abstract: Compositional generalization is a critical ability in learning and decision-making. We focus on the setting of reinforcement learning in object-oriented environments to study compositional generalization in world modeling. We (1) formalize the compositional generalization problem with an algebraic approach and (2) study how a world model can achieve that. We introduce a conceptual environment, Object Library, and two instances, and deploy a principled pipeline to measure the generalization ability. Motivated by the formulation, we analyze several methods with exact or no compositional generalization ability using our framework, and design a differentiable approach, Homomorphic Object-oriented World Model (HOWM), that achieves soft but more efficient compositional generalization.

paragraphs: Compositional generalization concerns using learned components in combinations beyond those previously encountered. This paper studies that ability in world models for reinforcement learning environments organized around objects. The central question is how a model of an environment can capture reusable structure that supports generalization across object compositions.

The authors give the problem an algebraic formulation, making compositional generalization something that can be analyzed explicitly. They introduce a conceptual environment called Object Library, provide two instances, and develop a principled evaluation pipeline. Within this framework, they examine methods that have exact compositional generalization and methods that lack the ability, clarifying distinctions between different modeling approaches.

The formulation also motivates a differentiable model called the Homomorphic Object-oriented World Model, or HOWM. It achieves a soft form of compositional generalization with greater efficiency, rather than the exact property considered for some of the analyzed methods. The contribution combines a formal account of the target ability, a way to measure it, and a model that makes an explicit tradeoff between exactness and efficiency.
summary.tldr: An algebraic framework analyzes compositional generalization in object-based world models and motivates HOWM, a differentiable approach offering soft but more efficient generalization.

title: Toward Compositional Generalization in Object-Oriented World Modeling

abstract: How to train deep neural networks (DNNs) to generalize well is a central concern in deep learning, especially for severely overparameterized networks nowadays. In this paper, we propose an effective method to improve the model generalization by additionally penalizing the gradient norm of loss function during optimization. We demonstrate that confining the gradient norm of loss function could help lead the optimizers towards finding flat minima. We leverage the first-order approximation to efficiently implement the corresponding gradient to fit well in the gradient descent framework. In our experiments, we confirm that when using our methods, generalization performance of various models could be improved on different datasets. Also, we show that the recent sharpness-aware minimization method (Foretet al., 2021) is a special, but not the best, case of our method, where the best case of our method could give new state-of-art performance on these tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/zhaoyang-0204/gnp.

paragraphs: A neural network can fit its training data well without generalizing equally well to new examples. This paper modifies training by adding a penalty on the norm of the loss gradient. The penalty controls how strongly the loss changes locally with the parameters, adding a geometric preference to the optimization objective.

The authors demonstrate that restricting the gradient norm can help guide optimization toward flat minima. To make the additional term practical within gradient descent, they use a first-order approximation when implementing its gradient. This connects the proposed generalization strategy to an efficient training procedure rather than leaving it solely as a property of desirable solutions.

Experiments show improved generalization across different models and datasets. The paper also establishes that sharpness-aware minimization is a special case of the proposed method, although it is not the best-performing case in the reported tasks. Better-performing choices within the method can achieve new state-of-the-art results on those tasks. The findings support gradient-norm control as a useful training mechanism, with the move toward flatter minima presented as something it can help achieve.
summary.tldr: Penalizing the loss-gradient norm can guide training toward flatter minima and improve generalization through an efficient first-order implementation.

title: Penalizing Gradient Norm for Efficiently Improving Generalization in Deep Learning

abstract: Learning a shared policy that guides the locomotion of different agents is of core interest in Reinforcement Learning (RL), which leads to the study of morphology-agnostic RL. However, existing benchmarks are highly restrictive in the choice of starting point and target point, constraining the movement of the agents within 2D space. In this work, we propose a novel setup for morphology-agnostic RL, dubbed Subequivariant Graph RL in 3D environments (3D-SGRL). Specifically, we first introduce a new set of more practical yet challenging benchmarks in 3D space that allows the agent to have full Degree-of-Freedoms to explore in arbitrary directions starting from arbitrary configurations. Moreover, to optimize the policy over the enlarged state-action space, we propose to inject geometric symmetry, i.e., subequivariance, into the modeling of the policy and Q-function such that the policy can generalize to all directions, improving exploration efficiency. This goal is achieved by a novel SubEquivariant Transformer (SET) that permits expressive message exchange. Finally, we evaluate the proposed method on the proposed benchmarks, where our method consistently and significantly outperforms existing approaches on single-task, multi-task, and zero-shot generalization scenarios. Extensive ablations are also conducted to verify our design.

paragraphs: Learning one locomotion policy for agents with different body structures requires handling both physical variation and movement goals. This paper argues that existing benchmarks restrict the problem through starting and target configurations that effectively confine movement to two dimensions. It introduces three-dimensional benchmarks with full degrees of freedom, arbitrary starting configurations, and exploration in arbitrary directions.

The larger state-action space makes policy learning more demanding. The proposed 3D-SGRL method incorporates geometric symmetry, specifically subequivariance, into both the policy and the Q-function. Its SubEquivariant Transformer enables expressive message exchange while imposing that structure. The intended benefit is generalization across directions, improving how efficiently the agent explores the expanded environment.

On the newly proposed benchmarks, the method consistently and significantly outperforms existing approaches in single-task, multitask, and zero-shot generalization scenarios. Ablation studies also examine the design choices. The paper therefore contributes both a broader evaluation setting for shared locomotion policies and a symmetry-aware modeling approach that performs well within that setting.
summary.tldr: New 3D locomotion benchmarks and a subequivariant Transformer improve shared-policy learning across agents and movement directions in reported evaluations.

title: Subequivariant Graph Reinforcement Learning in 3D Environments

abstract: Few-shot learning aims to transfer the knowledge acquired from training on a diverse set of tasks to unseen tasks from the same task distribution, with a limited amount of labeled data. The underlying requirement for effective few-shot generalization is to learn a good representation of the task manifold. This becomes more difficult when only a limited number of tasks are available for training. In such a few-task few-shot setting, it is beneficial to explicitly preserve the local neighborhoods from the task manifold and exploit this to generate artificial tasks for training. To this end, we introduce the notion of interval bounds from the provably robust training literature to few-shot learning. The interval bounds are used to characterize neighborhoods around the training tasks. These neighborhoods can then be preserved by minimizing the distance between a task and its respective bounds. We then use a novel strategy to artificially form new tasks for training by interpolating between the available tasks and their respective interval bounds. We apply our framework to both model-agnostic meta-learning as well as prototype-based metric-learning paradigms. The efficacy of our proposed approach is evident from the improved performance on several datasets from diverse domains in comparison to recent methods.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning transfers knowledge across tasks so that a model can handle a new task with little labeled data. This paper considers the additional difficulty of having only a few training tasks. In that setting, learning the structure of the task manifold—the relationships among tasks—is harder, making the local neighborhoods around available tasks especially valuable.

The authors bring interval bounds from robust training into this setting. The bounds characterize neighborhoods around training tasks, and minimizing the distance between each task and its bounds helps preserve that local structure. They then generate artificial training tasks by interpolating between the available tasks and their associated interval bounds, using the neighborhood descriptions to guide task augmentation.

The framework is applied to both model-agnostic meta-learning and prototype-based metric learning. Experiments across datasets from diverse domains show improved performance relative to recent methods. These findings support the use of explicit task-neighborhood information when training-task diversity is limited, and demonstrate that the proposed augmentation framework can operate within two different few-shot learning paradigms.
summary.tldr: Interval bounds preserve local task structure and guide artificial-task generation to improve few-shot learning when training tasks are scarce.

title: Interval Bound Interpolation for Few-shot Learning with Few Tasks

abstract: We study the class of location-scale or heteroscedastic noise models (LSNMs), in which the effect $Y$ can be written as a function of the cause $X$ and a noise source $N$ independent of $X$, which may be scaled by a positive function $g$ over the cause, i.e., $Y = f(X) + g(X)N$. Despite the generality of the model class, we show the causal direction is identifiable up to some pathological cases. To empirically validate these theoretical findings, we propose two estimators for LSNMs: an estimator based on (non-linear) feature maps, and one based on neural networks. Both model the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $X$ as a Gaussian parameterized by its natural parameters. When the feature maps are correctly specified, we prove that our estimator is jointly concave, and a consistent estimator for the cause-effect identification task. Although the the neural network does not inherit those guarantees, it can fit functions of arbitrary complexity, and reaches state-of-the-art performance across benchmarks.

Despite the generality of the model class, we show the causal direction is identifiable up to some pathological cases. To empirically validate these theoretical findings, we propose two estimators for LSNMs: an estimator based on (non-linear) feature maps, and one based on neural networks. paragraphs: This paper studies causal models in which a cause changes both the expected effect and the size of its noise. The model is Y = f(X) + g(X)N, with noise N independent of X and a positive scaling function g. This permits heteroscedasticity: the amount of variability can depend on the cause.

The authors show that causal direction is identifiable within this model class except for some pathological cases. They then propose two estimators to test these findings empirically. One uses nonlinear feature maps and the other uses neural networks. Both describe the conditional distribution of the effect as a Gaussian expressed through its natural parameters.

When the feature maps are correctly specified, the authors prove joint concavity for the estimation formulation and consistency for identifying cause and effect. Those guarantees do not transfer to the neural estimator. Its advantage is flexibility in fitting functions of arbitrary complexity, and it achieves state-of-the-art benchmark performance. The paper thus separates a conditional theoretical guarantee from the empirical benefits of a more expressive estimator.
summary.tldr: Location-scale noise models can identify causal direction except in pathological cases, with separate theoretical and empirical results for two estimators.

title: On the Identifiability and Estimation of Causal Location-Scale Noise Models

abstract: Agents must be able to adapt quickly as an environment changes. We find that existing model-based reinforcement learning agents are unable to do this well, in part because of how they use past experiences to train their world model. Here, we present Curious Replay—a form of prioritized experience replay tailored to model-based agents through use of a curiosity-based priority signal. Agents using Curious Replay exhibit improved performance in an exploration paradigm inspired by animal behavior and on the Crafter benchmark. DreamerV3 with Curious Replay surpasses state-of-the-art performance on Crafter, achieving a mean score of 19.4 that substantially improves on the previous high score of 14.5 by DreamerV3 with uniform replay, while also maintaining similar performance on the Deepmind Control Suite. Code for Curious Replay is available at github.com/AutonomousAgentsLab/curiousreplay.

paragraphs: An agent facing a changing environment needs to update its understanding quickly. The authors find that existing model-based reinforcement learning agents struggle with this, partly because of how they reuse past experiences to train their world models. The paper focuses on the selection of experiences for replay as a contributor to adaptation.

Curious Replay is a prioritized replay method designed specifically for model-based agents. It uses a curiosity-based signal to assign priority to stored experiences, changing which experiences receive attention during world-model training. This connects the replay mechanism to the agent's learning needs and makes the use of past experience part of the adaptation strategy.

Agents using Curious Replay improve on an exploration task inspired by animal behavior and on Crafter. Adding it to DreamerV3 raises the reported mean Crafter score from 14.5 with uniform replay to 19.4, exceeding the previous state of the art. Performance remains similar on the DeepMind Control Suite. The results show substantial gains in the reported exploration setting alongside retained performance on another benchmark.
summary.tldr: Curious Replay prioritizes stored experiences using curiosity to improve world-model learning and agent adaptation.

title: Curious Replay for Model-based Adaptation

abstract: We focus on addressing the dense backward propagation issue for training efficiency of N:M fine-grained sparsity that preserves at most N out of M consecutive weights and achieves practical speedups supported by the N:M sparse tensor core. Therefore, we present a novel method of Bi-directional Masks (Bi-Mask) with its two central innovations in: 1) Separate sparse masks in the two directions of forward and backward propagation to obtain training acceleration. It disentangles the forward and backward weight sparsity and overcomes the very dense gradient computation. 2) An efficient weight row permutation method to maintain performance. It picks up the permutation candidate with the most eligible N:M weight blocks in the backward to minimize the gradient gap between traditional unidirectional masks and our bi-directional masks. Compared with existing uni-directional scenario that applies a transposable mask and enables backward acceleration, our Bi-Mask is experimentally demonstrated to be more superior in performance. Also, our Bi-Mask performs on par with or even better than methods that fail to achieve backward acceleration. Project of this paper is available at https://github.com/zyxxmu/Bi-Mask.

It disentangles the forward and backward weight sparsity and overcomes the very dense gradient computation. 2) An efficient weight row permutation method to maintain performance. It picks up the permutation candidate with the most eligible N:M weight blocks in the backward to minimize the gradient gap between traditional unidirectional masks and our bi-directional masks. Also, our Bi-Mask performs on par with or even better than methods that fail to achieve backward acceleration. Project of this paper is available at https://github.com/zyxxmu/Bi-Mask.

paragraphs: N:M sparsity keeps at most N weights in each group of M consecutive weights, a structure that compatible sparse tensor cores can accelerate. However, making the forward computation sparse does not automatically make backpropagation efficient. Dense computations during the backward pass can therefore limit the training benefits of this sparsity pattern.

Bi-directional Masks, or Bi-Mask, uses separate masks for forward and backward propagation. This separates the sparsity requirements of the two directions so both can benefit from acceleration. Because changing the backward mask can alter gradient computation, the method also permutes weight rows efficiently. It selects a candidate permutation with many backward blocks that satisfy the N:M constraint, aiming to reduce the gradient discrepancy relative to traditional masking.

Experiments show better predictive performance than an existing approach that uses a transposable mask to accelerate the backward pass. Bi-Mask also matches or exceeds methods that do not provide backward acceleration. The contribution is therefore a way to combine efficient training computations with preserved model performance, using directional masks and weight arrangement together.
summary.tldr: Bi-Mask uses separate forward and backward sparsity masks plus weight-row permutations to accelerate training while maintaining predictive performance.

title: Bi-directional Masks for Efficient N:M Sparse Training

abstract: While Transformers have been the main architecture behind deep learning’s success in language modeling, state-space models (SSMs) such as Mamba have recently been shown to match or outperform Transformers at small to medium scale. We show that these families of models are actually quite closely related, and develop a rich framework of theoretical connections between SSMs and variants of attention, connected through various decompositions of a well-studied class of structured semiseparable matrices. Our state space duality (SSD) framework allows us to design a new architecture (Mamba-2) whose core layer is an a refinement of Mamba’s selective SSM that is 2-8$\times$ faster, while continuing to be competitive with Transformers on language modeling.

paragraphs: Transformers and state-space models are often presented as different approaches to sequence modeling. This paper develops a theoretical connection between state-space models and variants of attention. The connection is built through decompositions of semiseparable matrices, providing a shared mathematical framework for examining these model families.

The authors call this framework state space duality. Its value extends beyond describing a relationship: it guides the design of Mamba-2, a new architecture whose central layer refines Mamba's selective state-space model. The framework therefore links structural analysis of sequence models to a concrete change in how a model's core computation is organized.

The refined core layer is reported to be two to eight times faster, while Mamba-2 remains competitive with Transformers on language modeling. That speed claim applies to the core layer described in the abstract, rather than establishing the same gain for every complete training or inference workload. The contribution demonstrates how theoretical connections between model families can lead to more efficient architectures.
summary.tldr: State space duality connects SSMs with attention variants and leads to Mamba-2, whose refined core layer is reported to be two to eight times faster.

title: Transformers are SSMs: Generalized Models and Efficient Algorithms Through Structured State Space Duality

abstract: Second-order information is valuable for many applications but challenging to compute. Several works focus on computing or approximating Hessian diagonals, but even this simplification introduces significant additional costs compared to computing a gradient. In the absence of efficient exact computation schemes for Hessian diagonals, we revisit an early approximation scheme proposed by Becker and LeCun (1989, BL89), which has a cost similar to gradients and appears to have been overlooked by the community. We introduce HesScale, an improvement over BL89, which adds negligible extra computation. On small networks, we find that this improvement is of higher quality than all alternatives, even those with theoretical guarantees, such as unbiasedness, while being much cheaper to compute. We use this insight in reinforcement learning problems where small networks are used and demonstrate HesScale in second-order optimization and scaling the step-size parameter. In our experiments, HesScale optimizes faster than existing methods and improves stability through step-size scaling. These findings are promising for scaling second-order methods in larger models in the future.

paragraphs: Second-order information describes how the slope of a training objective changes, helping guide optimization beyond what a gradient alone provides. Computing it is expensive, and even approximating only the Hessian diagonal can add substantial cost. This paper revisits an older approximation whose computational expense is similar to obtaining gradients.

The authors introduce HesScale, an improvement to that earlier scheme with negligible additional computation. On small networks, it gives higher-quality approximations than the evaluated alternatives, including methods with guarantees such as unbiasedness, while costing much less. The finding highlights a practical distinction: a theoretical property of an estimator does not by itself determine its approximation quality in these experiments.

The paper applies HesScale to reinforcement-learning problems using small networks, both for second-order optimization and for scaling step sizes. Experiments show faster optimization than existing methods and improved stability from step-size scaling. These results establish evidence in the small-network setting; the authors present their relevance to larger models as a promising direction for future scaling.
summary.tldr: HesScale cheaply improves Hessian-diagonal estimates on small networks, accelerating tested reinforcement-learning optimization and stabilizing step sizes.

title: Revisiting Scalable Hessian Diagonal Approximations for Applications in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In this paper, we address the challenge of Perspective-Invariant Learning in machine learning and computer vision, which involves enabling a network to understand images from varying perspectives to achieve consistent semantic interpretation. While standard approaches rely on the labor-intensive collection of multi-view images or limited data augmentation techniques, we propose a novel framework, Discrete Latent Perspective Learning (DLPL), for latent multi-perspective fusion learning using conventional single-view images. DLPL comprises three main modules: Perspective Discrete Decomposition (PDD), Perspective Homography Transformation (PHT), and Perspective Invariant Attention (PIA), which work together to discretize visual features, transform perspectives, and fuse multi-perspective semantic information, respectively. DLPL is a universal perspective learning framework applicable to a variety of scenarios and vision tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DLPL significantly enhances the network’s capacity to depict images across diverse scenarios (daily photos, UAV, auto-driving) and tasks (detection, segmentation).

DLPL comprises three main modules: Perspective Discrete Decomposition (PDD), Perspective Homography Transformation (PHT), and Perspective Invariant Attention (PIA), which work together to discretize visual features, transform perspectives, and fuse multi-perspective semantic information, respectively. paragraphs: Recognizing the same meaning across different viewpoints is a challenge for image understanding. Standard approaches use collected images from multiple views or data augmentation, which the paper describes as labor-intensive or limited. Discrete Latent Perspective Learning, or DLPL, instead learns to combine perspective information using conventional images that each provide a single view.

Its three modules divide this work into distinct steps. Perspective Discrete Decomposition discretizes visual features. Perspective Homography Transformation transforms perspectives within the representation. Perspective Invariant Attention then combines semantic information across the resulting perspectives. Together, these stages let the network perform latent multi-perspective fusion without making a collected multi-view image set the basis of the framework.

The authors present DLPL as a general framework for perspective learning and evaluate it on detection and segmentation. Their experiments span everyday photographs, UAV imagery, and autonomous-driving scenarios, reporting significant improvements in the networks' representation capabilities. The findings support the value of explicitly transforming and combining perspective information inside learned features across the tested tasks and visual settings.
summary.tldr: DLPL learns and fuses latent perspectives from single-view images to improve detection and segmentation across varied visual settings.

title: Discrete Latent Perspective Learning for Segmentation and Detection

abstract: We study inductive bias in Transformers in the infinitely over-parameterized Gaussian process limit and argue transformers tend to be biased towards more permutation symmetric functions in sequence space. We show that the representation theory of the symmetric group can be used to give quantitative analytical predictions when the dataset is symmetric to permutations between tokens. We present a simplified transformer block and solve the model at the limit, including accurate predictions for the learning curves and network outputs. We show that in common setups, one can derive tight bounds in the form of a scaling law for the learnability as a function of the context length. Finally, we argue WikiText dataset, does indeed possess a degree of permutation symmetry.
originalAbstract: We study inductive bias in Transformers in the infinitely over-parameterized Gaussian process limit and argue transformers tend to be biased towards more permutation symmetric functions in sequence space. We show that the representation theory of the symmetric group can be used to give quantitative analytical predictions when the dataset is symmetric to permutations between tokens. We present a simplified transformer block and solve the model at the limit, including accurate predictions for the learning curves and network outputs. We show that in common setups, one can derive tight bounds in the form of a scaling law for the learnability as a function of the context length. Finally, we argue WikiText dataset, does indeed possess a degree of permutation symmetry.

paragraphs: This paper investigates which kinds of sequence functions Transformers tend to favor. It studies the infinitely overparameterized Gaussian process limit and argues that Transformers are biased toward functions with greater symmetry under token permutations. The limit provides a mathematically tractable setting for examining this architectural preference.

When a dataset is symmetric under permutations between tokens, the authors use representation theory of the symmetric group to make quantitative predictions. They introduce a simplified Transformer block and solve its limiting model, obtaining accurate predictions for learning curves and network outputs. The symmetry assumption is central to this analytical treatment.

The analysis also yields tight learnability bounds expressed as scaling laws in context length for common setups. This links the length of a sequence to how learnable a target is within the studied framework. Finally, the authors argue that WikiText exhibits some permutation symmetry, suggesting relevance to language data. The results provide an analytical perspective on Transformer bias grounded in a simplified infinite-width setting.
summary.tldr: An infinite-width analysis links Transformer learning preferences to token-permutation symmetry and derives context-length learnability bounds.

title: Towards Understanding Inductive Bias in Transformers: A View From Infinity

abstract: Combining Evolutionary Algorithms (EAs) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) for policy search has been proven to improve RL performance. However, previous works largely overlook value-based RL in favor of merging EAs with policy-based RL. This paper introduces Value-Evolutionary-Based Reinforcement Learning (VEB-RL) that focuses on the integration of EAs with value-based RL. The framework maintains a population of value functions instead of policies and leverages negative Temporal Difference error as the fitness metric for evolution. The metric is more sample-efficient for population evaluation than cumulative rewards and is closely associated with the accuracy of the value function approximation. Additionally, VEB-RL enables elites of the population to interact with the environment to offer high-quality samples for RL optimization, whereas the RL value function participates in the population’s evolution in each generation. Experiments on MinAtar and Atari demonstrate the superiority of VEB-RL in significantly improving DQN, Rainbow, and SPR. Our code is available on https://github.com/yeshenpy/VEB-RL.

paragraphs: Evolutionary algorithms can complement reinforcement learning by maintaining and improving a population of candidate solutions. This paper brings that approach to value-based reinforcement learning, an area the authors describe as relatively overlooked by earlier combinations. Its framework, VEB-RL, evolves a population of value functions.

Population fitness is measured using negative temporal-difference error, which connects evaluation to the accuracy of value approximation. The authors describe this measure as more sample-efficient for population evaluation than cumulative rewards. Elite population members interact with the environment to supply high-quality samples for reinforcement learning, while the reinforcement learner's value function participates in every generation of evolution.

This creates a two-way exchange between evolutionary search and value learning: the population contributes experience, and the learner contributes a value function to the evolving population. Experiments on MinAtar and Atari report significant improvements to DQN, Rainbow, and SPR. The findings support value functions as useful objects for evolutionary search and temporal-difference error as a practical evaluation signal within this framework.
summary.tldr: VEB-RL evolves value functions using temporal-difference error and exchanges experience with reinforcement learning to improve several value-based agents.

title: Value-Evolutionary-Based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In recent years, work has gone into developing deep interpretable methods for image classification that clearly attributes a model’s output to specific features of the data. One such of these methods is the Prototypical Part Network (ProtoPNet), which attempts to classify images based on meaningful parts of the input. While this architecture is able to produce visually interpretable classifications, it often learns to classify based on parts of the image that are not semantically meaningful. To address this problem, we propose the Reward Reweighing, Reselecting, and Retraining (R3) post-processing framework, which performs three additional corrective updates to a pretrained ProtoPNet in an offline and efficient manner. The first two steps involve learning a reward model based on collected human feedback and then aligning the prototypes with human preferences. The final step is retraining, which realigns the base features and the classifier layer of the original model with the updated prototypes. We find that our R3 framework consistently improves both the interpretability and the predictive accuracy of ProtoPNet and its variants.

paragraphs: ProtoPNet classifies images using parts intended to provide visually understandable evidence for its decisions. However, a visible image part is not necessarily meaningful to a person. The model can learn to rely on parts that make its classification display interpretable at a visual level without offering a semantically useful explanation.

The R3 framework corrects a pretrained model through reward reweighing, reselection, and retraining. Its first two stages learn a reward model from collected human feedback and align the prototypes with human preferences. This introduces an explicit human signal about which visual evidence should serve as a meaningful basis for classification.

The final stage retrains the original model's base features and classifier layer so they fit the updated prototypes. The authors describe these corrective updates as offline and efficient, and report consistent improvements in both interpretability and predictive accuracy for ProtoPNet and its variants. The findings support treating prototype quality and the surrounding classifier as connected: changing the explanatory parts is followed by realigning the model that uses them.
summary.tldr: R3 uses human feedback to revise visual prototypes and retrain their supporting model, improving reported interpretability and classification accuracy.

title: Improving Prototypical Visual Explanations with Reward Reweighing, Reselection, and Retraining

abstract: Efficient and effective Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection is essential for the safe deployment of AI systems. Existing feature space methods, while effective, often incur significant computational overhead due to their reliance on auxiliary models built from training features. In this paper, we propose a computationally-efficient OOD detector without using auxiliary models while still leveraging the rich information embedded in the feature space. Specifically, we detect OOD samples based on their feature distances to decision boundaries. To minimize computational cost, we introduce an efficient closed-form estimation, analytically proven to tightly lower bound the distance. Based on our estimation, we discover that In-Distribution (ID) features tend to be further from decision boundaries than OOD features. Additionally, ID and OOD samples are better separated when compared at equal deviation levels from the mean of training features. By regularizing the distances to decision boundaries based on feature deviation from the mean, we develop a hyperparameter-free, auxiliary model-free OOD detector. Our method matches or surpasses the effectiveness of state-of-the-art methods in extensive experiments while incurring negligible overhead in inference latency. Overall, our approach significantly improves the efficiency-effectiveness trade-off in OOD detection. Code is available at: https://github.com/litianliu/fDBD-OOD.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input differs from the data a model was trained to handle. Feature-based detectors can be effective, but building auxiliary models from training features adds computational overhead. This paper proposes using distances from an input’s features to the classifier’s decision boundaries without an auxiliary model.

To make this practical, the authors derive a closed-form estimate and prove that it tightly lower-bounds the distance. Using that estimate, they observe that in-distribution features tend to lie farther from decision boundaries than out-of-distribution features. They also find clearer separation when comparing samples with equal deviations from the mean training feature.

The detector therefore adjusts boundary distances according to that deviation, producing a method that requires neither hyperparameters nor an auxiliary model. Extensive experiments show effectiveness matching or exceeding state-of-the-art methods while adding negligible inference latency. The findings indicate that boundary geometry, interpreted alongside distance from the feature mean, can provide a useful detection signal at low computational cost.
summary.tldr: The detector uses efficiently estimated feature-to-boundary distances to detect unfamiliar inputs with strong reported accuracy and negligible inference overhead.

title: Fast Decision Boundary based Out-of-Distribution Detector

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in diverse areas, yet struggle with complex scientific reasoning, especially in the field of chemistry. Different from the simple chemistry tasks (e.g., molecule classification) addressed in previous studies, complex chemistry problems require not only vast knowledge and precise calculation, but also compositional reasoning about rich dynamic interactions of different concepts (e.g., temperature changes). Our study shows that even advanced LLMs, like GPT-4, can fail easily in different ways. Interestingly, the errors often stem not from a lack of domain knowledge within the LLMs, but rather from the absence of an effective reasoning structure that guides the LLMs to elicit the right knowledge, incorporate the knowledge in step-by-step reasoning, and iteratively refine results for further improved quality. On this basis, we introduce StructChem, a simple yet effective prompting strategy that offers the desired guidance and substantially boosts the LLMs’ chemical reasoning capability. Testing across four chemistry areas—quantum chemistry, mechanics, physical chemistry, and kinetics—StructChem substantially enhances GPT-4’s performance, with up to 30% peak improvement. Our analysis also underscores the unique difficulties of precise grounded reasoning in science with LLMs, highlighting a need for more research in this area.

paragraphs: StructChem addresses complex chemistry problems that require knowledge, precise calculation, and reasoning about interacting concepts. The authors find that even advanced language models can fail in multiple ways on these tasks. Their analysis points to an organizational problem: errors often arise because the model lacks an effective reasoning structure, rather than because it lacks the necessary chemistry knowledge.

The proposed prompting strategy guides the model to retrieve relevant knowledge, incorporate it into step-by-step reasoning, and iteratively refine the result. This structure is intended to help the model use what it knows in a coordinated way. The intervention therefore focuses on the process through which an answer is developed.

Tests cover quantum chemistry, mechanics, physical chemistry, and kinetics. StructChem substantially improves GPT-4’s performance, with a reported peak improvement of up to 30%. That figure describes the maximum reported gain, rather than a uniform improvement across all settings. The analysis also identifies continuing difficulties with precise, grounded scientific reasoning, showing why improved prompting is useful while further research remains necessary.
summary.tldr: StructChem structures knowledge retrieval, step-by-step reasoning, and refinement to improve language-model performance on complex chemistry problems.

title: Structured Chemistry Reasoning with Large Language Models

abstract: The weighted squared loss is a common component in several Collaborative Filtering (CF) algorithms for item recommendation, including the representative implicit Alternating Least Squares (iALS). Despite its widespread use, this loss function lacks a clear connection to ranking objectives such as Discounted Cumulative Gain (DCG), posing a fundamental challenge in explaining the exceptional ranking performance observed in these algorithms. In this work, we make a breakthrough by establishing a connection between squared loss and ranking metrics through a Taylor expansion of the DCG-consistent surrogate loss—softmax loss. We also discover a new surrogate squared loss function, namely Ranking-Generalizable Squared (RG$^2$) loss, and conduct thorough theoretical analyses on the DCG-consistency of the proposed loss function. Later, we present an example of utilizing the RG$^2$ loss with Matrix Factorization (MF), coupled with a generalization upper bound and an ALS optimization algorithm that leverages closed-form solutions over all items. Experimental results over three public datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the RG$^2$ loss, exhibiting ranking performance on par with, or even surpassing, the softmax loss while achieving faster convergence.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems often train collaborative filtering models with weighted squared loss, even though their practical goal is to rank items well. The relationship between that training objective and ranking measures such as Discounted Cumulative Gain has been unclear. This paper supplies a theoretical connection that helps explain the observed success of squared-loss methods.

The authors use a Taylor expansion of softmax loss, a surrogate consistent with DCG, to connect squared objectives with ranking quality. They introduce Ranking-Generalizable Squared loss, abbreviated RG², and analyze its DCG-consistency. They then combine it with matrix factorization, providing a generalization upper bound and an alternating least-squares algorithm with closed-form updates over all items.

Experiments on three public datasets find that RG² achieves ranking performance comparable to or better than softmax loss while converging faster. The result suggests that an efficiently optimized squared objective can also be deliberately aligned with ranking goals. The paper supports this alignment through both theoretical analysis and observed recommendation performance.
summary.tldr: RG² connects efficient squared-loss recommendation training with ranking objectives and matches or exceeds softmax ranking performance in experiments.

title: Learning-Efficient Yet Generalizable Collaborative Filtering for Item Recommendation

abstract: Pre-trained language models (LMs) are able to perform complex reasoning without explicit fine-tuning. To understand how pre-training with a next-token prediction objective contributes to the emergence of such reasoning capability, we propose that we can view an LM as deriving new conclusions by aggregating indirect reasoning paths seen at pre-training time. We found this perspective effective in two important cases of reasoning: logic reasoning with knowledge graphs (KGs) and chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. More specifically, we formalize the reasoning paths as random walk paths on the knowledge/reasoning graphs. Analyses of learned LM distributions suggest that a weighted sum of relevant random walk path probabilities is a reasonable way to explain how LMs reason. Experiments and analysis on multiple KG and CoT datasets reveal the effect of training on random walk paths and suggest that augmenting unlabeled random walk reasoning paths can improve real-world multi-step reasoning performance.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how next-token pretraining might produce reasoning ability without explicit reasoning fine-tuning. It proposes viewing a language model as combining indirect reasoning paths encountered during training to derive new conclusions. The authors examine this perspective in two settings: logical reasoning over knowledge graphs and chain-of-thought reasoning.

They formalize reasoning paths as random walks through knowledge or reasoning graphs. Analysis of learned model distributions suggests that a weighted sum of relevant path probabilities can reasonably explain the models' reasoning behavior. This provides a mathematical way to connect exposure to individual paths during training with conclusions that depend on combining those paths.

Experiments and analyses across several knowledge-graph and chain-of-thought datasets explore the effects of training on random-walk paths. The results suggest that adding unlabeled reasoning paths can improve real-world multi-step reasoning. The paper therefore offers both an explanatory perspective and a possible training-data intervention. Its account is presented as supported and useful in the studied cases, rather than as a complete explanation of every form of language-model reasoning.
summary.tldr: Language-model reasoning can be usefully viewed as aggregating learned reasoning paths, and experiments suggest that adding unlabeled paths can improve multi-step reasoning.

title: Understanding Reasoning Ability of Language Models From the Perspective of Reasoning Paths Aggregation

abstract: This paper presents FedType, a simple yet pioneering framework designed to fill research gaps in heterogeneous model aggregation within federated learning (FL). FedType introduces small identical proxy models for clients, serving as agents for information exchange, ensuring model security, and achieving efficient communication simultaneously. To transfer knowledge between large private and small proxy models on clients, we propose a novel uncertainty-based asymmetrical reciprocity learning method, eliminating the need for any public data. Comprehensive experiments conducted on benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficacy and generalization ability of FedType across diverse settings. Our approach redefines federated learning paradigms by bridging model heterogeneity, eliminating reliance on public data, prioritizing client privacy, and reducing communication costs (The codes are available in the supplementation materials).

paragraphs: Federated learning becomes harder when participants use different kinds of models. FedType addresses this model heterogeneity by giving each client a small proxy model with the same design. These proxies provide a common mechanism for exchanging information while clients retain their larger private models.

The central challenge is transferring knowledge between each private model and its smaller proxy. FedType uses uncertainty-based asymmetrical reciprocity learning for this exchange, allowing the two models to contribute through an asymmetric learning relationship. The approach does not require public data, so its knowledge-transfer mechanism avoids depending on a shared public dataset.

The small, identical proxies serve several purposes together: bridging differences between private models, supporting model security, and lowering communication costs. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate effectiveness and generalization across diverse settings. The contribution is a framework in which clients can collaborate despite model differences, with knowledge exchange handled through lightweight intermediaries. Its reported benefits concern that combination of heterogeneous participation, private models, and efficient communication.
summary.tldr: FedType uses small shared-design proxy models to connect heterogeneous private models without requiring public data.

title: Bridging Model Heterogeneity in Federated Learning via Uncertainty-based Asymmetrical Reciprocity Learning

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in graph classification tasks. However, ensuring the explainability of their predictions remains a challenge. To address this, graph rationalization methods have been introduced to generate concise subsets of the original graph, known as rationales, which serve to explain the predictions made by GNNs. Existing rationalizations often rely on shortcuts in data for prediction and rationale composition. In response, de-shortcut rationalization methods have been proposed, which commonly leverage counterfactual augmentation to enhance data diversity for mitigating the shortcut problem. Nevertheless, these methods have predominantly focused on centralized datasets and have not been extensively explored in the Federated Learning (FL) scenarios. To this end, in this paper, we propose a Federated Graph Rationalization (FedGR) with anti-shortcut augmentations to achieve self-explaining GNNs, which involves two data augmenters. These augmenters are employed to produce client-specific shortcut conflicted samples at each client, which contributes to mitigating the shortcut problem under the FL scenarios. Experiments on real-world benchmarks and synthetic datasets validate the effectiveness of FedGR under the FL scenarios.

paragraphs: Graph rationalization explains a graph classifier’s prediction by selecting a concise subset of the original graph. However, a small explanation is not automatically reliable: both the prediction and its selected rationale can depend on shortcuts in the data. Existing methods that counter these shortcuts have largely studied centralized datasets.

FedGR brings this problem into federated learning, where the method must address shortcuts associated with individual clients. It introduces two data augmenters that produce client-specific samples conflicting with those shortcuts. These examples are intended to weaken the usefulness of shortcut information during learning and help the model produce more meaningful rationales.

The approach matters because explainability and shortcut resistance are treated as connected learning problems within the federated setting. Rather than relying solely on concise graph subsets, it changes the training examples used to learn those subsets and predictions. Experiments on real-world benchmarks and synthetic datasets support FedGR’s effectiveness in federated learning. The stated result is mitigation of shortcut reliance, rather than a guarantee that every explanation is shortcut-free.
summary.tldr: FedGR uses client-specific augmentations that conflict with shortcuts to improve graph rationalization in federated learning.

title: Federated Self-Explaining GNNs with Anti-shortcut Augmentations

abstract: We study online learning in adversarial nonstationary environments. Since the future can be very different from the past, a critical challenge is to gracefully forget the history while new data comes in. To formalize this intuition, we revisit the discounted regret in online convex optimization, and propose an adaptive (i.e., instance optimal), FTRL-based algorithm that improves the widespread non-adaptive baseline – gradient descent with a constant learning rate. From a practical perspective, this refines the classical idea of regularization in lifelong learning: we show that designing better regularizers can be guided by the principled theory of adaptive online optimization. Complementing this result, we also consider the (Gibbs & Candes, 2021)-style online conformal prediction problem, where the goal is to sequentially predict the uncertainty sets of a black-box machine learning model. We show that the FTRL nature of our algorithm can simplify the conventional gradient-descent-based analysis, leading to instance-dependent performance guarantees.

paragraphs: Online learning must update decisions as data arrives, but older observations can become less useful when conditions change. This paper studies that problem in adversarial, nonstationary environments. It revisits discounted regret in online convex optimization, giving formal expression to the idea that a learner should gradually reduce the influence of its history.

The proposed algorithm uses Follow-the-Regularized-Leader, or FTRL, and adapts to the particular learning instance. The authors establish instance-optimal behavior and improve on the non-adaptive baseline of gradient descent with a constant learning rate. This connects forgetting to regularization: the theory of adaptive online optimization can guide the design of regularizers for lifelong learning.

The paper also applies the approach to online conformal prediction, where a system repeatedly produces uncertainty sets for a black-box model. The FTRL structure simplifies the conventional gradient-descent-based analysis and yields guarantees that depend on the instance. Together, these results connect adaptive learning rules with both changing environments and sequential uncertainty prediction.
summary.tldr: An adaptive FTRL algorithm uses discounted regret to guide forgetting and regularization, with additional guarantees for online uncertainty prediction.

title: Discounted Adaptive Online Learning: Towards Better Regularization

abstract: Software engineering activities frequently involve edits to existing code. However, contemporary code language models (LMs) lack the ability to handle diverse types of code-edit requirements. In this work, we attempt to overcome this shortcoming through (1) a novel synthetic data generation pipeline and (2) a robust model adaptation algorithm. Starting with seed code examples and diverse editing criteria, our pipeline generates high-quality samples comprising original and modified code, along with natural language instructions in different styles and verbosity. Today’s code LMs come bundled with strong abilities, such as code generation and instruction following, which should not be lost due to fine-tuning. To ensure this, we propose a novel adaptation algorithm, SeleKT, that (a) leverages a dense gradient-based step to identify the weights that are most important for code editing, and (b) does a sparse projection onto the base model to avoid overfitting. Using our approach, we obtain a new series of models NextCoder (adapted from QwenCoder-2.5) that achieves strong results on five code-editing benchmarks, outperforming comparable size models and even several larger ones. We show the generality of our approach on two model families DeepSeekCoder and QwenCoder), compare against other fine-tuning approaches, and demonstrate robustness by showing retention of code generation and general problem-solving abilities post adaptation. We opensource the models, synthetic dataset, and implementation at https://aka.ms/nextcoder.

paragraphs: Software development often requires modifying existing code according to varied instructions. NextCoder addresses this capability through both training data and model adaptation. Its synthetic-data pipeline starts from seed programs and editing criteria, producing original code, modified code, and instructions that vary in wording style and level of detail.

The adaptation algorithm, SeleKT, aims to improve editing while retaining abilities already present in the base model. It first uses a dense gradient-based step to identify weights important for editing, then applies a sparse projection onto the base model to avoid overfitting. This design makes preservation of existing capabilities part of the adaptation procedure, alongside learning the new task.

NextCoder models adapted from QwenCoder-2.5 perform strongly on five editing benchmarks, surpassing comparable-size models and several larger ones. The authors also test their approach with DeepSeekCoder and QwenCoder, compare it with other fine-tuning methods, and show retention of code generation and general problem-solving abilities. These results support the combination of diverse synthetic edits and selective adaptation, with models, data, and implementation released for reuse.
summary.tldr: NextCoder combines diverse synthetic editing data with selective adaptation to improve code edits while retaining broader coding abilities.

title: NextCoder: Robust Adaptation of Code LMs to Diverse Code Edits

abstract: Quality statistical inference requires a sufficient amount of data, which can be missing or hard to obtain. To this end, prediction-powered inference has risen as a promising methodology, but existing approaches are largely limited to Z-estimation problems such as inference of means and quantiles. In this paper, we apply ideas of prediction-powered inference to e-values. By doing so, we inherit all the usual benefits of e-values – such as anytime-validity, post-hoc validity and versatile sequential inference – as well as greatly expand the set of inferences achievable in a prediction-powered manner. In particular, we show that every inference procedure that can be framed in terms of e-values has a prediction-powered counterpart, given by our method. We showcase the effectiveness of our framework across a wide range of inference tasks, from simple hypothesis testing and confidence intervals to more involved procedures for change-point detection and causal discovery, which were out of reach of previous techniques. Our approach is modular and easily integrable into existing algorithms, making it a compelling choice for practical applications.
