paragraphs: Prediction-powered inference uses machine learning predictions to help make statistical conclusions when directly obtained data is scarce or costly. Existing approaches largely focus on Z-estimation problems, including means and quantiles. This paper extends the idea to e-values, opening a broader route for incorporating predictions into statistical procedures.

The central result is that every inference procedure expressible through e-values has a prediction-powered counterpart under the proposed method. This preserves the usual benefits of e-values, including anytime validity, post-hoc validity, and flexible sequential inference. The scope is broad but specific: the result applies to procedures that can be framed in terms of e-values.

The authors demonstrate the framework on hypothesis tests, confidence intervals, change-point detection, and causal discovery. The latter tasks extend beyond what the previous techniques described in the abstract could handle. Because the approach is modular, it can be integrated into existing algorithms. Its significance is the expansion of prediction-powered inference from a relatively narrow set of estimation tasks to a general family of evidence-based procedures.
summary.tldr: The framework gives e-value-based inference procedures prediction-powered counterparts while retaining their sequential and validity benefits.

title: Prediction-Powered E-Values

abstract: Conformal Prediction is a widely studied technique to construct prediction sets of future observations. Most conformal prediction methods focus on achieving the necessary coverage guarantees, but do not provide formal guarantees on the size (volume) of the prediction sets. We first prove the impossibility of volume optimality where any distribution-free method can only find a trivial solution. We then introduce a new notion of volume optimality by restricting the prediction sets to belong to a set family (of finite VC-dimension), specifically a union of $k$-intervals. Our main contribution is an efficient distribution-free algorithm based on dynamic programming (DP) to find a union of $k$-intervals that is guaranteed for any distribution to have near-optimal volume among all unions of $k$-intervals satisfying the desired coverage property. By adopting the framework of distributional conformal prediction (Chernozhukov et al., 2021), the new DP based conformity score can also be applied to achieve approximate conditional coverage and conditional restricted volume optimality, as long as a reasonable estimator of the conditional CDF is available. While the theoretical results already establish volume-optimality guarantees, they are complemented by experiments that demonstrate that our method can significantly outperform existing methods in many settings.

paragraphs: A prediction set can meet its coverage target yet remain too large to be informative. This paper studies formal guarantees on set volume in conformal prediction. It first proves an impossibility result for unrestricted distribution-free volume optimality, then changes the objective by limiting the family of prediction sets under consideration.

The main construction uses unions of k intervals, a structured family with finite VC-dimension. An efficient dynamic-programming algorithm finds a set whose volume is near-optimal among unions of k intervals satisfying the desired coverage property, for any distribution. The restriction is central: the comparison is against other sets in the same family, making a meaningful volume guarantee possible.

The authors also extend the conformity score through distributional conformal prediction. With a reasonable estimator of the conditional cumulative distribution function, this supports approximate conditional coverage and conditional restricted volume optimality. Experiments show substantial improvements over existing methods in many settings. The results connect informative set size with explicit structural choices, while keeping the conditional claims dependent on the stated estimation requirement.
summary.tldr: Restricting prediction sets to unions of k intervals enables efficient, distribution-free near-optimal volume guarantees that are unavailable without such structure.

title: Volume Optimality in Conformal Prediction with Structured Prediction Sets

abstract: Personalized Federated Learning (PFL) has become a promising learning paradigm, enabling the training of high-quality personalized models through multiple communication rounds between clients and a central server. However, directly applying traditional PFL in real-world environments where communication is expensive, limited, or infeasible is challenging, as seen in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite constellations, which face severe communication constraints due to their high mobility, limited contact windows. To address these issues, we introduce Federated Oriented Learning (FOL), a novel four-stage one-shot PFL algorithm designed to enhance local model performance by leveraging neighboring models within stringent communication constraints. FOL comprises model pretraining, model collection, model alignment (via fine-tuning, pruning, post fine-tuning, and ensemble refinement), and knowledge distillation stages. We establish two theoretical guarantees on empirical risk discrepancy between student and teacher models and the convergence of the distillation process. Extensive experiments on datasets Wildfire, Hurricane, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN demonstrate that FOL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art one-shot Federated Learning (OFL) methods; for example, it achieves accuracy improvements of up to 39.24% over the baselines on the Wildfire dataset.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning usually improves local models through repeated communication between clients and a server. That process is difficult when connections are expensive or brief, as in low Earth orbit satellite constellations. Federated Oriented Learning addresses this setting with a one-shot framework that uses neighboring models to improve local performance under strict communication constraints.

FOL has four stages: pretraining models, collecting models, aligning them, and distilling their knowledge. Alignment includes fine-tuning, pruning, further fine-tuning, and ensemble refinement. The final distillation stage transfers knowledge from teacher models into a student. This sequence concentrates the work of adapting and combining collected models into a local learning process suitable for limited communication.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees concerning the empirical-risk discrepancy between teacher and student and convergence of distillation. Experiments on Wildfire, Hurricane, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN consistently outperform the compared one-shot federated methods. On Wildfire, reported accuracy improvements reach up to 39.24% over baselines, supporting the usefulness of the framework in the evaluated communication-constrained setting.
summary.tldr: FOL improves personalized local models through one-shot model sharing, alignment, and knowledge distillation under severe communication constraints.

title: Federated Oriented Learning: A Practical One-Shot Personalized Federated Learning Framework

abstract: Several recent studies have attempted to autoregressively generate continuous speech representations without discrete speech tokens by combining diffusion and autoregressive models, yet they often face challenges with excessive computational loads or suboptimal outcomes. In this work, we propose Diffusion Transformer Autoregressive Modeling (DiTAR), a patch-based autoregressive framework combining a language model with a diffusion transformer. This approach significantly enhances the efficacy of autoregressive models for continuous tokens and reduces computational demands. DiTAR utilizes a divide-and-conquer strategy for patch generation, where the language model processes aggregated patch embeddings, and the diffusion transformer subsequently generates the next patch based on the output of the language model. For inference, we propose defining temperature as the time point of introducing noise during the reverse diffusion ODE to balance diversity and determinism. We also show in the extensive scaling analysis that DiTAR has superb scalability. In zero-shot speech generation, DiTAR achieves state-of-the-art performance in robustness, speaker similarity, and naturalness.

paragraphs: DiTAR generates speech using continuous representations without first converting speech into discrete tokens. The paper addresses the computational burden and quality difficulties encountered when combining autoregressive generation with diffusion. Its approach divides speech generation into patches and assigns different parts of the work to a language model and a diffusion transformer.

The language model processes aggregated embeddings that summarize patches. Its output then conditions the diffusion transformer, which generates the next patch. This division lets the autoregressive component work with summaries while the diffusion component constructs the patch itself. The authors report that this organization improves the effectiveness of continuous-token autoregression and reduces computational demands.

The paper also introduces an inference-time temperature defined by when noise enters the reverse diffusion ordinary differential equation, providing a control over diversity and determinism. A scaling analysis reports strong scalability, and zero-shot speech experiments achieve state-of-the-art robustness, speaker similarity, and naturalness. Together, these results support patch-based division of work as an effective architecture for continuous speech generation.
summary.tldr: DiTAR combines patch-level autoregression with diffusion to improve the efficiency and quality of continuous speech generation.

title: DiTAR: Diffusion Transformer Autoregressive Modeling for Speech Generation

abstract: We obtain an analytic, interpretable and predictive theory of creativity in convolutional diffusion models. Indeed, score-matching diffusion models can generate highly original images that lie far from their training data. However, optimal score-matching theory suggests that these models should only be able to produce memorized training examples. To reconcile this theory-experiment gap, we identify two simple inductive biases, locality and equivariance, that: (1) induce a form of combinatorial creativity by preventing optimal score-matching; (2) result in fully analytic, completely mechanistically interpretable, local score (LS) and equivariant local score (ELS) machines that, (3) after calibrating a single time-dependent hyperparameter can quantitatively predict the outputs of trained convolution only diffusion models (like ResNets and UNets) with high accuracy (median $r^2$ of $0.95, 0.94, 0.94, 0.96$ for our top model on CIFAR10, FashionMNIST, MNIST, and CelebA). Our model reveals a locally consistent patch mosaic mechanism of creativity, in which diffusion models create exponentially many novel images by mixing and matching different local training set patches at different scales and image locations. Our theory also partially predicts the outputs of pre-trained self-attention enabled UNets (median $r^2 \sim 0.77$ on CIFAR10), revealing an intriguing role for attention in carving out semantic coherence from local patch mosaics.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate images that differ greatly from their training examples, yet optimal score-matching theory suggests memorization. This paper explains that apparent conflict through two architectural biases: locality and equivariance. These biases prevent the idealized optimum and enable a form of creativity based on recombining information from training images.

The authors derive analytic local score and equivariant local score models whose operations can be interpreted directly. After calibrating one time-dependent hyperparameter, these models predict the outputs of trained convolution-only diffusion networks with high accuracy. The proposed mechanism constructs locally consistent mosaics by combining training-image patches across locations and scales, supporting exponentially many novel combinations.

Across four image datasets, the strongest analytic model achieves median r-squared values between 0.94 and 0.96 for convolution-only networks. Its predictions are less complete for an attention-enabled UNet, reaching about 0.77 on CIFAR10. This difference suggests a role for attention in organizing local patch combinations into semantically coherent images, while the theory explains much of the convolutional contribution.
summary.tldr: An analytic theory explains convolutional diffusion creativity as locally consistent recombination of training-image patches.

title: An analytic theory of creativity in convolutional diffusion models

abstract: The optimal transport barycenter (a.k.a. Wasserstein barycenter) is a fundamental notion of averaging that extends from the Euclidean space to the Wasserstein space of probability distributions. Computation of the unregularized barycenter for discretized probability distributions on point clouds is a challenging task when the domain dimension $d > 1$. Most practical algorithms for approximating the barycenter problem are based on entropic regularization. In this paper, we introduce a nearly linear time $O(m \log{m})$ and linear space complexity $O(m)$ primal-dual algorithm, the Wasserstein-Descent $\dot{\mathbb{H}}^1$-Ascent (WDHA) algorithm, for computing the exact barycenter when the input probability density functions are discretized on an $m$-point grid. The key success of the WDHA algorithm hinges on alternating between two different yet closely related Wasserstein and Sobolev optimization geometries for the primal barycenter and dual Kantorovich potential subproblems. Under reasonable assumptions, we establish the convergence rate and iteration complexity of WDHA to its stationary point when the step size is appropriately chosen. Superior computational efficacy, scalability, and accuracy over the existing Sinkhorn-type algorithms are demonstrated on high-resolution (e.g., $1024 \times 1024$ images) 2D synthetic and real data.

paragraphs: A Wasserstein barycenter extends averaging to probability distributions using optimal transport. Computing an unregularized barycenter becomes challenging beyond one dimension, so practical methods often introduce entropic regularization. This paper introduces WDHA to compute the exact, unregularized barycenter for probability densities discretized on an m-point grid.

WDHA is a primal-dual algorithm that alternates between two optimization geometries. It uses Wasserstein geometry for the barycenter subproblem and Sobolev geometry for the dual Kantorovich potential subproblem. The paper reports nearly linear time complexity, O(m log m), and linear space complexity, O(m), making the grid size central to its computational scaling.

Under stated reasonable assumptions and an appropriate step size, the authors establish convergence rates and iteration complexity to a stationary point. That guarantee should be distinguished from an unconditional guarantee of reaching a global optimum. Evaluations on synthetic and real two-dimensional data, including 1024-by-1024 images, demonstrate better computational efficacy, scalability, and accuracy than existing Sinkhorn-type algorithms. The results support the value of matching the two subproblems to different optimization geometries.
summary.tldr: WDHA tackles unregularized Wasserstein barycenters with complementary optimization geometries and conditional convergence guarantees to a stationary point.

title: Optimal Transport Barycenter via Nonconvex-Concave Minimax Optimization

abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative audio synthesis and editing technologies has raised significant concerns about copyright infringement, data provenance, and the spread of misinformation through deepfake audio. Watermarking offers a proactive solution by embedding imperceptible, identifiable, and traceable marks into audio content. While recent neural network-based watermarking methods like WavMark and AudioSeal have improved robustness and quality, they struggle to achieve both robust detection and accurate attribution simultaneously. This paper introduces the Cross-Attention Robust Audio Watermark (XAttnMark), which bridges this gap by leveraging partial parameter sharing between the generator and the detector, a cross-attention mechanism for efficient message retrieval, and a temporal conditioning module for improved message distribution. Additionally, we propose a psychoacoustic-aligned temporal-frequency masking loss that captures fine-grained auditory masking effects, enhancing watermark imperceptibility. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in both detection and attribution, demonstrating superior robustness against a wide range of audio transformations, including challenging generative editing with strong editing strength. This work represents a significant step forward in protecting intellectual property and ensuring the authenticity of audio content in the era of generative AI.

paragraphs: Audio watermarking embeds identifiable information into sound while aiming to keep the mark imperceptible. A useful system must both detect the presence of a watermark and recover information for attribution. This paper addresses the difficulty of achieving both goals robustly, especially when audio undergoes transformations or generative editing.

XAttnMark partially shares parameters between the watermark generator and detector. It uses cross-attention to retrieve the embedded message and a temporal conditioning module to improve how that message is distributed. These components connect watermark creation with the later task of finding and reading it after the audio has changed.

The training objective also includes a temporal-frequency masking loss aligned with auditory masking effects, helping the watermark remain imperceptible. Reported evaluations achieve state-of-the-art detection and attribution performance, with superior robustness across a wide range of transformations, including strong generative edits. The findings support jointly designing message insertion, retrieval, and perceptual quality when building audio watermarks intended to survive subsequent modification.
summary.tldr: XAttnMark combines cross-attention message retrieval and perceptually informed training to improve audio watermark detection, attribution, and robustness.

title: XAttnMark: Learning Robust Audio Watermarking with Cross-Attention

abstract: Conformal prediction is a powerful tool for constructing prediction intervals for black-box models, providing a finite sample coverage guarantee for exchangeable data. However, this exchangeability is compromised when some entries of the test feature are contaminated, such as in the case of cellwise outliers. To address this issue, this paper introduces a novel framework called detect-then-impute conformal prediction. This framework first employs an outlier detection procedure on the test feature and then utilizes an imputation method to fill in those cells identified as outliers. To quantify the uncertainty in the processed test feature, we adaptively apply the detection and imputation procedures to the calibration set, thereby constructing exchangeable features for the conformal prediction interval of the test label. We develop two practical algorithms, $\texttt{PDI-CP}$ and $\texttt{JDI-CP}$, and provide a distribution-free coverage analysis under some commonly used detection and imputation procedures. Notably, $\texttt{JDI-CP}$ achieves a finite sample $1-2\alpha$ coverage guarantee. Numerical experiments on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that our proposed algorithms exhibit robust coverage properties and comparable efficiency to the oracle baseline.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction constructs prediction intervals with finite-sample coverage guarantees when data are exchangeable. Corruption in individual entries of a test example can undermine that condition. This paper addresses such cellwise outliers, where the difficulty comes from contaminated features rather than necessarily from an entirely unusable example.

The proposed framework first detects suspicious feature entries and then replaces them through imputation. Crucially, it also adaptively applies detection and imputation to the calibration data. That additional step accounts for uncertainty in the processed test features and constructs exchangeable features for forming the test-label interval. The method therefore connects data repair with the calibration procedure needed for uncertainty guarantees.

The authors develop two algorithms, PDI-CP and JDI-CP, and analyze distribution-free coverage under commonly used detection and imputation procedures. In particular, JDI-CP has a finite-sample coverage guarantee of 1−2α. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show robust coverage and efficiency comparable to an oracle baseline, supporting the value of coordinating outlier handling with conformal calibration.
summary.tldr: Coordinating outlier detection and imputation with conformal calibration supports reliable prediction intervals for partially corrupted test features.

title: Conformal Prediction with Cellwise Outliers: A Detect-then-Impute Approach

abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge models generate chain-of-thought (CoT) sequences intended to capture the step-by-step reasoning process that underlies the final evaluation of a response. However, due to the lack of human-annotated CoTs for evaluation, the required components and structure of effective reasoning traces remain understudied. Consequently, previous approaches often (1) constrain reasoning traces to hand-designed components, such as a list of criteria, reference answers, or verification questions and (2) structure them such that planning is intertwined with the reasoning for evaluation. In this work, we propose EvalPlanner, a preference optimization algorithm for Thinking-LLM-as-a-Judge that first generates an unconstrained evaluation plan, followed by its execution, and then the final judgment. In a self-training loop, EvalPlanner iteratively optimizes over synthetically constructed evaluation plans and executions, leading to better final verdicts. Our method achieves a new state-of-the-art performance for generative reward models on RewardBench and PPE, despite being trained on fewer amount of, and synthetically generated, preference pairs. Additional experiments on other benchmarks like RM-Bench, JudgeBench, and FollowBenchEval further highlight the utility of both planning and reasoning for building robust LLM-as-a-Judge reasoning models.

paragraphs: Language models used as judges often explain their evaluations through step-by-step reasoning. However, effective evaluation reasoning is difficult to study without human-annotated examples. Existing designs frequently prescribe specific components, such as criteria or verification questions, and mix deciding how to evaluate with carrying out the evaluation. This paper separates those activities.

EvalPlanner first produces an unconstrained evaluation plan, then executes that plan, and finally gives a judgment. A preference-optimization algorithm trains this process through repeated self-training on synthetically constructed plans and executions. The model therefore learns how to organize its evaluation as well as how to reason toward a verdict.

The authors report state-of-the-art results for generative reward models on RewardBench and PPE despite training with fewer preference pairs that were synthetically generated. Further experiments on RM-Bench, JudgeBench, and FollowBenchEval support the usefulness of planning and reasoning. The findings indicate that explicitly separating planning from execution can improve the final evaluations produced by an LLM judge.
summary.tldr: EvalPlanner trains LLM judges to plan, execute their evaluation, and then decide, improving benchmark performance through synthetic self-training.

title: Learning to Plan & Reason for Evaluation with Thinking-LLM-as-a-Judge

abstract: In this work, we unveil and study idiosyncrasies in Large Language Models (LLMs) – unique patterns in their outputs that can be used to distinguish the models. To do so, we consider a simple classification task: given a particular text output, the objective is to predict the source LLM that generates the text. We evaluate this synthetic task across various groups of LLMs and find that simply fine-tuning text embedding models on LLM-generated texts yields excellent classification accuracy. Notably, we achieve 97.1% accuracy on held-out validation data in the five-way classification problem involving ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini, and DeepSeek. Our further investigation reveals that these idiosyncrasies are rooted in word-level distributions. These patterns persist even when the texts are rewritten, translated, or summarized by an external LLM, suggesting that they are also encoded in the semantic content. Additionally, we leverage LLM as judges to generate detailed, open-ended descriptions of each model’s idiosyncrasies. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of our findings, including training on synthetic data, inferring model similarity, and robust evaluation of LLMs.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether a language model leaves recognizable patterns in the text it generates. The authors turn that question into a classification task: given a passage, predict which model produced it. Fine-tuning text embedding models on generated examples yields strong classification performance across several groups of language models.

For a five-way task involving ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini, and DeepSeek, the classifier reaches 97.1% accuracy on held-out validation data. Further analysis connects these distinctive patterns to word-level distributions. The patterns also persist when another language model rewrites, translates, or summarizes the text, suggesting that semantic content carries some of the distinguishing information.

The authors additionally use language models as judges to describe each model's tendencies in open-ended language. These descriptions complement the classification results by examining what the differences look like. The findings raise questions for synthetic-data training, assessments of model similarity, and robust evaluation, because generated text can retain information about its source through substantial transformations.
summary.tldr: Language models leave distinguishable textual patterns that can persist through rewriting, translation, and summarization.

title: Idiosyncrasies in Large Language Models

abstract: Armijo line-search (Armijo-LS) is a standard method to set the step-size for gradient descent (GD). For smooth functions, Armijo-LS alleviates the need to know the global smoothness constant $L$ and adapts to the “local” smoothness, enabling GD to converge faster. Existing theoretical analyses show that GD with Armijo-LS ($\texttt{GD-LS}$) can result in constant factor improvements over GD with a $1/L$ step-size (denoted as $\texttt{GD(1/L)}$). We strengthen these results and show that if the objective function satisfies a certain non-uniform smoothness condition, $\texttt{GD-LS}$ can result in a faster convergence rate than $\texttt{GD(1/L)}$. In particular, we prove that for convex objectives corresponding to logistic regression and multi-class classification, $\texttt{GD-LS}$ can converge to the optimum at a linear rate, and hence improves over the sublinear convergence of $\texttt{GD(1/L)}$. Furthermore, for non-convex objectives satisfying gradient domination (e.g., those corresponding to the softmax policy gradient in RL or generalized linear models with a logistic link function), $\texttt{GD-LS}$ can match the fast convergence of algorithms tailored for these specific settings. Finally, we analyze the convergence of stochastic GD with a stochastic line-search on convex losses under the interpolation assumption.

Armijo line-search instead chooses steps adaptively, responding to local behavior without requiring that global constant in advance.

Earlier theory established constant-factor improvements from this adaptation. There, the method can match fast algorithms designed for those settings. A separate stochastic analysis covers convex losses under interpolation. Together, these results explain when a standard adaptive step-size rule can provide more than a modest speed improvement.
summary.tldr: Under specified objective conditions, Armijo line-search improves gradient descent's convergence rate rather than merely its constant factors.

title: Armijo Line-search Can Make (Stochastic) Gradient Descent Provably Faster

abstract: Off-Policy Evaluation (OPE) aims to estimate the value of a target policy using offline data collected from potentially different policies. In real-world applications, however, logged data often suffers from missingness. While OPE has been extensively studied in the literature, a theoretical understanding of how missing data affects OPE results remains unclear. In this paper, we investigate OPE in the presence of monotone missingness and theoretically demonstrate that the value estimates remain unbiased under ignorable missingness but can be biased under nonignorable (informative) missingness. To retain the consistency of value estimation, we propose an inverse probability weighting value estimator and conduct statistical inference to quantify the uncertainty of the estimates. Through a series of numerical experiments, we empirically demonstrate that our proposed estimator yields a more reliable value inference under missing data.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a target decision policy would perform using data collected under other policies. Missing entries in that historical data can complicate the estimate. This paper studies how missingness affects policy-value estimation, focusing specifically on the setting of monotone missingness.

The theoretical analysis distinguishes ignorable missingness from nonignorable, or informative, missingness. It shows that value estimates remain unbiased in the former case but can become biased in the latter. The distinction matters because the reasons observations are absent can affect what the remaining logged data tells us about a policy's value.

To retain consistent estimation, the authors propose an estimator based on inverse probability weighting. They also develop statistical inference to quantify uncertainty around the value estimates. Numerical experiments find more reliable value inference under missing data. The contribution combines an explanation of when missingness can distort evaluation with a corrective estimation method and uncertainty analysis, within the missing-data setting studied by the paper.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes missing-data bias in off-policy evaluation and proposes inverse probability weighting with uncertainty quantification.

title: Off-Policy Evaluation under Nonignorable Missing Data

abstract: Learning lighting adaptation is a crucial step in achieving good visual perception and supporting downstream vision tasks. Current research often addresses individual light-related challenges, such as high dynamic range imaging and exposure correction, in isolation. However, we identify shared fundamental properties across these tasks: i) different color channels have different light properties, and ii) the channel differences reflected in the spatial and frequency domains are different. Leveraging these insights, we introduce the channel-aware Learning Adaptive Lighting Network (LALNet), a multi-task framework designed to handle multiple light-related tasks efficiently. Specifically, LALNet incorporates color-separated features that highlight the unique light properties of each color channel, integrated with traditional color-mixed features by Light Guided Attention (LGA). The LGA utilizes color-separated features to guide color-mixed features focusing on channel differences and ensuring visual consistency across all channels. Additionally, LALNet employs dual domain channel modulation for generating color-separated features and a mixed channel modulation and light state space module for producing color-mixed features. Extensive experiments on four representative light-related tasks demonstrate that LALNet significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on benchmark tests and requires fewer computational resources. We provide an anonymous online demo at LALNet.

paragraphs: Lighting problems such as exposure correction and high dynamic range imaging are often studied separately. This paper looks for shared structure across those tasks. It identifies two relevant properties: color channels respond differently to light, and those differences appear differently in spatial and frequency representations. LALNet uses these observations to build a multitask lighting-adaptation framework.

The network maintains both color-separated features and conventional features that mix channels. Light Guided Attention uses the separated features to guide the mixed features toward relevant channel differences while preserving visual consistency across channels. Dual-domain channel modulation generates the separated features, while mixed-channel modulation and a light state space module produce the mixed features.

This arrangement gives the network access to channel-specific lighting information without losing a combined representation of the image. Experiments on four representative lighting tasks report substantial improvements over state-of-the-art methods on benchmark tests while using fewer computational resources. The findings support a shared channel-aware approach to several lighting problems, rather than requiring each task to be handled in isolation.
summary.tldr: LALNet combines channel-specific and mixed-color features to improve multiple lighting tasks with lower computational requirements.

title: Learning Adaptive Lighting via Channel-Aware Guidance

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential in scientific domains, yet a fundamental question remains unanswered: Can we simulate human research communities with LLMs? Addressing this question can deepen our understanding of the processes behind idea brainstorming and inspire the automatic discovery of novel scientific insights. In this work, we propose ResearchTown, a multi-agent framework for research community simulation. Within this framework, the human research community is simplified as an agent-data graph, where researchers and papers are represented as agent-type and data-type nodes, respectively, and connected based on their collaboration relationships. We also introduce TextGNN, a text-based inference framework that models various research activities (e.g., paper reading, paper writing, and review writing) as special forms of a unified message-passing process on the agent-data graph. To evaluate the quality of the research community simulation, we present ResearchBench, a benchmark that uses a node-masking prediction task for scalable and objective assessment based on similarity. Our experiments reveal three key findings: (1) ResearchTown can provide a realistic simulation of collaborative research activities, including paper writing and review writing; (2) ResearchTown can maintain robust simulation with multiple researchers and diverse papers; (3) ResearchTown can generate interdisciplinary research ideas that potentially inspire pioneering research directions.

paragraphs: ResearchTown investigates whether language-model agents can simulate collaborative research communities. It simplifies a community into a graph containing researcher agents and paper data nodes, connected through collaboration relationships. This representation provides a shared structure for studying activities involving multiple researchers and bodies of work.

Its TextGNN framework treats reading papers, writing papers, and writing reviews as variations of text-based message passing through that graph. The authors also introduce ResearchBench to evaluate simulation quality. Its node-masking task asks the system to predict hidden graph content and assesses similarity, creating a scalable way to compare simulations with the information being reconstructed.

Experiments indicate realistic simulations of collaborative writing and reviewing, with robust behavior across multiple researchers and diverse papers. ResearchTown also generates interdisciplinary ideas that could inspire new research directions. That potential is distinct from demonstrating a scientific discovery: the stated result concerns useful idea generation. The work combines a community representation, a unified activity model, and an evaluation benchmark for studying this possibility.
summary.tldr: ResearchTown simulates collaborative research through language-model agents and text-based graph message passing, including potentially useful interdisciplinary idea generation.

title: ResearchTown: Simulator of Human Research Community

abstract: Detecting a minor average treatment effect is a major challenge in large-scale applications, where even minimal improvements can have a significant economic impact. Traditional methods, reliant on normal distribution-based or expanded statistics, often fail to identify such minor effects because of their inability to handle small discrepancies with sufficient sensitivity. This work leverages a counterfactual outcome framework and proposes a maximum probability-driven two-armed bandit (TAB) process by weighting the mean volatility statistic, which controls Type I error. The implementation of permutation methods further enhances the robustness and efficacy. The established strategic central limit theorem (SCLT) demonstrates that our approach yields a more concentrated distribution under the null hypothesis and a less concentrated one under the alternative hypothesis, greatly improving statistical power. The experimental results indicate a significant improvement in the A/B testing, highlighting the potential to reduce experimental costs while maintaining high statistical power.

paragraphs: Small average treatment effects can matter economically in large-scale applications while remaining difficult to detect statistically. This paper develops an A/B testing method intended to improve sensitivity to these small differences. It uses a counterfactual outcome framework and a maximum probability-driven two-armed bandit process to construct the testing approach.

The method weights a mean volatility statistic while controlling Type I error, the risk of declaring an effect when the null hypothesis holds. Permutation methods further strengthen robustness and effectiveness. The authors establish a strategic central limit theorem showing that the resulting distribution is more concentrated under the null hypothesis and less concentrated under the alternative.

This difference in concentration underlies the reported improvement in statistical power, or the ability to detect an effect when one exists. Experiments show significant gains in A/B testing performance. The findings point to the potential for reducing experimental costs while retaining high power; cost reduction is presented as a possible benefit of the improved testing approach.
summary.tldr: A bandit-based A/B testing method improves sensitivity to small effects while controlling Type I error.

title: Strategic A/B testing via Maximum Probability-driven Two-armed Bandit

abstract: Sampling from unnormalized densities using diffusion models has emerged as a powerful paradigm. However, while recent approaches that use least-squares ‘matching’ objectives have improved scalability, they often necessitate significant trade-offs, such as restricting prior distributions or relying on unstable optimization schemes. By generalizing these methods as special forms of fixed-point iterations rooted in Nelson’s relation, we develop a new method that addresses these limitations. Our approach enables learning a stochastic transport map between arbitrary prior and target distributions with a single, scalable, and stable objective. Furthermore, we introduce a damped variant of this iteration that incorporates a regularization term to mitigate mode collapse. Empirically, we demonstrate that our method enables sampling at unprecedented scales while preserving mode diversity, achieving state-of-the-art results on complex synthetic densities and high-dimensional molecular benchmarks.

paragraphs: Sampling from an unnormalized density means generating examples when the target is specified without its overall normalization constant. Diffusion-based approaches can tackle this problem, and matching objectives have made them more scalable. However, existing approaches can require restrictive starting distributions or optimization procedures that are unstable, creating trade-offs in practical use.

The paper interprets these matching methods as particular fixed-point iterations based on Nelson’s relation. These findings support the proposed formulation as a way to expand sampling scale without sacrificing the diversity observed in those evaluations.
summary.tldr: Bridge Matching Sampler learns flexible diffusion transports with a stable objective and regularization that helps preserve sampling diversity.

title: Bridge Matching Sampler: Scalable Sampling via Generalized Fixed-Point Diffusion Matching

abstract: Concept unlearning in diffusion models is hampered by feature splitting, where concepts are distributed across many latent features, making their removal challenging and computationally expensive. We introduce SAEmnesia, a supervised sparse autoencoder framework that overcomes this by enforcing one-to-one concept-neuron mappings. By systematically labeling concepts during training, our method achieves feature centralization, binding each concept to a single, interpretable neuron. This enables highly targeted and efficient concept erasure. Compared to the state-of-the-art sparse autoencoder-based unlearning approach, SAEmnesia reduces hyperparameter search by 96.67% and achieves a 9.22% improvement on the UnlearnCanvas benchmark for objects. Our method also shows superior scalability in sequential unlearning, improving accuracy by 28.4% when removing nine objects, establishing a step forward for precise and controllable concept erasure. Moreover, SAEmnesia effectively suppresses nudity on the I2P benchmark and remains robust to adversarial attacks. Source code available at https://github.com/EIDOSLAB/SAEmnesia.

paragraphs: Removing a concept from a diffusion model is difficult when that concept is spread across many internal features. SAEmnesia addresses this feature-splitting problem with supervised sparse autoencoders. Additional evaluations show nudity suppression on I2P and robustness to adversarial attacks. Together, the reported results support supervised feature organization as a way to make concept erasure more precise and scalable across the tested settings.
summary.tldr: SAEmnesia concentrates concepts into individual sparse-autoencoder neurons to make diffusion-model concept erasure more targeted and efficient.

title: SAEmnesia: Erasing Concepts in Diffusion Models with Supervised Sparse Autoencoders

abstract: Many modern generative models can be viewed as minimizing divergences between probability distributions, yet they rely on different algorithmic and geometric principles. Wasserstein gradient flows provide a continuous-time formulation for optimizing over distributions, and can be approximated through their implicit discretization via the Jordan–Kinderlehrer–Otto (JKO) scheme. In this work, we present a unified theoretical framework for generative modeling based on Wasserstein gradient flows, which we refer to as Generative Wasserstein Flows (GWF). We show that a broad class of existing methods can be derived as instances of parametric JKO schemes for $f$-divergence objectives, and we establish equivalences between several recently proposed algorithms. We extend this framework beyond $f$-divergences to Integral Probability Metrics and squared Maximum Mean Discrepancy, deriving new JKO-based generative algorithms, and clarifying their connections with GANs. We study empirically the impact of the JKO regularization for a wide set of objectives. Finally, we analyze parametric Wasserstein flows, where the dynamics are restricted to distributions induced by parametrized maps.

paragraphs: Generative models often learn by making one probability distribution resemble another, but their training procedures can look quite different. This paper develops Generative Wasserstein Flows, a theoretical framework that places many such procedures within a common account of optimization over distributions. Its starting point is a continuous evolution described by Wasserstein gradient flows.

The connection to practical algorithms comes through the Jordan–Kinderlehrer–Otto scheme, which turns that continuous evolution into discrete optimization steps. The authors show that a broad class of existing methods follows from parameterized versions of this scheme for objectives based on f-divergences. They also establish equivalences between several recent algorithms, explaining how apparently different constructions can share the same underlying formulation.

The framework extends to Integral Probability Metrics and squared Maximum Mean Discrepancy, yielding additional generative algorithms and clarifying relationships with GANs. The paper empirically studies JKO regularization across objectives and analyzes flows restricted to distributions generated by parameterized maps. Its contribution is both organizational and constructive: it connects existing approaches while providing a route to new ones.
summary.tldr: A Wasserstein-flow framework connects existing generative algorithms and derives new ones through a shared optimization scheme.

title: A Unifying View of Variational Generative Wasserstein Flows

abstract: Plasticity—a neural network’s ability to adapt to new tasks—is critical for continual and transfer learning. Existing measures, such as effective rank, dead neuron fraction, and weight norm, lack theoretical grounding and correlate poorly with performance on new tasks. We introduce local redundancy, an information-theoretic measure derived from universal compression theory. We define local redundancy as the worst-case redundancy of a local model family—parameters in an infinitesimal neighborhood along gradient directions—and show this is a principled measure of plasticity. Although local redundancy is intractable to compute exactly, we prove that the expected squared gradient norm on a synthetic memorization task provides an efficiently computable lower bound. Experiments on continual image classification and time series transfer learning demonstrate that local redundancy predicts downstream performance better than existing measures and enables pretraining checkpoint selection where validation loss plateaus.

The paper introduces local redundancy to measure it, motivated by the weak theoretical grounding and poor downstream correlations of measures such as effective rank, dead neuron fraction, and weight norm.

This gives an efficiently measurable quantity with a formal connection to the proposed plasticity measure.

Experiments in continual image classification and time series transfer learning show better prediction of downstream performance than existing measures. The approach also supports choosing pretraining checkpoints when validation loss has plateaued. That finding matters because checkpoints with similar validation loss can still differ in their usefulness for later adaptation, and the proposed measure provides additional information for selecting among them.
summary.tldr: Local redundancy gives a theoretically motivated measure of adaptability, with a computable lower bound derived from synthetic memorization gradients.

title: Local Redundancy: An Information-Theoretic Measure of Plasticity from Synthetic Memorization

abstract: Agentic systems solve complex tasks by coordinating multiple agents that iteratively reason, invoke tools, and exchange intermediate results. To improve robustness and solution quality, recent approaches deploy multiple agent teams running in parallel to explore diverse reasoning trajectories. However, parallel execution comes at a significant computational cost: when different teams independently reason about similar sub-problems or execute analogous steps, they repeatedly perform substantial overlapping computation. To address these limitations, in this paper, we propose Learning to Share (LTS), a learned shared-memory mechanism for parallel agentic frameworks that enables selective cross-team information reuse while controlling context growth. LTS introduces a global memory bank accessible to all teams and a lightweight controller that decides whether intermediate agent steps should be added to memory or not. The controller is trained using stepwise reinforcement learning with usage-aware credit assignment, allowing it to identify information that is globally useful across parallel executions. Experiments on the AssistantBench and GAIA benchmarks show that LTS significantly reduces overall runtime while matching or improving task performance compared to memory-free parallel baselines, demonstrating that learned memory admission is an effective strategy for improving the efficiency of parallel agentic systems.

paragraphs: Running several agent teams in parallel can explore different routes to a solution, but it also duplicates work. Teams may independently solve similar subproblems or repeat analogous tool-driven steps. Learning to Share addresses this computational overlap by allowing teams to reuse selected intermediate results through a common memory bank.

The central component is a lightweight controller that decides which intermediate steps should enter shared memory. It is trained with stepwise reinforcement learning and usage-aware credit assignment, so its learning signal reflects information’s usefulness across parallel executions. Selective admission also controls context growth: the mechanism seeks valuable shared information rather than indiscriminately accumulating every step.

The results support learned memory admission as a way to preserve the benefits of multiple reasoning trajectories while reducing repeated computation. The contribution centers on deciding what deserves to be shared, alongside making cross-team reuse possible.
summary.tldr: Learning to Share trains a selective memory controller that reduces parallel-agent runtime while matching or improving benchmark task performance.

title: Learning to Share: Selective Memory for Efficient Parallel Agentic Systems

abstract: Black box auditing of language models is an essential pre-deployment tool, but it may miss subtle forms of misalignment and hidden information. To better elicit hidden information during an auditing process, we introduce overthinking: the process of using reasoning task vectors to amplify the chain-of-thought faithfulness of reasoning models. Given the parameters of a base instruct model M and reasoning-distilled model R, we define the overthinking model as $\mathcal{O}_\alpha = M + \alpha(R - M)$, where $\alpha > 1$ amplifies reasoning beyond the pure reasoning model R. Additionally, we introduce new layer-wise attenuation strategies that selectively amplify reasoning without losing quality and coherence of model outputs. We demonstrate that overthinking models are more likely to reveal hidden information across four experimental settings, across 2B-32B models. Our findings suggest that reasoning amplification may surface secrets or unintended behaviors acquired during training up to $10\times$ more frequently than the original reasoning model. How secrets surface depends on the secret type: some require perturbation along the reasoning direction, while others yield to any sufficiently large weight perturbation.

paragraphs: This paper explores a model-auditing technique for surfacing hidden information that black-box testing may miss. Called overthinking, it amplifies the parameter changes associated with reasoning distillation. The method requires the weights of a base instruction model and a corresponding reasoning-distilled model, making the intervention a direct modification of model parameters.

The authors subtract the base model’s weights from the reasoning model’s weights, scale that difference by a factor greater than one, and add it back to the base. This extrapolates beyond the reasoning model along the same parameter direction. Layer-wise attenuation strategies selectively control amplification to preserve output quality and coherence.

Across four experimental settings and models ranging from 2B to 32B parameters, amplified models are more likely to reveal hidden information. The findings suggest that secrets or unintended learned behaviors may surface up to ten times more frequently than in the original reasoning model. The mechanism varies by secret type: some disclosures require the reasoning direction, while others occur under any sufficiently large weight perturbation. This distinction qualifies how specifically the effects can be attributed to reasoning amplification.
summary.tldr: Amplifying reasoning-related weight changes can expose hidden learned information more frequently, with effects that depend on the type of secret.

title: Overthinking: Amplifying Reasoning Weights to Extract Learned Secrets

abstract: We introduce a new mechanism within the Utility-Optimized Local Differential Privacy (ULDP) framework that enables censoring with plausible deniability when collecting and analyzing sensitive data. Our approach addresses scenarios where certain values, such as large numerical responses, are more privacy-sensitive than others, while accompanying categorical information may not be private on its own but could still be identifying. The mechanism selectively withholds identifying details when a response might indicate sensitive content, offering asymmetric privacy protection. Unlike previous methods, it avoids the need to predefine an exact sensitive region, making it more adaptable and practical. Although the mechanism is designed for ULDP, it can also be applied under symmetric LDP settings, where it still benefits from censoring and reduced perturbation cost. We provide theoretical guarantees, including uniform consistency and pointwise weak convergence results. Numerical experiments on both synthetic data and real-world data demonstrate the validity of the proposed methodology.

paragraphs: This paper studies private estimation of cumulative distributions across categories when some numerical responses are more sensitive than others. A category may seem harmless by itself yet become identifying when paired with a sensitive value. The proposed mechanism handles this interaction by selectively withholding identifying details when a response could reveal sensitive content.

The mechanism operates within utility-optimized local differential privacy, allowing protection to reflect unequal sensitivity across responses. Its censoring provides plausible deniability without requiring an exact sensitive region to be specified in advance. That flexibility matters when privacy concerns cannot be captured by a fixed boundary. The method can also be used with symmetric local differential privacy, where censoring still reduces the need for perturbation.

The authors establish uniform consistency and pointwise weak convergence results, providing theoretical support for the resulting estimates and their limiting statistical behavior. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real data further support the methodology. The contribution joins a more adaptable privacy mechanism with statistical guarantees for distribution estimation, while accounting for the identifying potential of accompanying categories.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces selective censoring for private distribution estimation when numerical values and accompanying categories carry unequal privacy risks.

title: Censoring with Plausible Deniability: Asymmetric Local Privacy for Multi-Category CDF Estimation

abstract: Repository-level automated program repair (APR) requires long-horizon reasoning over interdependent decisions. However, most LLM-based approaches reconstruct repair reasoning independently for each issue, failing to reuse successful patterns from prior repairs, even though real-world repositories contain many related issues with shared structure or constraints. Existing methods typically rely on forward exploration, which operates under outcome uncertainty, incurs substantial inference-time overhead, and can drift from the final correct patch. We propose Conditional Reasoning Distillation (ConRAD), which leverages in-repository resolved issues by reconstructing repair reasoning backward from verified patches and distilling outcome-consistent, stage-wise repair reasoning plans. Injected at inference time, these plans guide fault localization and patch generation, replacing open-ended exploration with constrained inference without fine-tuning or search. On SWE-Bench Lite, ConRAD improves Pass@1 by 10.4% (GPT-4o), 8.6% (DeepSeek-V3), and 10.3% (GPT-5), demonstrating a scalable inference-time alternative to forward exploration for long-horizon APR.

paragraphs: Repairing a software repository involves linked decisions about where a bug originates and how a change should fix it. Many language-model approaches rebuild that reasoning for every issue, even when the repository already contains related successful repairs. Exploring forward without knowing the correct outcome can also consume substantial inference effort and lead reasoning away from the eventual fix.

ConRAD uses resolved issues from the same repository as a source of guidance. Starting from verified patches, it reconstructs reasoning backward and distills stage-by-stage repair plans consistent with those outcomes. At inference time, these plans guide fault localization and patch generation. The method provides this guidance without fine-tuning the repair model or conducting search.

On SWE-Bench Lite, the paper reports Pass@1 improvements of 10.4% for GPT-4o, 8.6% for DeepSeek-V3, and 10.3% for GPT-5. The findings support reusing successful repair structure through inference-time plans. The central idea is that a known correct historical outcome can help organize reasoning for a new issue, reducing reliance on open-ended exploration.
summary.tldr: ConRAD turns verified historical patches into reusable repair plans that improve repository-level bug fixing without fine-tuning or search.

title: From Historical Patches to Repair Plans: Outcome-Conditioned Reasoning for Repository-Level Program Repair

abstract: We present MoST (Mixture of Speech and Text), a novel multimodal large language model that seamlessly integrates speech and text processing through our proposed Modality-Aware Mixture of Experts (MAMoE) architecture. While current multimodal models typically process diverse modality representations with identical parameters—disregarding their inherent representational differences, we introduce specialized routing pathways that direct tokens to modality-appropriate experts based on input type. MAMoE simultaneously enhances modality-specific learning and cross-modal understanding through two complementary components: modality-specific expert groups that capture domain-specific patterns and shared experts that facilitate information transfer between modalities. Building on this architecture, we develop an efficient transformation pipeline that adapts the pretrained MoE language model through strategic post-training on ASR and TTS datasets, followed by fine-tuning with a carefully curated speech-text instruction dataset. A key feature of this pipeline is that it relies exclusively on fully accessible, open-source datasets to achieve strong performance and data efficiency. Comprehensive evaluations across ASR, TTS, audio language modeling, and spoken question answering benchmarks show that MoST consistently outperforms existing models of comparable parameter counts. Our ablation studies confirm that the modality-specific routing mechanism and shared experts design significantly contribute to performance gains across all tested domains. To our knowledge, MoST represents the first fully open-source speech-text LLM built on a Mixture of Experts architecture.

paragraphs: MoST integrates speech and text in a mixture-of-experts language model. Its starting point is that speech and text have different representational patterns, so applying identical parameters to both can overlook useful distinctions. The architecture routes tokens according to modality while retaining shared components that allow information to transfer between speech and language.

Modality-specific expert groups learn patterns particular to each input type, and shared experts support cross-modal understanding. The training pipeline adapts a pretrained mixture-of-experts language model using speech recognition and speech synthesis datasets, then fine-tunes it on speech-text instructions. All datasets used in this pipeline are fully accessible and open source.

Evaluations cover speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio language modeling, and spoken question answering. MoST consistently outperforms existing models with comparable parameter counts, and ablations show that both modality-specific routing and shared experts contribute significantly across tested domains. The findings support combining specialization with sharing, and the authors describe MoST as, to their knowledge, the first fully open-source speech-text LLM based on mixture-of-experts architecture.
summary.tldr: MoST combines modality-specific and shared experts to improve speech-text tasks using an adaptation pipeline built entirely from open datasets.

title: MoST: Mixing Speech and Text with Modality-Aware Mixture of Experts

abstract: As Text-to-Image (T2I) diffusion models are increasingly used in real-world creative workflows, a principled framework for valuing contributors who provide a collection of data is essential for fair compensation and sustainable data marketplaces. While the Shapley value offers a theoretically grounded approach to attribution, it faces a dual computational bottleneck: (i) the prohibitive cost of exhaustive model retraining for each sampled subset of players (i.e., data contributors) and (ii) the combinatorial number of subsets needed to estimate marginal contributions due to contributor interactions. To this end, we propose SurrogateSHAP, a retraining-free framework that approximates the expensive retraining game through inference from a pretrained model. To further improve efficiency, we employ a gradient-boosted tree to approximate the utility function and derive Shapley values analytically from the tree-based model. We evaluate SurrogateSHAP across three diverse attribution tasks: (i) image quality for DDPM-CFG on CIFAR-20, (ii) aesthetics for Stable Diffusion on Post-Impressionist artworks, and (iii) product diversity for FLUX.1 on Fashion-Product data. Across settings, SurrogateSHAP outperforms prior methods while substantially reducing computational overhead, consistently identifying influential contributors across multiple utility metrics. Finally, we demonstrate that SurrogateSHAP effectively localizes data sources responsible for spurious correlations in clinical images, providing a scalable path toward auditing safety-critical generative models. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CFG-Attribution-15DD/

paragraphs: SurrogateSHAP estimates how much different data contributors matter to a text-to-image model’s outputs. Shapley values provide a principled attribution framework, but computing them is costly when it requires retraining models on many contributor subsets. Interactions among contributors also make the number of combinations difficult to manage.

The method approximates the retraining-based attribution problem using inference from a pretrained model. It then fits a gradient-boosted tree to approximate the utility function and derives Shapley values analytically from that tree. This avoids repeated retraining of the image generator while making the attribution calculation more tractable. The resulting values describe contributions to the chosen utility measure.

Evaluations cover image quality, artistic aesthetics, and product diversity across three generation settings. The authors report better performance than prior attribution methods, substantially lower computational overhead, and consistent identification of influential contributors. They also demonstrate localization of data sources behind spurious correlations in clinical images. This connects contributor valuation with auditing which data sources influence undesirable generation behavior.
summary.tldr: SurrogateSHAP approximates contributor Shapley values without retraining image generators, supporting efficient valuation and data-source auditing.

title: SurrogateSHAP: Training-Free Contributor Attribution for Text-to-Image (T2I) Models

abstract: Group fairness can ensure equitable performance across different demographic subgroups for medical image analysis. However, the current fine-tuned foundation models (FMs) exhibit significant subgroup disparity. One-shot federated learning (OFL) can potentially mitigate this by leveraging cross-institutional data diversity within a single communication round. However, heterogeneous distributions across medical institutions may cause OFL local models to diverge severely, resulting in parameter conflicts that amplify disparity upon aggregation. To address these challenges, we propose Fair-FedMOE, a group-fair OFL framework for medical FMs. During local training, Fairness-aware Expert Routing leverages learnable prototypes to route samples to group-specific experts, enabling subgroup-specialized learning to capture group-specific features without inter-group interference. During model aggregation, Prototype-guided Differential Aggregation computes personalized weights based on prototype similarity and applies differentiated aggregation strategies to filter conflicting updates. We propose RES-AUC, a Rawlsian justice-inspired metric based on worst-group performance that remains stable as groups increase. Extensive experiments on retinal and chest X-ray datasets with multiple FMs demonstrate consistent fairness gains without sacrificing accuracy.

paragraphs: Medical imaging models can perform unevenly across demographic groups. Combining models trained at different institutions could help by drawing on more diverse data, but differences between institutions can also produce conflicting updates. In one-shot federated learning, those conflicts must be handled within a single communication round.

Fair-FedMOE addresses the problem during both local training and aggregation. Locally, learnable prototypes route samples to group-specific experts, supporting specialized learning of subgroup features without inter-group interference. During aggregation, prototype similarities determine personalized weights, while differentiated aggregation strategies filter conflicting updates. The prototypes thus guide both where learning happens and how institutional contributions are combined.

The paper also introduces RES-AUC, a fairness measure inspired by Rawlsian justice that emphasizes worst-group performance and remains stable as the number of groups increases. Experiments using retinal and chest X-ray datasets with multiple foundation models report consistent fairness improvements without sacrificing accuracy. The findings support coordinating subgroup specialization and model aggregation to reduce disparities in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Fair-FedMOE uses subgroup experts and prototype-guided aggregation to improve medical imaging fairness in one-shot federated learning without sacrificing reported accuracy.

title: Fair-FedMOE: Group-Fair One-Shot Federated Learning via Prototype-Guided Experts for Medical Imaging Analysis

abstract: Distributed stochastic optimization intertwines (i) stochastic gradient noise, (ii) communication compression, and (iii) adaptive/normalized updates. While each factor has been studied in isolation, their joint effect under realistic assumptions remains poorly understood. In this work, we develop a unified theoretical framework for Distributed Compressed SGD (DCSGD) and its sign variant Distributed SignSGD (DSignSGD) under the recently introduced $(L_0, L_1)$-smoothness condition. From a conceptual perspective, we show that the first- and second-order modified equations from the literature do not accurately model the discrete-time step-size/stability restrictions, especially under $(L_0,L_1)$-smoothness. From a technical perspective, we propose new first-order SDEs by carefully incorporating curvature-dependent terms into their drift: This helps capture the fine-grained relationship between learning rate restrictions, gradient noise, compression, and the geometry of the loss landscape. Importantly, we do so under general gradient noise assumptions, including heavy-tailed and affine-variance regimes, which extend beyond the classical bounded-variance setting. Our results suggest that normalizing the updates of DCSGD emerges as a natural condition for stability, with the degree of normalization precisely determined by the gradient noise structure, the landscape’s regularity, and the compression rate. In contrast, DSignSGD converges even under heavy-tailed noise with standard learning rate schedules. Together, these findings offer both new theoretical insights and perspectives, and practical guidance.

paragraphs: Distributed optimization combines noisy gradient estimates, compressed communication, and sometimes normalized updates. Analyzing these ingredients separately can miss how they jointly affect stability. This paper develops a unified account of Distributed Compressed SGD and Distributed SignSGD under the stated (L0, L1)-smoothness condition, connecting their behavior to the geometry of the loss landscape.

The authors argue that existing modified-equation descriptions do not accurately reproduce discrete algorithms’ step-size and stability restrictions. They propose first-order stochastic differential equations whose drift includes curvature-dependent terms. This construction is designed to capture how permissible learning rates depend on noise, compression, and landscape geometry. The analysis includes heavy-tailed noise and affine-variance regimes, extending beyond a uniformly bounded-variance setting.

The results suggest that normalizing Distributed Compressed SGD updates is a natural route to stability, with the required degree determined jointly by noise structure, landscape regularity, and compression rate. Distributed SignSGD, by contrast, converges under heavy-tailed noise with standard learning-rate schedules in the analyzed setting. The contribution is a more faithful theoretical description that helps explain why update normalization and learning-rate choices should reflect all three interacting factors.
summary.tldr: Curvature-aware stochastic equations explain how gradient noise, compression, and normalization jointly shape distributed optimization stability.

title: On the Interaction of Batch Noise, Adaptivity, and Compression, under $(L_0,L_1)$-Smoothness: An SDE Approach

abstract: New AI accelerators with novel instruction set architectures (ISAs) often require developers to manually craft low-level kernels — a time-consuming and error-prone process that does not scale across hardware targets. This delays emerging hardware platforms from reaching the market. While prior LLM-based code generation has shown promise in mature GPU ecosystems, it remains unclear whether agentic LLM systems can quickly produce valid and efficient kernels for emerging hardware with new ISAs. We present KernelCraft: the first benchmark for evaluating an LLM agent’s ability to generate and optimize low-level kernels for customized accelerators through a function-calling, feedback-driven workflow. We evaluate agent performance across three emerging accelerators on more than 20 machine-learning tasks, each with five diverse task configurations. Across four leading reasoning models, the strongest agents generate functionally correct kernels for unseen ISAs within a few refinement steps, and produce optimized kernels that match or outperform compiler baselines. These results demonstrate KernelCraft’s potential to accelerate the accelerator chip development cycle. KernelCraft is available at https://kernelcraft-cam.github.io/.

paragraphs: New AI accelerators need low-level kernels that fit their instruction sets. Writing these kernels manually is slow and error-prone, and success with LLM coding in established GPU environments does not settle whether agents can handle unfamiliar hardware. KernelCraft creates a benchmark focused on that question.

The benchmark evaluates agents through a function-calling workflow in which feedback supports repeated refinement of generated kernels. It covers three emerging accelerators and more than 20 machine-learning tasks, each with five configurations. This tests whether an agent can both produce valid hardware-specific code and improve its efficiency across varied workloads.

Across four leading reasoning models, the strongest agents produce functionally correct kernels for previously unseen instruction sets within a few refinement steps. Their optimized kernels match or exceed compiler baselines in the reported evaluation. These results indicate that feedback-driven agents can contribute to software development for emerging accelerators. The authors present faster accelerator development as a potential consequence, with the benchmark supplying evidence about kernel-generation capability rather than a direct measurement of hardware time to market.
summary.tldr: KernelCraft evaluates feedback-driven agents on unfamiliar accelerators, where the strongest agents generate correct kernels and competitive optimizations.

title: KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-Metal Kernel Generation on Emerging Hardware

abstract: Data-Free Quantization (DFQ) addresses data security concerns by synthesizing samples, without accessing real data. It has garnered increasing attention in the context of Vision Transformers (ViTs), owing to the superiority of the self-attention mechanism compared to classical convolutional operation. However, previous DFQ arts for ViTs often suffer from a distribution mismatch between synthetic samples and input distribution expected by quantized models $Q$, resulting in the suboptimal performance. In this paper, we propose a novel Masked Attention Alignment approach for Data-Free Quantization of ViTs, named MaskAQ, revealing that: 1) the semantics in the self-attention mechanism is predominantly localized to a sparse subset of patches, called informative regions; 2) the informative regions dominate the mutual information between synthetic samples and $Q$’s outputs. To these ends, we incorporate differential entropy maximum over patch similarity of synthetic samples, to decouple informative regions from noisy background. To couple with varied $Q$, the informative regions are selected to align full-precision models with $Q$ via a masked attention alignment objective, thus yielding high-quality synthetic samples. Furthermore, a periodic sample refreshing strategy comes up to endow MaskAQ with the capacity to continually adapt to the evolving state of $Q$ throughout the training process, to preserve desirable mutual information with synthetic samples. Extensive experiments verify the merits of MaskAQ over state-of-the-art approaches across multiple backbones and downstream tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/hfutqian/MaskAQ.

paragraphs: Data-free quantization uses synthesized examples to prepare lower-precision models without accessing real data. For vision Transformers, those examples may differ from the input distribution that the quantized model needs, reducing performance. MaskAQ addresses this mismatch by focusing synthesis and alignment on the image regions that carry useful semantic information.

The paper identifies a sparse subset of patches, called informative regions, that dominates the mutual information between synthetic inputs and quantized outputs. An entropy-based objective over patch similarity helps separate these regions from noisy backgrounds. A masked attention objective then selects informative regions for aligning the full-precision and quantized models, tailoring synthetic samples to the particular quantized model.

Because that model changes during training, MaskAQ periodically refreshes the synthetic samples to preserve their usefulness. Experiments across multiple backbones and downstream tasks support improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The approach links sample quality to both spatial selectivity and continued adaptation: it concentrates alignment on informative patches while updating the training material as the quantized model evolves.
summary.tldr: MaskAQ improves data-free vision Transformer quantization by aligning informative image patches and periodically refreshing synthetic training samples.

title: Selective Coupling of Decoupled Informative Regions: Masked Attention Alignment for Data-Free Quantization of Vision Transformers

abstract: Predicting transcriptional responses to genetic perturbations is a central problem in functional genomics. In practice, perturbation responses are rarely gene-independent but instead manifest as coordinated, program-level transcriptional changes among functionally related genes. However, most existing methods do not explicitly model such coordination, due to gene-wise modeling paradigms and reliance on static biological priors that cannot capture dynamic program reorganization. To address these limitations, we propose scBIG, a module-inductive perturbation prediction framework that explicitly models coordinated gene programs. scBIG induces coherent gene programs from data via Gene-Relation Clustering, captures inter-program interactions through a Gene-Cluster-Aware Encoder, and preserves modular coordination using structure-aware alignment objectives. These structured representations are then modeled using conditional flow matching to enable flexible and generalizable perturbation prediction. Extensive experiments on multiple single-cell perturbation benchmarks show that scBIG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly on unseen and combinatorial perturbation settings, achieving an average improvement of 6.7% over the strongest baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/ttruan2426-dot/scBIG.
