paragraphs: Predicting how genetic interventions change a cell requires accounting for genes that respond together. The paper argues that treating genes independently, or relying on fixed biological relationships, misses coordinated changes in gene programs. Its proposed framework, scBIG, learns representations organized around these programs so that predictions can reflect relationships among groups of genes.

The method first discovers coherent programs from data through Gene-Relation Clustering. A Gene-Cluster-Aware Encoder then represents interactions between programs, while structure-aware alignment objectives help preserve their internal coordination. Conditional flow matching models the resulting structured representations to predict responses to perturbations. Together, these components make coordinated gene behavior an explicit part of the prediction process.

Across multiple single-cell perturbation benchmarks, the authors report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, averaging 6.7% over the strongest baselines. The gains are particularly pronounced for previously unseen interventions and combinations of interventions. These findings support the value of learning gene-program structure when the prediction task requires generalizing beyond perturbations already represented in training.
summary.tldr: scBIG learns coordinated gene programs to improve predictions of cellular responses, especially for unseen and combined genetic perturbations.

title: Beyond Independent Genes: Learning Module-Inductive Representations for Single-Cell Gene Perturbation Prediction

abstract: Innovation is a key driving force of human civilization. As the body of knowledge has grown considerably, bridging knowledge across different disciplines, where significant innovation often emerges, has become increasingly challenging. The recent advancements in machine learning models, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), have provided effective access to extensive knowledge sources and shown impressive abilities in reasoning, rendering significant opportunities for interdisciplinary discovery. Our research aims to understand the capabilities of state-of-the-art LLMs in integrating knowledge from different fields for interdisciplinary research (IDR). To address this fundamental problem, we introduce IDRBench, a pioneering framework that includes both datasets and evaluation tasks: (1) IDR Paper Identification, (2) IDR Idea Integration, and (3) IDR Idea Recommendation. Our study on ten mainstream LLMs provides a comprehensive analysis of their behavior and establishes benchmarks and baselines for future research. To the best of our knowledge, IDRBench is the first to provide a comprehensive investigation of LLMs’ IDR capability.

Recognizing existing connections is one capability; combining ideas and proposing further directions place additional demands on how a model uses knowledge from multiple fields.

The authors evaluate ten mainstream language models, analyze their behavior, and establish benchmarks and baselines for subsequent work. The abstract presents the resulting evaluation framework as the main contribution rather than reporting a particular model’s superiority. Its significance is to give interdisciplinary research assistance a concrete set of tasks, allowing future studies to investigate capabilities more systematically than broad claims about general reasoning would permit.
summary.tldr: IDRBench evaluates ten language models on identifying, integrating, and recommending interdisciplinary research ideas.

title: IDRBench: Understanding the Capability of Large Language Models on Interdisciplinary Research

abstract: All-in-one image restoration aims to address diverse degradation types using a single unified model. Existing methods typically rely on degradation priors to guide restoration, yet often struggle to reconstruct content in severely degraded regions. Although recent works leverage semantic information to facilitate content generation, integrating it into the shallow layers of diffusion models often disrupts spatial structures (e.g., blurring artifacts). To address this issue, we propose a Triple-Prior Guided Diffusion (TPGDiff) network for unified image restoration. TPGDiff incorporates degradation priors throughout the diffusion trajectory, while introducing structural priors into shallow layers and semantic priors into deep layers, enabling hierarchical and complementary prior guidance for image reconstruction. Specifically, we leverage multi-source structural cues as structural priors to capture fine-grained details and guide shallow layers representations. To complement this design, we further develop a distillation-driven semantic extractor that yields robust semantic priors, ensuring reliable high-level guidance at deep layers even under severe degradations. Furthermore, a degradation extractor is employed to learn degradation-aware priors, enabling stage-adaptive control of the diffusion process across all timesteps. Extensive experiments on both single- and multi-degradation benchmarks demonstrate that TPGDiff achieves superior performance and generalization across diverse restoration scenarios.

paragraphs: A single image-restoration model must handle different forms of damage while preserving both detail and recognizable content. Guidance about degradation alone can be insufficient in heavily damaged regions. Semantic guidance can help reconstruct content, but introducing it into shallow diffusion layers can disrupt spatial structure and produce blur.

TPGDiff assigns three kinds of guidance to complementary roles. Structural priors enter shallow layers to support fine spatial detail, while semantic priors enter deeper layers to guide high-level content. Degradation priors operate throughout the diffusion trajectory, adapting the restoration process across timesteps. This arrangement makes the placement of information within the model part of the restoration strategy.

The structural guidance draws on multiple sources of cues. A distillation-driven extractor supplies robust semantic information even under severe degradation, and a separate degradation extractor provides stage-adaptive control. Experiments on benchmarks with single and multiple degradations report superior performance and generalization across restoration scenarios. The findings support coordinating information about damage, structure, and meaning at the layers and stages where each is intended to help.
summary.tldr: TPGDiff places structural, semantic, and degradation guidance at complementary layers and timesteps to improve unified image restoration.

title: TPGDiff : Hierarchical Triple-Prior Guided Diffusion for Image Restoration

abstract: 3D CT analysis spans a continuum from low-level perception to high-level clinical understanding. Existing 3D-oriented analysis methods adopt either isolated task-specific modeling or task-agnostic end-to-end paradigms to produce one-hop outputs, impeding the systematic accumulation of perceptual evidence for downstream reasoning. In parallel, recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) exhibit improved visual perception and can integrate visual and textual information effectively, yet their predominantly 2D-oriented designs fundamentally limit their ability to perceive and analysis volumetric medical data. To bridge this gap, we propose 3DMedAgent, an unified agent that enables 2D MLLMs to perform general 3D CT analysis without 3D-specific fine-tuning. 3DMedAgent coordinates heterogeneous visual and textual tools through a flexible MLLM agent, progressively decomposing complex 3D analysis into tractable subtasks that transition from global to regional views, from 3D volumes to informative 2D slices, and from visual evidence to structured textual representations. Central to this design, 3DMedAgent maintains a long-term structured memory that aggregates intermediate tool outputs and supports query-adaptive, evidence-driven multi-step reasoning. We further introduce the DeepChestVQA benchmark for evaluating unified perception-to-understanding capabilities in 3D thoracic imaging. Experiments across over 40 tasks demonstrate that 3DMedAgent consistently outperforms general, medical, and 3D-specific MLLMs, highlighting a scalable path toward general-purpose 3D clinical assistants. Code and data are available https://github.com/jinlab-imvr/3DMedAgent.

paragraphs: 3DMedAgent addresses the gap between recognizing structures in a CT scan and reasoning about what those structures mean. Many existing systems produce an answer in a single step, making it difficult to accumulate evidence across tasks. Meanwhile, multimodal language models designed mainly for two-dimensional images have difficulty working directly with full three-dimensional scans.

The proposed agent lets a 2D multimodal model coordinate visual and textual tools without requiring 3D-specific fine-tuning. It breaks a complex question into smaller tasks, moving between whole volumes, regions, and informative slices. A structured long-term memory collects intermediate results, turning tool outputs into evidence that can support later reasoning and adapt to the current question.

The authors also introduce DeepChestVQA to evaluate this progression from perception to understanding in thoracic imaging. Across more than 40 tasks, the agent consistently outperforms the general, medical, and 3D-specific multimodal models evaluated. These findings support tool coordination and accumulated evidence as a promising approach to broader 3D medical analysis.
summary.tldr: 3DMedAgent combines tools and structured memory to let 2D multimodal models reason over 3D CT scans without 3D-specific fine-tuning.

title: 3DMedAgent: Unified Perception-to-Understanding for 3D Medical Analysis

abstract: Despite rapid progress in generative 3D creation, producing high-fidelity 3D face assets from a single image remains challenging, as it requires both identity-critical facial micro-structures and fine-grained view-consistent textures. To address this, we present a two-stage framework named SAMT for monocular 3D avatar generation and texture synthesis. Specifically, a latent 3D diffusion model for facial mesh generation is pretrained and then further adapted to generate high-quality facial geometry through large-scale domain-specific finetuning on 35K curated 3D avatar models. Subsequently, the generated facial mesh is textured through a multi-view-aware texturing strategy. It incorporates multi-view facial priors along with the mesh geometry to guide a 2D texturing diffusion, enabling cross-view consistent and mesh-aligned texture synthesis. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAMT improves over existing baselines by producing more coherent facial geometry together with more fine-grained and view-consistent textures. Project page is available at https://github.com/muyuWang/SAMT.

paragraphs: Creating a 3D face from one image requires both convincing geometry and surface appearance that remains coherent from different viewpoints. Small facial structures are particularly important because they contribute to identity. SAMT divides this problem into two linked stages: generating the facial mesh and then producing textures aligned with that mesh.

For geometry, the authors pretrain a latent 3D diffusion model and adapt it through domain-specific fine-tuning on 35,000 curated 3D avatar models. The second stage uses a 2D diffusion model for texturing. It receives guidance from both the generated geometry and multi-view facial priors, so texture synthesis accounts for how the face should appear across views.

Experiments show improvements over existing baselines in facial geometry coherence, texture detail, and consistency between viewpoints. The two stages matter together: a detailed texture must agree with the mesh, while a well-formed mesh still needs appearance that remains consistent when viewed from different directions. The reported results support combining specialized geometry learning with explicitly multi-view-aware texture generation for single-image avatar creation.
summary.tldr: SAMT generates facial geometry and then applies mesh-guided, multi-view-aware textures to create more coherent 3D avatars from one image.

title: SAMT: Generating Structured Avatar Meshes and Textures from a Single Image

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has powered many recent breakthroughs in large language models (LLMs), especially for tasks where rewards can be computed automatically, such as code generation. However, it is less effective in open-ended medical dialogue, where feedback is ambiguous, context-dependent, and difficult to simply summarize into a single scalar signal—often requiring heavily supervised reward models and creating risks of reward hacking. Thus, we introduce ORBIT, an open-ended rubric-based incremental training framework tailored for critical medical dialogues. ORBIT integrates medical dialogue construction with dynamically generated case-conditioned rubrics that serve as adaptive guides for incremental RL. Unlike approaches that rely on external medical knowledge bases or handcrafted rules, ORBIT uses rubric-guided evaluation and can be implemented with general-purpose instruction-following LLMs, avoiding task-specific judge fine-tuning. With only 2k training samples, ORBIT raises Qwen3-4B-Instruct’s HealthBench-Hard score from 7.0 to 27.5, achieving state-of-the-art performance among similarly sized open-source models while maintaining strong consultation quality as rubric coverage broadens. Project page: https://pidneuralode.github.io/ORBIT.

paragraphs: Medical dialogue presents a difficult reinforcement-learning problem because a good response depends on context and cannot easily be summarized by a simple reward. ORBIT addresses this with evaluation rubrics generated for individual cases. These rubrics provide adaptive guidance for incremental training, connecting feedback to the particular medical conversation being learned.

The framework combines dialogue construction with rubric-guided evaluation. It can use general-purpose instruction-following language models without specialized judge fine-tuning, external medical knowledge bases, or handcrafted rules. Its central design choice is to make the evaluation criteria responsive to the case, giving the training process more structured guidance for an open-ended task with ambiguous feedback.

Using 2,000 training samples, ORBIT raises Qwen3-4B-Instruct’s HealthBench-Hard score from 7.0 to 27.5. The authors report state-of-the-art performance among similarly sized open-source models and strong consultation quality as rubric coverage expands. These findings show substantial benchmark gains from case-conditioned feedback and incremental training in the evaluated medical-dialogue setting.
summary.tldr: ORBIT uses dynamically generated medical-case rubrics to guide incremental reinforcement learning, substantially improving a small model’s HealthBench-Hard score.

title: InfiMed-ORBIT: Aligning LLMs on Open-Ended Complex Tasks via Rubric-Based Incremental Training

abstract: While current software agents powered by large language models (LLMs) and reinforcement learning (RL) can boost programmer productivity, their reliance on human-curated training data and environments creates a fundamental barrier to superintelligence. In this paper, we present Self-play SWE-RL (SSR), a first step toward training superintelligent software agents under minimal data assumptions. SSR requires only access to sandboxed repositories with source code and dependencies, no need for human-labeled issues or test commands. Grounded in real-world codebases, a single LLM agent is trained via RL in a self-play setting to inject and repair increasingly complex bugs. The bugs are formally specified by test suite improvements proposed by the agent rather than natural language issue descriptions. On the SWE-bench Verified and SWE-Bench Pro benchmarks, SSR achieves clear self-improvement (+10.4 and +7.8 points) and consistently outperforms the human-data baseline throughout training, generalizing to natural language bug descriptions not seen in training. Overall, our results point toward a paradigm where agents autonomously gather extensive learning experiences from real software repositories, ultimately enabling superintelligent systems that exceed human capabilities in understanding, modifying, and creating software from scratch.

paragraphs: Self-play SWE-RL explores how software agents can generate their own training experiences from real repositories. Its starting requirement is access to sandboxed codebases containing source code and dependencies. It does not require human-labeled issues or supplied test commands, addressing dependence on manually curated tasks and environments for reinforcement learning.

A single language-model agent learns through self-play to introduce and repair increasingly complex bugs. Instead of specifying bugs through written issue descriptions, it proposes test-suite improvements that formally define them. This links task generation to executable software behavior and provides a way to create learning experiences grounded in the repositories themselves.

The authors report self-improvement of 10.4 points on SWE-bench Verified and 7.8 points on SWE-Bench Pro, with performance above the human-data baseline throughout training. The agent also generalizes to natural-language bug descriptions absent from training. These results demonstrate progress in autonomous training-data generation and software repair. The paper presents exceeding human software capabilities as a longer-term direction enabled by this paradigm, rather than as a capability established by these benchmark gains.
summary.tldr: Self-play SWE-RL trains an agent to create and repair repository bugs without human-labeled issues, producing gains on two software-repair benchmarks.

title: Toward Training Superintelligent Software Agents through Self-Play SWE-RL

abstract: GPU kernel optimization challenges LLMs beyond standard coding tasks, as it requires an understanding of hardware architecture, parallel computing optimization strategies, and profiling outputs. However, most existing approaches leveraging LLMs for kernel generation apply standard prompting and feedback loops, considering hardware only through profiling feedback. We introduce KernelFoundry, an evolutionary framework that efficiently explores the space of GPU kernels through (1) MAP-Elites quality-diversity search with kernel-specific behavioral dimensions to sustain exploration; (2) meta-prompt evolution that co-evolves prompts with kernels to uncover task-specific optimization strategies, and (3) a template-based parameter optimization approach to tune kernels to inputs and hardware. We evaluate this framework on KernelBench, robust-kbench and custom tasks, generating SYCL kernels as a cross-platform GPU programming paradigm, and CUDA kernels for comparison to prior work. Our approach consistently outperforms the baseline methods and achieves an average speedup of 2.3 on KernelBench for SYCL. Moreover, KernelFoundry is implemented as a distributed framework with remote access to diverse hardware, allowing quick benchmarking and featuring a flexible user input layer to support kernel generation for a wide range of real use cases beyond benchmarking.

paragraphs: Generating a fast GPU kernel requires understanding hardware, parallel execution, and profiling results as well as producing working code. KernelFoundry addresses this with an evolutionary search framework that incorporates hardware-sensitive optimization into the search process. It explores alternative kernels while also adapting how the language model is prompted.

Three mechanisms work together. MAP-Elites search maintains diverse candidates along kernel-specific behavioral dimensions, helping sustain exploration. Meta-prompt evolution changes prompts alongside kernels to discover strategies suited to the task. Template-based parameter optimization then tunes candidate kernels for particular inputs and hardware. These mechanisms target different parts of the optimization problem.

The authors evaluate SYCL and CUDA kernel generation on KernelBench, robust-kbench, and custom tasks. KernelFoundry consistently outperforms the compared baselines and reports an average SYCL speedup of 2.3 on KernelBench. Its distributed implementation can benchmark remotely on different hardware and accepts flexible user inputs. The findings support combining diverse code search, evolving prompts, and parameter tuning for the evaluated kernel-generation tasks.
summary.tldr: KernelFoundry co-evolves GPU kernels and prompts, combining diverse search with hardware-specific tuning to improve benchmark performance.

title: KernelFoundry: Hardware-Aware Evolutionary GPU Kernel Optimization

abstract: Visual causal reasoning is essential for understanding and intervening in the physical world, requiring identification of causal variables from visual inputs and reasoning over intervention effects. Despite recent progress, large vision-language models (VLMs) remain brittle at such tasks, especially for interventional and counterfactual queries over multi-image inputs. Most existing explorations inject causal knowledge via textual prompts, leaving causal mechanisms external to model execution and limiting reliable control during inference. To address this problem, we propose BridgeVLM, which internalizes visual causal reasoning by inducing a causal graph from multi-image inputs and converting it into structured Causal Tokens executed by RAMP layers injected into the LLM decoder for causal message passing. We further introduce a unified training interface M3S for fine-grained causal supervision from different granularities (local/global level). BridgeVLM achieves 54.4% accuracy on intervention tasks on CausalVLBench (vs. 33.2% with prompt-level supervision), improves results on Causal3D from 43.6% to 49.0%, and substantially improves causal structure learning on CausalVLBench ($F_1$: 33.4% $\rightarrow$ 75.1%).

paragraphs: Reasoning about causes across images requires identifying relevant variables and understanding what changes when an intervention occurs. The paper addresses the brittleness of vision-language models on these tasks, especially intervention and counterfactual questions. It argues that causal guidance supplied only through text prompts leaves the mechanisms outside the model’s execution.

BridgeVLM first infers a causal graph from multiple images. It converts that graph into structured Causal Tokens, which added RAMP layers process inside the language-model decoder through causal message passing. A training interface called M3S combines fine-grained supervision at local and global levels, connecting the learned structure with the model’s reasoning process.

These results support integrating causal structure into model execution as a useful approach to the evaluated multi-image reasoning tasks.
summary.tldr: BridgeVLM embeds causal graphs into decoder execution through structured tokens, improving multi-image intervention reasoning and causal structure learning.

title: From Prompts to Tokens: Internalizing Causal Supervision in Vision-Language Model for Multi-Image Causal Reasoning

abstract: Off-policy reinforcement learning is vulnerable to overestimation bias, which is rooted in the total value uncertainty. However, existing methods typically misaddress this by targeting the epistemic component, neglecting the aleatoric component. We identify for the first time that this oversight fails to contain a massive bias surge, termed Aleatoric Impulse. Although transient, this impulse fundamentally derails the learning trajectory, permanently locking the agent into suboptimal policies. To counteract this, we propose Aleatoric Impulse Damping (AID), the first mechanism that models total value uncertainty by disentangling the return variance into epistemic and aleatoric components, followed by their adaptive weighted recombination. Leveraging this derived uncertainty, the critic constructs a pessimistic lower confidence bound to surgically suppress the impulse. Complementing this, the actor utilizes a symmetrical upper confidence bound to drive optimistic exploration, ensuring that the necessary pessimism does not compromise exploration efficiency. We integrate this mechanism into the Distributional Soft Actor-Critic algorithm to establish DSAC-AID. Extensive experiments on the high-dimensional Gym-MuJoCo and DeepMind Control Suite benchmarks demonstrate that it achieves state-of-the-art results in final performance.

paragraphs: Off-policy reinforcement learning can overestimate how valuable an action is. The paper connects this bias to total value uncertainty and argues that existing methods focus too heavily on epistemic uncertainty, associated with incomplete knowledge. Neglecting aleatoric uncertainty, associated with randomness in returns, can allow a brief but large bias surge that the authors call an Aleatoric Impulse.

The authors find that this transient surge can derail learning and lock an agent into a suboptimal policy. Aleatoric Impulse Damping separates return variance into epistemic and aleatoric components, then recombines them with adaptive weights. The critic uses the resulting uncertainty to form a pessimistic lower confidence bound that suppresses excessive value estimates.

The actor uses a corresponding optimistic upper confidence bound to support exploration, balancing conservative value learning with the incentive to try uncertain actions. Integrating the mechanism into Distributional Soft Actor-Critic produces DSAC-AID. Experiments on high-dimensional Gym-MuJoCo and DeepMind Control Suite tasks report state-of-the-art final performance, supporting the value of addressing both uncertainty components in the tested control settings.
summary.tldr: AID separates and recombines two sources of value uncertainty to suppress damaging overestimation surges while supporting exploration.

title: Taming Aleatoric Impulse in Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Long-form video understanding remains challenging for Vision-Language Models (VLMs) due to the inherent tension between computational constraints and the need to capture information distributed across thousands of frames. Existing approaches either sample frames uniformly (risking information loss) or select keyframes in a single pass (with no recovery from poor choices). We propose VideoBrain, an end-to-end framework that enables VLMs to adaptively acquire visual information through learned sampling policies. Our approach features dual complementary agents: a CLIP-based agent for semantic retrieval across the video and a Uniform agent for dense temporal sampling within intervals. Unlike prior agent-based methods that rely on text-only LLMs orchestrating visual tools, our VLM directly perceives frames and reasons about information sufficiency. To prevent models from invoking agents indiscriminately to maximize rewards, we introduce a behavior-aware reward function coupled with a data classification pipeline that teaches the model when agent invocation is genuinely beneficial. Experiments on four long video benchmarks demonstrate that VideoBrain achieves +3.5% to +9.0% improvement over the baseline while using 30-40% fewer frames, with strong cross-dataset generalization to short video benchmarks. The code is available at https://github.com/junbo-zou/VideoBrain.

Uniform sampling can miss important content, while a single keyframe-selection pass cannot recover from poor choices. VideoBrain trains a vision-language model to acquire additional visual information adaptively and judge whether it has seen enough.

The framework combines two complementary agents. A CLIP-based agent retrieves frames by semantic relevance across the video, while a Uniform agent samples densely within time intervals. The vision-language model directly inspects frames and reasons about information sufficiency. A behavior-aware reward and data classification pipeline teach it when invoking these agents is beneficial, discouraging indiscriminate calls.

Across four long-video benchmarks, VideoBrain improves over the baseline by 3.5% to 9.0% while using 30–40% fewer frames. It also shows strong cross-dataset generalization to short-video benchmarks. The findings suggest that learned decisions about where and when to look can improve understanding while reducing the visual information a model needs to process.
summary.tldr: VideoBrain learns when and where to sample video frames, improving reported benchmark performance while using 30–40% fewer frames.

title: VideoBrain: Learning Adaptive Frame Sampling for Long Video Understanding

abstract: Machine learning research increasingly bifurcates into two disconnected modes: benchmark-driven engineering that prioritizes metrics over understanding, and idealized theory that often fails to transfer to modern systems . In this position paper, we argue that the field focuses too heavily on these endpoints, neglecting the central scientific object: the idea. We propose an Ideas First framework in which ideas are valued for the behavioral signatures they predict in modern models, and these signatures are tested through tailored experiments designed to detect the relevant patterns rather than to win leaderboards. This shift not only bridges the gap between theory and practice but also promotes equity by removing the "complexity premium", enabling rigorous scientific contributions from researchers with modest computational, financial, and human resources. Ultimately, we advocate for a research culture centered on ideas, treating benchmarks and theorems as instruments for testing mechanistic hypotheses rather than as ends in themselves.

The authors propose putting explanatory ideas at the center. An idea should earn attention through the observable patterns of behavior it predicts in actual models.

Their Ideas First framework connects those predictions to experiments designed specifically to detect the relevant patterns. Such experiments test whether a proposed explanation captures how a model behaves. Benchmarks and mathematical results remain useful, but their role becomes supporting the investigation of mechanisms rather than serving as the final objective of research.

The authors also connect this shift to participation in the field. They argue that rewarding clear ideas and targeted tests can remove a premium placed on complexity, allowing researchers with modest computational, financial, and personnel resources to make rigorous contributions. The proposal is therefore both a scientific framework for linking theory with practice and a call to change what research culture rewards.
summary.tldr: The Ideas First framework centers research on mechanistic ideas, their predicted behaviors, and experiments tailored to test those predictions.

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) research typically develops algorithms for helping an RL agent best achieve its goals ---however they came to be defined--- while ignoring the relationship of those goals to the goals of the agent designer. We extend agent design to include the meta-optimization problem of selecting internal agent goals (rewards)which optimize the designer's goals. Our claim is that well-designed internal rewards can help improve the performance of RL agents which are computationally bounded in some way (as practical agents are). We present a formal framework for understanding both bounded agents and the meta-optimization problem, and we empirically demonstrate several instances of common agent bounds being mitigated by general internal reward functions.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often starts with an agent’s reward already specified and asks how the agent can pursue it effectively. This paper expands the design problem to include the choice of that reward. It distinguishes the agent’s internal goal from the designer’s goal, then asks which internal rewards best serve what the designer ultimately wants.

The motivation is that practical agents have computational bounds. A reward that guides a limited agent well may improve its performance against the designer’s objective. The authors express reward selection as a meta-optimization problem: the design process chooses the internal objective, while the agent learns or acts according to that objective.

The paper supplies a formal framework for both bounded agents and this additional optimization problem. It also empirically demonstrates several cases in which general internal reward functions mitigate common agent bounds. The stated claim is that well-designed internal rewards can help computationally bounded agents. The examples support that possibility without establishing that every reward redesign or every agent bound will benefit.
summary.tldr: Choosing an agent’s internal rewards to serve the designer’s objective can mitigate computational limitations, as shown in a formal framework and empirical examples.

title: Internal Rewards Mitigate Agent Boundedness

abstract: In many network domains, labeled data may be costly to acquire---indicating a need for {\em relational active learning} methods. Recent work has demonstrated that relational model performance can be improved by taking network structure into account when choosing instances to label. However, in collective inference settings, {\em both} model estimation {\em and} prediction can be improved by acquiring a node's label---since relational models estimate a joint distribution over labels in the network and collective classification methods propagate information from labeled training data during prediction. This conflates improvement in learning with improvement in inference, since labeling nodes can reduce inference error without improving the overall quality of the learned model. Here, we use {\em across-network} classification to separate the effects on learning and prediction, and focus on reduction of learning error. When label propagation is used for learning, we find that labeling based on prediction {\em certainty} is more effective than labeling based on {\em uncertainty}. As such, we propose a novel active learning method that combines a network-based {\em certainty} metric with semi-supervised learning and relational resampling. We evaluate our approach on synthetic and real-world networks and show faster learning compared to several baselines, including the network based method of Bilgic et al. 2010.

paragraphs: In network classification, obtaining a node's label can help in two different ways. It can improve the learned model, and it can directly improve predictions as label information propagates through the network. The paper argues that evaluating both effects together can obscure whether an active-learning strategy actually learns a better model.

The authors use classification across networks to separate learning improvements from prediction improvements and focus on reducing learning error. When label propagation is part of learning, they find that choosing nodes whose predictions are more certain is more effective than choosing uncertain nodes. This conclusion is tied to that learning setting, rather than a general rejection of uncertainty-based active learning.

They propose a method combining a network-based certainty measure, semi-supervised learning, and relational resampling. Experiments on synthetic and real-world networks show faster learning than several baselines. The main implication is that label selection should be judged against the intended benefit: improving a transferable model can favor different queries from those that immediately improve collective predictions within one network.
summary.tldr: When label propagation supports learning, certainty-based network queries can improve model learning more effectively than uncertainty-based queries.

title: Relational Active Learning for Joint Collective Classification Models

abstract: In probabilistic PCA, the fully Bayesian estimation is computationally intractable. To cope with this problem, two types of approximation schemes were introduced: the partially Bayesian PCA (PB-PCA) where only the latent variables are integrated out, and the variational Bayesian PCA (VB-PCA) where the loading vectors are also integrated out. The VB-PCA was proposed as an improved variant of PB-PCA for enabling automatic dimensionality selection (ADS). In this paper, we investigate whether VB-PCA is really the best choice from the viewpoints of computational efficiency and ADS. We first show that ADS is not the unique feature of VB-PCA---PB-PCA is also actually equipped with ADS. We further show that PB-PCA is more advantageous in computational efficiency than VB-PCA because the global solution of PB-PCA can be computed analytically. However, we also show the negative fact that PB-PCA results in a trivial solution in the empirical Bayesian framework. We next consider a simplified variant of VB-PCA, where the latent variables and loading vectors are assumed to be mutually independent (while the ordinary VB-PCA only requires matrix-wise independence). We show that this simplified VB-PCA is the most advantageous in practice because its empirical Bayes solution experimentally works as well as the original VB-PCA, and its global optimal solution can be computed efficiently in a closed form.

paragraphs: Fully Bayesian estimation for probabilistic PCA is computationally intractable, motivating approximations. The paper compares partially Bayesian PCA, which integrates out latent variables, with variational Bayesian PCA, which also integrates out loading vectors. It asks whether the variational approach is preferable for computational efficiency and automatic selection of the representation's dimensionality.

The authors show that automatic dimensionality selection is available in partially Bayesian PCA as well. Its global solution can also be computed analytically, giving it a computational advantage. However, they establish an important drawback: in the empirical Bayesian framework, partially Bayesian PCA produces a trivial solution. Its analytical convenience therefore does not settle the practical comparison.

The paper then examines a simplified variational formulation with stronger independence assumptions between latent variables and loading vectors than ordinary variational Bayesian PCA. Its global optimum has an efficiently computable closed form. Experiments show that its empirical Bayes solution performs as well as the original variational approach, supporting the authors' conclusion that this simplified formulation offers the most advantageous practical combination among the approaches considered.
summary.tldr: A simplified variational Bayesian PCA admits an efficient closed-form optimum and experimentally matches the original formulation's empirical Bayes performance.

title: On Bayesian PCA: Automatic Dimensionality Selection and Analytic Solution

abstract: Sparse coding is a common approach to learning local features for object recognition. Recently, there has been an increasing interest in learning features from spatio-temporal, binocular, or other multi-observation data, where the goal is to encode the relationship between images rather than the content of a single image. We discuss the role of multiplicative interactions and of squaring non-linearities in learning such relations. In particular, we show that training a sparse coding model whose filter responses are multiplied or squared amounts to jointly diagonalizing a set of matrices that encode image transformations. Inference amounts to detecting rotations in the shared eigenspaces. Our analysis helps explain recent experimental results showing that Fourier features and circular Fourier features emerge when training complex cell models on translating or rotating images. It also shows how learning about transformations makes it possible to learn invariant features.

paragraphs: Learning features from multiple observations can require representing how images relate, rather than only what each image contains. This paper examines that problem for settings such as image sequences and binocular observations. It focuses on the role of multiplying filter responses or applying squaring nonlinearities in sparse-coding models that learn image relationships.

The analysis shows that training these models amounts to jointly diagonalizing matrices that encode image transformations. Inference, in turn, corresponds to detecting rotations within shared eigenspaces. This gives a mathematical interpretation of the learned representation: the multiplicative or squared responses are connected to the structure of transformations between images.

The framework helps explain earlier experimental observations that Fourier features and circular Fourier features emerge when complex-cell models are trained on translating or rotating images. It also shows how learning transformations can make it possible to learn invariant features. The contribution is an explanatory link between model operations, transformation structure, and representations that can remain stable under changes to an image.
summary.tldr: The paper connects multiplicative multi-view feature learning to joint matrix diagonalization and transformation-dependent rotations in shared eigenspaces.
